İbrət: Yaxşı fikir söyləmək hələ işin yarısıdır. Bir planı alqışlamazdan əvvəl onu kimin və necə həyata keçirəcəyini də düşünmək lazımdır.

title: Quzuların dərisi
paragraphs: «Quzuların dərisini soymaqdansa, qoçların yununu qırxmaq yaxşıdır.»
Bu deyim Osmanlı dövründə Dəməşq valisi olmuş Azmzadə Əsəd Paşanın adı ilə bağlı bir rəvayətdə işlənir.
Deyilənə görə, bir gün xəzinənin boşaldığını görən Əsəd Paşa müşavirlərini yanına çağırıb çıxış yolu axtarır. Onlar Dəməşqdəki toxucuların üzərinə əlavə vergi qoymağı təklif edirlər.
— Bu vergidən nə qədər gəlir əldə edə bilərik? — deyə Paşa soruşur.
— Əlli-altmış kisə qızıl, — deyə cavab verirlər.
— Axı bu adamlar onsuz da güclə dolanırlar. Vergini nə ilə ödəyəcəklər?
— Evlərindəki qızılı, zinət əşyalarını satarlar, Paşa.
Əsəd Paşa bu təkliflə razılaşmır:
— Mən həmin pulu başqa yolla taparam.
Ertəsi gün müftiyə xəbər göndərib onu gecə gizli görüşə çağırır. Müfti gələndə Paşa deyir:

— Müfti əfəndi, bizə məlumat çatıb ki, evinizdə gizlicə içki içirsiniz. Bu, tutduğunuz vəzifəyə və müdafiə etdiyiniz qaydalara ziddir. Məsələni İstanbula bildirməliyəm. Amma əvvəlcə sizinlə danışmaq istədim.

Müfti təşvişə düşüb yalvarmağa başlayır. Xəbərin İstanbula çatmaması üçün min qızıl pul təklif edir. Paşa razılaşmır. Müfti məbləği ikiqat artırır, amma yenə rədd cavabı alır. Nəhayət, altı min qızıl pula razılaşırlar.
Sonrakı gün Paşa qazını yanına çağırır:
— Qazı əfəndi, etibarlı mənbələrdən öyrənmişik ki, rüşvət alır, vəzifənizdən şəxsi qazancınız üçün istifadə edirsiniz.
Qazı da vəzifəsini və nüfuzunu itirməkdən qorxaraq yalvarmağa başlayır:
— Məni vəzifəmdən uzaqlaşdırmayın, əfəndim. El içində rüsvay olaram.
Uzun sövdələşmədən sonra o da altı min qızıl pul verməyə razı olur.
Ardınca Paşa xəzinədarı, asayiş rəisini, tacirləri və başqa varlı adamları bir-bir yanına çağırır. Rəvayətə görə, bu yolla iki yüz kisə qızıl toplayır.
Sonra müşavirlərini yenidən çağırıb soruşur:
— Dəməşq əhalisinə əlavə vergi qoyduğumu eşitmisinizmi?
— Xeyr, Paşa.
— Amma mən əlli deyil, iki yüz kisə qızıl toplamışam.
— Bunu necə bacardınız?
Paşa cavab verir:
— Quzuların dərisini soymaqdansa, qoçların yununu qırxmaq yaxşıdır.

İbrət: Ədalət gücsüzün son tikəsinə əl uzatmaq deyil, yükü insanların imkanına uyğun bölməkdir. Haqsız qazanca görə isə gizli sövdələşmə ilə deyil, hamıya eyni qaydada tətbiq olunan qanun əsasında hesab soruşulmalıdır.

title: Vətən və torpaq
paragraphs: Torpağa su qatsan, palçıq olar; uğrunda qan tökülsə, Vətən olar.

İbrət: Vətən sadəcə yaşadığımız yer deyil; onu qoruyanların fədakarlığını və xatirəsini yaşadan, bizə əmanət edilmiş yurddur. Bu əmanətə sahib çıxmaq həm keçmişi unutmamaq, həm də gələcək nəsillər üçün əmin-amanlıq içində bir həyat qurmaqdır.

title: Altmışdan sonra nə dəyişdi?
paragraphs: Altmışı keçib yetmişə yaxınlaşan bir dostumdan yaşa dolduqca özündə hansı dəyişiklikləri hiss etdiyini soruşdum. Belə cavab verdi:
Yaşlılara «Bu əhvalatı artıq danışmısan» demirəm. Qoy danışsınlar. Bəzən bir xatirəni bölüşmək onlara ömrün gözəl anlarını yenidən yaşadır.
Hər səhvi düzəltməyə çalışmıram. Hamını qüsursuz etmək mənim vəzifəm deyil. Könül rahatlığı çox vaxt hər şeyin mükəmməl olmasından daha qiymətlidir.
Xoş sözümü əsirgəmirəm. Səmimi bir iltifat həm qarşımdakı insanın, həm də mənim könlümü açır.
Geyimimdəki kiçik bir qırışığı, bir ləkəni dərd etmirəm. Səliqəli olmaq yaxşıdır, amma insanın dəyəri təkcə görünüşü ilə ölçülmür.
Məni daxilən yoran münasibətlərdən uzaq durmağı öyrəndim. Hər kəslə yaxın olmaq məcburiyyətində deyiləm; qarşılıqlı hörmət və anlayış olan münasibətlərin qədrini bilirəm.
Duyğularımdan utanmıram. Sevinmək də, kövrəlmək də, darıxmaq da insan olmağın bir parçasıdır.
Münasibəti qorumaq üçün yersiz qürurumdan keçməyi öyrəndim. Hər dəfə haqlı çıxmaq insanı xoşbəxt etmir; bəzən bir addım yaxınlaşmaq daha dəyərlidir.
Mənə sevinc verən şeylərə vaxt ayırıram. Öz xoşbəxtliyimin qayğısını da çəkməli olduğumu başa düşmüşəm.
Kömək etməzdən əvvəl buna ehtiyac və istək olub-olmadığını soruşuram. Yaxşı niyyətim başqasının seçiminə hörmət etməyimə mane olmamalıdır.
Sağlamlığımdan, qonşularımdan, qohumlarımdan, təqaüddə olmağımdan durmadan şikayət etmirəm. Çətinlikləri görməzdən gəlmirəm, amma yaşadığıma, sevdiklərimin yanımda olduğuna da şükür edirəm.

Gənclərə «Mən sənin yaşında olanda...» deyib öz həyatımı nümunə göstərməyə tələsmirəm. «Ən yaxşı illərimi sənə verdim» deyərək heç kimi borclu çıxarmıram. Hər dövrün öz şərtləri var; bu günü yalnız keçmişin ölçüsü ilə ölçmək olmaz.

Həyat yoldaşıma daha çox diqqət göstərirəm. Onun bir vaxtlar necə gənc, güclü və şən olduğunu unutmuram. İndi illərin yorğunluğunu daşıyırsa, qayğıma daha çox ehtiyac duyursa, yanında olmağa çalışıram. Birlikdə keçirdiyimiz ömrün qədrini bilirəm.
Hər şeyə görə özümü qınamaqdan əl çəkmişəm. Səhvlərim də olub, amma həm özüm, həm də övladlarım üçün bacardığım qədər çalışmışam. Keçmişdən dərs alıram, özümü onunla cəzalandırmıram.

Və nəhayət, Rəbbimdən dəyişdirə biləcəklərim üçün güc, dəyişdirə bilməyəcəklərim üçün səbir, bunları bir-birindən ayırmaq üçün isə hikmət diləməyi öyrənmişəm. İnsan olduğumu, hər şeyə gücüm çatmadığını qəbul edirəm.
İbrət: Yaşa dolduqca anlayırsan ki, dinclik mükəmməllikdən, anlayış isə hər dəfə haqlı çıxmaqdan daha qiymətlidir. Ömrü gözəlləşdirən özünə və başqalarına mərhəmətlə yanaşmağı bacarmaqdır.

title: Altmışı haqlayanlara
paragraphs: Altmış yaş həyatın kənarına çəkilmək vaxtı deyil. Bəlkə də, illərlə təxirə saldığın istəklərə yer açmaq, özünə daha çox qayğı göstərmək zamanıdır.

Zəhmətlə qazandığın imkanlardan özün üçün də istifadə et. Gələcək ehtiyaclarını nəzərə alaraq rahatlığına, sevincinə və çoxdan arzuladığın şeylərə pay ayır. Hər şeyi başqalarına saxlamaq üçün özünü hər şeydən məhrum etmə.

Övladlarını, nəvələrini sevməyə və bacardığın qədər dəstəkləməyə davam et. Amma onların bütün qayğılarını öz çiyinlərinə yükləmə. Böyümüş övladlarına öz qərarlarını vermək, məsuliyyət daşımaq və yollarını tapmaq üçün yer ver. Özünə ayırdığın vaxt və imkan səni daha az qayğıkeş etmir.

Bədəninə diqqətlə yanaş. Gücünə və sağlamlığına uyğun hərəkət et, gəz, dincəl. Sağlamlığınla bağlı ehtiyacların barədə həkiminlə danış, müayinələrini onunla birlikdə planlaşdır. Nə özünü gərəksiz yerə yüklə, nə də yaşını bəhanə edib sevdiyin məşğuliyyətlərdən uzaqlaş.
Özünə baxmağı unutma. Təmiz, rahat, zövqünə uyğun geyin. Səliqəni başqalarının bəyənməsi üçün deyil, özünü yaxşı hiss etmək üçün qoru. Yaşın sənin üslubunu və rənglərini əlindən almasın.

Marağını və öyrənmək həvəsini yaşat. Kitab oxu, musiqi dinlə, yeni bir şey öyrən. İstəsən, texnologiyadan yaxınlarınla əlaqə saxlamaq və dünyanı tanımaq üçün istifadə et. Hər yeniliyin ardınca qaçmaq məcburiyyətində deyilsən; sənə fayda və sevinc verəni seç.

Gəncləri dinlə. Onların həyatını öz keçmişinin ölçüsü ilə qiymətləndirmə. Təcrübəni bölüş, amma nəsihət verməzdən əvvəl onların fikrini də soruş. Bəzən sənin onlara öyrədəcəyin qədər onların da sənə öyrədəcəyi var.
“Bizim vaxtımızda…” deyəndə unutma: indi də sənin vaxtındır. Xatirələrin keçmişdə olsa da, həyatın bu gün davam edir.
Sənə hörmət edən, yanında özün ola bildiyin insanlarla münasibətlərini qoru. Başqalarının dərdinə şərik ol, amma səni daim alçaldan və tükəndirən münasibətlərə sərhəd qoy.
Həvəs göstərdiyin işlərdən əl çəkmə. Bağçılıq et, yemək bişir, yaz, rəqs et, səyahətə çıx — imkanın və istəyin nədirsə, ona yer ayır. Böyük planların olmadığı günlərdə də kiçik sevinclər tapmaq olar.

İmkan olduqca evdən çıx. Bir dostla görüş, parkda otur, sərgiyə get. Çölə çıxmaq çətindirsə, bir telefon zəngi, evdə içilən bir stəkan çay da yaxınlıq yarada bilər. Həyatla əlaqəni özünə uyğun yollarla qoru.

İncikliklərini yüngülləşdirməyə çalış. Qəlbini qırdığın insandan üzr istə. Bağışlamağa hazır olmaq isə vaxt ala bilər; özünü tələsdirmə. Bağışlamaq hər şeyi unutmaq və ya səni incidən münasibətə qayıtmaq demək deyil.
Kədərlənəndə danış, köməyə ehtiyacın olanda istə. Həmişə güclü, həmişə gülərüz görünməyə borclu deyilsən.
Sev, gül, maraqlan, plan qur. Özünə yalnız dincəlməyə deyil, yenidən başlamağa da icazə ver. Ömrünün bu çağını başqalarının gözləntilərinə görə deyil, öz dəyərlərinə və imkanlarına uyğun yaşa.
İbrət: Özünə qayğı göstərmək üçün başqalarına sevgini azaltmaq lazım deyil. Yaşın neçə olursa olsun, vaxtının, rahatlığının və arzularının dəyəri var. Bu gün də sənin həyatındır.

title: Yaşa dolmaq
paragraphs: Yaşa dolmaq dağa qalxmağa bənzəyir: yüksəldikcə addımların ağırlaşır, nəfəsin təngiyir, amma qarşında daha geniş mənzərə açılır.
İbrət: İllər keçdikcə gücümüz azala bilər, amma qazandığımız təcrübə bizə daha uzağı görməyi, həyatı daha dərindən anlamağı öyrədir.

title: Zaman — səssiz axan ömür
paragraphs: Zaman qəribə bir möcüzədir... Onu nə görmək, nə tutmaq, nə də geri qaytarmaq mümkündür. O, səssizcə keçir — saatların əqrəblərində, günlərin dəyişməsində, saçlara düşən ağlarda, uşaqların böyüməsində, xatirələrin uzaqlaşmasında...

İnsan çox vaxt zamanı yalnız itirdikdən sonra dərk edir. Dünən adi görünən bir gün illər keçəndən sonra ən qiymətli xatirəyə çevrilir. Bir vaxtlar əhəmiyyətsiz hesab etdiyimiz bir söhbət, bir baxış, bir gülüş, sevdiyimiz insanla keçirdiyimiz sadə bir axşam sonralar həyatımızın ən gözəl anlarından birinə çevrilə bilir.

Zaman heç kim üçün dayanmır. Nə var-dövlətə, nə şöhrətə, nə də insanın istəyinə boyun əyir. O, hamıya eyni ölçüdə verilən, lakin hər kəs tərəfindən fərqli qiymətləndirilən ən böyük sərvətdir. İnsanın ömrü, əslində, illərlə deyil, yaşadığı mənalı anlarla ölçülür.
Bəzən düşünürük ki, həyat qarşıdadır və hələ çox vaxtımız var. Sabah edərik, gələn həftə gedərik, bir gün danışarıq, sonra görüşərik... Amma “sonra” dediyimiz zaman heç də həmişə gəlmir.
Zaman bizdən çox şey aparır: gəncliyimizi, bəzi insanları, bəzi arzuları, bəzi fürsətləri... Amma əvəzində bizə xatirələr, təcrübə və həyatın həqiqi mənasını anlamaq imkanı verir.

Ona görə zamanı sadəcə keçən illərlə ölçməyək. Vaxtımızı nə qədər yaşadığımızla deyil, necə yaşadığımızla qiymətləndirək. Sevdiklərimizə sevgimizi bu gün söyləyək. Dostlarımızla görüşməyi sonraya saxlamayaq. Gözəl mənzərələrə baxaq, günəşin doğuşunu seyr edək, dənizin səsini dinləyək, ürəyimizi sevindirən anları yaşayaq.
Çünki zaman keçir...
İbrət: Sevgimizi bildirməyi, doğmalarımıza vaxt ayırmağı sonraya saxlamayaq. Ötən an geri qayıtmır, bu günün qədrini elə bu gün bilmək lazımdır.
Etibar Siracsoy

title: Aslanın izi
paragraphs: Qorxaq, amma lovğalanmağı sevən bir ovçu aslan axtara-axtara meşəyə gəlib çıxır. Qarşısına çıxan odunçudan soruşur:
— Qardaş, buralarda aslan görməmisən? Heç olmasa, izinə rast gəlmisən?
Odunçu cavab verir:
— Aslanın özünü görmüşəm. İstəsən, gəl, səni olduğu yerə aparım.
Ovçunun rəngi qaçır:
— Yox, yox, sağ ol! Mən aslanın özünü yox, sadəcə izini axtarırdım.
İbrət: Cəsarət sözdə deyil, sınaq anında üzə çıxır. Lovğalıqla yaradılan qəhrəman obrazı ilk çətinlikdə dağıla bilər.

title: Eşşəyin qanunu
paragraphs: Bir gün eşşək meşənin şahı oldu. Taxta çıxandan bir neçə gün sonra fərman verdi:
— Hamı axşam saat altıda yatmalı, səhər saat altıda oyanmalıdır. Bu on iki saat ərzində meşədə bir səs belə eşidilməməlidir. Qanunu pozan cəzalandırılacaq!
Heyvanlar təəccüblənsələr də, etiraz etmədilər. Axşam düşən kimi meşəni sükut bürüdü.
Bir səhər xoruz saat beşdə banladı. Meşəyə çaxnaşma düşdü. Xoruzu dərhal məhkəməyə çıxardılar və şahın hökmü ilə edam etdilər.
Bundan sonra heç kim qanunu pozmağa cürət etmədi. Hamı həyatını eşşəyin müəyyən etdiyi saatlara uyğunlaşdırdı.
İllər keçdi. Eşşək qocaldı, taqətdən düşdü. Ömrünün son günlərində şir onu görməyə gəldi. Halını soruşandan sonra dedi:

— İllərdir bir sual bizi düşündürür: hamının axşam altıda yatıb səhər altıda oyanmasının hikməti nə idi? Dəfələrlə bu qanuna qarşı çıxmaq istədik. Amma asayiş pozular deyə çəkindik. Düşündük ki, yəqin, sənin bildiyin, bizim anlamadığımız bir şey var.
Eşşək acı-acı gülümsədi:
— Heç bir hikməti yox idi. Eşşəkliyimdən elə bir qanun çıxarmışdım. Məni təəccübləndirən o oldu ki, siz illərlə mənim ağılsızlığımda hikmət axtardınız.
Şir susdu. Eşşək sözünə davam etdi:
— Əvvəlcə məndən qorxdunuz. Sonra öyrəşdiniz. Axırda isə başqa cür yaşamağın mümkün olduğunu unutdunuz.

İbrət: Hər əmrin arxasında hikmət, hər köhnə qaydanın arxasında ağlabatan səbəb olmur. Qorxu ilə qəbul edilən bir qayda zamanla vərdişə, vərdiş isə sorğulanmayan həqiqətə çevrilə bilər. “Bu qayda nəyə xidmət edir?” sualını unutma.

title: Fil və ip
paragraphs: Bir rəvayətdə deyilir ki, səyyah fillərin saxlandığı bir yerdən keçərkən qəribə mənzərə ilə qarşılaşdı: nəhəng heyvanların hər biri ön ayağından nazik bir iplə qazığa bağlanmışdı. Nə zəncir vardı, nə də qəfəs.
Səyyah düşündü: “Bu qədər güclü heyvanlar istəsələr, ipi asanlıqla qıra bilərlər. Bəs niyə heç cəhd etmirlər?”
Yaxınlıqdakı təlimçidən bunun səbəbini soruşdu.
Təlimçi dedi:

— Balaca olanda onları belə bir iplə bağlayırıq. Nə qədər dartınsalar da, qıra bilmirlər. Bir müddət sonra cəhd etməkdən vaz keçirlər. Böyüyəndə gücləri artır, amma ipi qıra bilməyəcəklərinə inamları dəyişmir.
Səyyah yenidən fillərə baxdı. Onları yerində saxlayan təkcə ayaqlarındakı ip deyildi; keçmişdə bacarmadıqları işi bu gün də bacarmayacaqlarına inanmaları idi.
İbrət: Dünən bacarmadığın bir şeyi bu gün də bacarmayacağını düşünmə. Təcrübən, gücün və imkanların dəyişə bilər. Keçmiş uğursuzluğu gələcəyinin sərhədinə çevirmə.

title: İki uzunqulaq
paragraphs: İki uzunqulaq yolla gedərkən ağacda oturmuş bir meymun görür. Biri o birinə deyir:
— Gəl bu meymuna sataşaq. Soruşaq ki, dostun varmı? «Var» desə, deyərik: «Hansı axmaq səninlə dostluq edir?» «Yoxdur» desə, deyərik: «Hansı axmaq səninlə dost olar ki?»
Ağaca yaxınlaşıb səslənirlər:
— Meymun, sənin dostun varmı?
Meymun yuxarıdan onlara baxıb cavab verir:
— Hara baxıram, ancaq eşşək görürəm. Kimlə dostluq edim?
İbrət: Başqasını gülünc vəziyyətə salmaq istəyən bəzən özü gülüş hədəfinə çevrilir. İnsan başqasını alçaltmaqla ucalmaz.

title: Milçək çini qablar dükanında
paragraphs: Bir milçək çini qablarla dolu dükanı dağıtmaq istəsə, buna gücü çatmaz. Amma dükanın içindəki öküzün qulağına girib onu təlaşa salsa, öküz sağa-sola çırpınaraq hər şeyi sındıra bilər.
Bu bənzətmədə milçək yalanı, mövhumatı və qərəzi təmsil edir. Öküz isə eşitdiyini düşünmədən qəbul edən, qəzəbinin və qorxusunun təsiri ilə hərəkətə keçən insanı.
Bəzən böyük dağıntını yaradan yalanın öz gücü deyil, ona inananın düşünmədən işə saldığı gücdür.
İbrət: Eşitdiyin hər sözün ardınca getmə. Mənbəyini yoxla, doğruluğunu araşdır, sonra qərar ver. Başqasının yalanı sənin əlinlə zərərə çevrilməsin.

title: Ovçunun vəsfi
paragraphs: Aslan yazmağı öyrənənədək bütün hekayələr ovçunu tərifləyəcək.
— Afrika atalar sözü kimi tanınan deyim

İbrət: Hekayəni danışan çox vaxt özünü qəhrəman göstərir. Həqiqəti anlamaq üçün yalnız danışanın deyil, səsi eşidilməyənin də tərəfini dinlə. Öz yaşadıqlarını dilə gətirməsən, sənin hekayəni başqaları öz baxışlarına görə yazar.

title: Su daşıyan qarışqa
paragraphs: Rəvayətə görə, zalım hökmdar Nəmrud İbrahim peyğəmbəri oda atdırmaq üçün meydanın ortasında nəhəng bir tonqal qalatdırdı. Alov getdikcə yüksəlir, bütün canlılar dözülməz istidən uzaqlaşmağa çalışırdı.
Təkcə balaca bir qarışqa oda doğru tələsirdi. Ağzında bir damla su aparırdı.
Başqa bir qarışqa onu səslədi: — Hara gedirsən? O boyda alovu görmürsən?
— Nəmrud İbrahim peyğəmbəri yandırmaq istəyir. Odu söndürməyə su aparıram.
— Bir damla su ilə? — o biri qarışqa istehza ilə soruşdu. — O damla heç közə çatmamış buxarlanacaq! Bununla nəyi dəyişə bilərsən?
Su daşıyan qarışqa bir anlıq dayandı: — Bəlkə, bu damla tonqalı söndürməz. Amma heç olmasa, kimin tərəfində olduğum bəlli olar.
Bunu deyib yoluna davam etdi.
İbrət: Zülmün qarşısını almağa hər zaman gücümüz çatmaya bilər. Amma ona laqeyd qalmamaq öz əlimizdədir. Darda olanın müdafiəsi üçün atılan ən kiçik addımın da dəyəri var.

title: Tısbağanın yanlış hesabı
paragraphs: Tısbağadan soruşdular:
— Yaxınlıqdakı kəndə nə qədər vaxta çatarsan?
— Yağışı, palçığı, küləyi, eniş-yoxuşu nəzərə alsaq, üç günlük yoldur. Amma ehtiyat üçün altı gün deyək, — deyə tısbağa cavab verdi.
Altı gün keçdi, tısbağa isə kəndə çatmadı. Onu axtarmağa çıxdılar və yolun yarısında tapdılar.
— Nə olub? Üç günlük yolu altı günə də gələ bilməmisən? — deyə təəccüblə soruşdular.
Tısbağa pərişan halda cavab verdi:
— Heç soruşmayın, dostlar. Yağışı da, palçığı da, küləyi də, eniş-yoxuşu da hesablamışdım. Bir pis niyyətli adamları unutmuşdum. Hər dəfə bir az sürət yığanda məni tutub arxam üstə çevirirdilər.
İbrət: Yolumuzu təkcə çətin şərait deyil, başqalarının pis niyyəti də kəsə bilər. Allah qarşına səni yıxanları deyil, yıxılanda əlindən tutanları çıxarsın.

title: Albrext Dürer
paragraphs: Albrext Dürer haqqında rəvayət

Deyilənə görə, Nürnberq yaxınlığında yaşayan kasıb, çoxuşaqlı bir ailədə iki qardaş böyüyürdü: Albrext və Albert. Hər ikisi rəssam olmaq arzusunda idi. Səhərdən axşamadək çalışan atalarının isə onları oxutmağa imkanı çatmırdı.

Qardaşlar gecələr şam işığında uzun-uzadı söhbət edir, arzularına yol axtarırdılar. Axırda püşk atmağa qərar verdilər. Birinə oxumaq, o birinə isə mədəndə işləyib qardaşının təhsil xərcini ödəmək düşəcəkdi. Dörd ildən sonra yerlərini dəyişəcəkdilər.
Püşk Albrextə düşdü.

O, rəssamlığı öyrənməyə yollandı, Albert isə mədəndə işə başladı. Biri fırça tutmağın incəliklərini öyrənir, rənglərin dünyasına baş vururdu. Digəri hər gün yerin dərinliklərinə enir, ağır zəhməti ilə qardaşının təhsilini davam etdirməsinə kömək edirdi.

Dörd il keçdi. Albrextin istedadı diqqət çəkdi, əsərləri ona ad-san və qazanc gətirməyə başladı. Evə qayıdanda qardaşını qucaqlayıb sevinclə dedi: — İndi növbə sənindir, Albert. Get, oxu, arzunu gerçəkləşdir. Sən mənə dayaq oldun, indi də mən sənə dayaq olacağam.
Albert isə başını yavaşca buladı: — Yox, qardaşım… Mənim üçün artıq gecdir.
O, əllərini uzatdı. Ovucları qabar bağlamış, barmaqları ağır işdən əyilmişdi. — Bu əllər daha əvvəlki kimi fırça tuta bilməz.
Albrext qardaşının əllərini ehtiyatla ovuclarına aldı. Nəsə demək istədi, amma söz tapa bilmədi. Göz yaşları Albertin yorğun əllərinə damladı.
Öz arzusuna çatmağın qardaşına nəyin bahasına başa gəldiyini yalnız indi bütün ağırlığı ilə anladı.
Rəvayətdə Dürerin məşhur “Dua edən əllər” rəsmi bu fədakarlıqla əlaqələndirilir. O əllər qardaş sevgisinin, minnətdarlığın və başqasının uğuru naminə çəkilən səssiz zəhmətin rəmzi kimi təqdim olunur.
İbrət: Uğurlarımızda vaxtını, gücünü və imkanlarını bizdən əsirgəməyən insanların da payı var. Onların fədakarlığını görmək, unutmamaq və qayğılarına qayğı ilə cavab vermək əsl minnətdarlıqdır.

title: Memar Sinanın susuz evi
paragraphs: Memar Sinan haqqında rəvayət

Qanuni Sultan Süleymanın dövründə İstanbul sürətlə böyüyür, şəhərdə su çatışmazlığı getdikcə artırdı. Rəvayətə görə, bir gün sultan Memar Sinanı hüzuruna çağırıb soruşdu: — Xalq suyu baha qiymətə alır, böyük əziyyət çəkir. İstanbulu bu darlıqdan qurtarmağın bir yolu varmı?
Sinan şəhərin ətrafını araşdırmaq üçün vaxt istədi. Köməkçiləri ilə bulaqları, çay yataqlarını və dərələri gəzdi, suyu şəhərə çatdırmağın yollarını axtardı.
Sonra sultanın yanına qayıdıb dedi: — Su gətirmək mümkündür. Amma bu iş böyük zəhmət və çoxlu vəsait tələb edəcək.
— Təki mümkün olsun, — sultan cavab verdi. — Lazım olan vəsait ayrılacaq.
Sinan işə başladı. Zamanla qurduğu su kəmərləri və tağlı körpülərlə şəhərin çeşmələrinə su gəldi. Əvvəllər hər damlası əziyyətlə əldə olunan su indi insanların gündəlik ehtiyacını ödəyirdi.
Sultan ümumi suyun qorunmasını əmr etmiş, icazəsiz olaraq evlərə ayrıca xətt çəkilməsini qadağan etmişdi. Sinana isə xidmətinin əvəzində bir istisna etdi: evinə su çəkdirməsinə şifahi icazə verdi.
İllər keçdi. Sultan Süleyman dünyadan köçdü. Onun verdiyi icazəni xatırlayan adamlar da getdikcə azaldı.
Bir gün ahıl memarı saraya çağırdılar. Divana şikayət olunmuşdu: başqalarına qadağan olduğu halda, niyə Sinanın evinə ayrıca su gəlirdi?
— Bu, Sultan Süleymanın icazəsi ilə olub, — Sinan izah etdi.
— Yazılı fərmanın varmı?
Sinan sakitcə cavab verdi: — Yoxdur. Sultanın sözünü yetərli bildim. Ondan bir də yazılı sənəd istəməyə çəkindim.
Uzun müzakirədən sonra qərar verdilər: əvvəlki istifadəsinə görə memar cəzalandırılmasın, amma evinə gələn su kəsilsin.
Rəvayətə görə, ömrünün son günlərində ağır xəstələnən Sinan qurumuş dodaqlarını islatmaq üçün su istədi. Lakin evinin kranından su gəlmirdi.

Onda bir şəhəri suya qovuşduran memar asta səslə dedi: — Biz bu işi öz mənfəətimiz üçün deyil, Allah rizası üçün gördük. Mükafatını da Ondan gözləyirik. Evimizdə su olmasa da, çəkdiyimiz zəhmət xalqa xidmət edir.
İbrət: İnsanlar onlara edilən yaxşılığı unuda bilərlər, amma bu, görülən yaxşılığın dəyərini azaltmır. Təmənnasız xidmət etmək insanın ucalığı, ona xidmət edənləri unutmamaq isə cəmiyyətin borcudur.

title: Mihrimah Sultan və Memar Sinan
paragraphs: İstanbulun iki məscidini birləşdirən gözəl bir rəvayət var: Mihrimah Sultanla Memar Sinanın hekayəsi.
Qanuni Sultan Süleymanın qızı Mihrimahın adı fars mənşəlidir: «mihr» günəş, «mah» isə ay deməkdir.
Rəvayətə görə, Mihrimah on yeddi yaşına çatanda onunla evlənmək istəyən iki nəfər vardı: Rüstəm Paşa və Memar Sinan. Lakin şahzadə Rüstəm Paşa ilə evləndi. Bu evlilik 1539-cu ildə baş tutmuşdu.
Əfsanəyə görə, o vaxt artıq evli və əlli yaşına yaxın olan Sinan sevgisini qəlbində saxladı. Sevdiyinə qovuşa bilməyən memar duyğularını sənətində yaşatdı.

Sinan əvvəlcə Üsküdarda Mihrimah Sultanın adını daşıyan məscidi inşa etdi. Sonra Ədirnəqapıda onun adına ikinci məscid ucaltdı. Bu iki abidə həqiqətən də Sinanın əsərləridir; onları gizli bir məhəbbətin ifadəsi saymaq isə rəvayətin yozumudur.

Rəvayəti danışanlar Üsküdardakı məscidin siluetində ətəkləri yerə süzülən bir qadın görürlər. Ədirnəqapıdakı məscidin incə minarəsində, işıqlı məkanında və zərif bəzəklərində isə Mihrimahın gözəlliyini axtarırlar. Hətta bəzi naxışları onun uzun saçlarına bənzədirlər.
Hekayənin ən yaddaqalan hissəsi Günəşlə Ayın görüşüdür.

Deyilənə görə, İstanbulda elə bir nöqtə var ki, oradan baxanda Günəş Ədirnəqapıdakı məscidin arxasında batarkən Ay Üsküdardakı məscidin arxasından doğur. Rəvayət bu mənzərəni bahar gecə-gündüz bərabərliyi ilə bağlayır və onu Sinanın sevdiyinə ünvanladığı səssiz bir etiraf kimi təsvir edir.
Mihrimah — Günəş və Ay…
Sinan bu mənzərəni qəsdən yaratmışdı, yoxsa insanlar sonradan onun sənətinə belə bir məna vermişdilər? Bunu təsdiqlənmiş tarix kimi söyləmək mümkün deyil.
Amma rəvayət yaşayır. İki məscidə baxan insan yalnız daş, günbəz və minarə görmür; bəzən orada sözə çevrilməmiş bir duyğunun izini də axtarır.
İbrət: Hər sevgi qovuşmaqla tamamlanmır. İnsan duyğularını yaradıcılığa yönəltdikdə, onlar başqalarına da gözəllik bəxş edən bir əsərdə yaşaya bilər.

title: Möhtəşəm dərs
paragraphs: Osmanlı padşahı II Muradla oğlu Mehmed haqqında belə bir rəvayət danışılır.
Gələcəyin Fateh Sultan Mehmedi uşaq vaxtı dərsdə sakit oturmaz, tez-tez dəcəllik edərmiş. Müəllimi Ağşəmsəddin ona irad bildirəndə isə deyərmiş:
— Sən mənə heç nə deyə bilməzsən. Mən padşah oğluyam!
Ağşəmsəddin şahzadənin bu davranışından narahat idi. Əvvəlcə padşaha şikayət etməyə çəkinsə də, bir gün cəsarətini toplayıb onun hüzuruna çıxdı və vəziyyəti danışdı.
II Murad bir qədər düşündü, sonra ağlına gələn planı müəllimin qulağına pıçıldadı. Ağşəmsəddin etiraz etdi:
— Padşahım, mən bunu edə bilmərəm!
Lakin hökmdar qərarından dönmədi:
— Oğlumun dərs alması üçün bunu etməliyik.
Ertəsi gün şahzadə yenə dərsi pozdu. Müəllimin xəbərdarlığına da həmişəki cavabı verdi:
— Mən padşah oğluyam!
Elə bu vaxt qapı açıldı və II Murad sinfə girdi.
Əvvəlcədən razılaşdıqları kimi, Ağşəmsəddin qəzəblənmiş görkəm alıb padşaha tərəf döndü. İcazəsiz içəri girdiyinə görə onu danladı, hətta bir şillə vurub sinifdən çıxmasını tələb etdi.
Padşah başını aşağı saldı, üzr istəyib çıxdı.
Mehmed heyrətdən donub qalmışdı. Hamının qarşısında baş əydiyi atası müəllimin iradını qəbul etmiş, sinfin qaydasına tabe olmuşdu.
Bir az sonra qapı döyüldü. II Murad bu dəfə içəri girmək üçün icazə istədi və yenidən üzr istədi.
Rəvayətə görə, həmin gündən şahzadənin dərsdə davranışı dəyişdi. Atası ona uzun nəsihətlə deyil, öz nümunəsi ilə göstərmişdi ki, padşah oğlu olmaq insana başqalarına hörmətsizlik etmək haqqı vermir.
İbrət: Tərbiyədə şəxsi nümunə uzun nəsihətdən təsirlidir. Valideynin nüfuzu özünü qaydalardan üstün tutmasında deyil, övladından gözlədiyi hörmət və məsuliyyəti öz davranışında göstərməsindədir.

title: Şəhər üçün üç vacib şey
paragraphs: Hər şəhərə üç şey lazımdır: kanalizasiya, hamam və kitabxana. Kanalizasiya şəhəri, hamam bədəni, kitabxana isə ruhu təmizləyir.
— Fateh Sultan Mehmedə aid edilən söz
İbrət: Şəhərin və bədənin təmizliyinə olduğu qədər insanın mənəvi dünyasına da qayğı göstərmək lazımdır. Kitab düşüncəni aydınlaşdırır, insanın özünə və dünyaya daha dərindən baxmasına kömək edir.

title: An Honestly Earned Morsel
paragraphs: Even when the flour is fresh and the water pure, dough will not rise properly if the yeast is spoiled. Nor will it make good bread.
To raise a child of good character, nourish them with food earned honestly.
— Attributed to Imam al-Ghazali
Moral: A child’s moral upbringing begins with the example set at home. An honest livelihood, integrity, and respect for the rights of others provide a firm foundation.

title: Adversity and Blessing
paragraphs: A hardship that draws you closer to God may hold a hidden blessing.
A blessing that draws you away from God may become a misfortune.
Moral: Do not judge your experiences only by the pain or comfort they bring. Consider how they change your heart and where they lead you.

title: The Church Bell
paragraphs: Long ago, so the story goes, a country had a custom: when an ordinary citizen died, the church bell tolled once. For a noble, it tolled twice; for someone close to the king, three times; and for the king himself, four times.
One day, the court—the very place people turned to in the hope of finding justice—convicted an innocent man.
That day, the church bell tolled five times.
Bewildered, the townspeople gathered outside the church and asked the priest:
“Who could be more important than the king? Why did you ring the bell five times?”
The priest answered sorrowfully:
“Justice. Today, justice died.”
Moral: An unjust verdict harms more than one person: it shakes everyone’s faith in justice. Speaking out against injustice protects both those who suffer and the conscience of society.

title: Confidence Is Half the Battle
paragraphs: A teaching story tells of a principal who called several teachers into his office and gave them an assignment.

“You are among our most capable teachers. We are therefore putting a class of specially selected, talented pupils in your care. This year, we want you to help them develop their abilities even further.”

Encouraged by this trust, the teachers prepared their lessons enthusiastically, tried new approaches, and patiently supported pupils who struggled. The children sensed that their teachers believed in them. They became more willing to ask questions and attempt difficult tasks.
By the end of the school year, the class had achieved excellent results. Teachers and pupils alike were delighted.
The principal congratulated the teachers.
“There is something I need to tell you. These children were not selected for exceptional ability. They were chosen at random.”
The teachers exchanged glances. Their hard work must have played a considerable part in the children’s progress.
The principal continued:
“And you were not selected through a competition either. I drew your names by lot.”
The room fell silent.
“You believed in your own abilities and in the children’s,” he said. “Then you turned that belief into effort, patience, and care. That is what made the difference.”
Moral: Belief alone does not create success, but it can encourage people to try, learn, and persevere. If you believe someone can succeed, show them that belief and support their growth.

title: The Dervish's Long Spoons
paragraphs: One day, a dervish was asked:
“What is the difference between those who truly love and those who only talk about love?”
“Let me show you,” he replied.
First, he invited a group of people who spoke a great deal about love to share a meal. Bowls of hot soup were set before them, along with spoons that had very long handles.
“There is one condition,” he said. “You must hold your spoons at the very end of the handle.”

The guests began to eat. But the spoons were so long that no one could bring the soup to their own mouth. However hard they tried, the soup spilled and the spoons knocked against one another. Each person was intent on feeding only themselves. Eventually, they left the table tired and hungry.
Then the dervish invited people who showed their love through their actions. They were served the same soup and given the same spoons, and the same rule applied.

One guest filled a spoon and offered it to the person opposite. That person returned the gesture. Soon, everyone was feeding one another. Conversation and laughter rose around the table, and no one went hungry.
After the guests had left, the dervish turned to those who had asked the question.

“The spoons were the same. So was the soup. The difference was in how the people treated one another. At the first table, everyone thought only of themselves. At the second, everyone cared for the person opposite them too.”
Moral: Love shows itself in acts of care, not words alone. When we notice one another’s needs and offer our help, we can overcome difficulties together.

title: The Dervish’s Robe
paragraphs: One day, an injured bird came before the king with a complaint.
“A dervish has broken my wing. I ask you for justice.”
The king summoned the man.
“Why did you break this bird’s wing?”
The man in the dervish’s robe tried to defend himself.

“Your Majesty, I was trying to catch it. I approached, but it did not fly away. I moved closer, and still it stayed where it was. I thought I could catch it easily. But when I reached for it, it struggled to escape. That was when its wing broke.”
The king turned to the bird.
“Why didn’t you fly away when you saw him approaching?”
The bird replied:

“He was wearing a dervish’s robe. Had I known he was a hunter, I would have flown away. I thought he was a compassionate man who feared God and would do me no harm. I stayed because I trusted what his robe stood for.”
The king was silent for a moment. Then he ordered angrily:
“Break his arm as well!”
The bird spoke up at once.
“No, Your Majesty! Please don’t!”
“Why not?” asked the king in surprise.
“His arm will heal, and he may hurt someone again. Have him take off the dervish’s robe, so that others like me won’t be deceived into trusting him because of what he wears.”
Moral: Wearing something that inspires trust does not make a person worthy of it. Judge people by their actions, not their clothing or titles.

title: Hands at Work, Hope in God
paragraphs: There was once a dervish who spent much of his day praying in solitude. He supported himself through his own labor: each day, he worked for a while, bought bread with his earnings and shared whatever he did not need with the poor.
One day, while praying in the desert, he noticed a fox that could barely use its legs. The animal struggled to drag itself along. The dervish wondered:
“How does this fox survive? It cannot hunt or even walk properly. How does God provide for it?”
Just then, a lion appeared in the distance, dragging a gazelle it had caught. It set down its prey, ate its fill and walked away, leaving the rest.
The fox, which had been waiting nearby, dragged itself over and ate until it was no longer hungry.
The dervish marveled at what he had seen. He praised God for providing for the fox through the lion. Then he thought:
“God, who feeds this fox, will surely feed me too. I can spend the time I usually work in prayer instead. There is no need to work any longer.”

From that day on, he stopped working and devoted all his time to worship. But the food he expected never arrived. No one knocked on his door or brought him even a piece of bread. Day by day, he grew weaker.
At last, one day, he heard an unseen voice:

“I gave you the strength and health to work. Why did you choose to imitate the fox that could not walk? Why did you not learn from the lion? Get up, work and earn your living. Let those who need help benefit from your labor too. Feed yourself, and feed someone in need.”
The dervish realized that he had drawn the wrong lesson from what he had witnessed. He repented and returned to his former way of life, earning his bread and sharing it with those in need.

Moral: Trusting in God does not mean giving up your efforts. It means doing what you can and placing your trust in Him. If you have the strength and opportunity, work both to support yourself and to help others.

catalog_metadata.title: Hands at Work, Hope in God

title: Drinking the Sherbet of Martyrdom
paragraphs: According to a traditional account, mortally wounded soldiers in Ottoman times were given sherbet—a sweet drink—to leave a pleasant taste in their mouths during their final moments. Doctors are said to have prepared it with water from the sacred Zamzam well and carried it in small barrels.

The expression “to drink the sherbet of martyrdom,” meaning to die a martyr, is sometimes linked to this account. However, the story should be treated as a traditional explanation rather than an established account of the expression’s origin.
Its most moving element is the idea that a person should not be deprived of tenderness and care, even at the end of life.
Moral: Language preserves memories, beliefs, and stories from the past. Honoring that inheritance means appreciating its meaning while distinguishing tradition from documented history.

title: Fasting
paragraphs: During Ramadan, a few young men noticed an elderly man sitting quietly to one side, eating. They approached him and asked mockingly:
“What’s this? You’re eating? Aren’t you fasting?”
The old man answered calmly:
“I am, my boys. I just happen to be eating and drinking.”
They laughed.
“What kind of fasting is that?”
He replied:

“I keep my tongue from lying, my eyes from looking at others with ill intent, and my hands from taking what belongs to someone else. I don’t mock people, belittle them, or gossip about them. I avoid wastefulness. My illness prevents me from going without food, but I try to make my words and actions reflect the spirit of this month.”
Then he asked:
“And what about you? Are you fasting?”
The young men lowered their heads in shame.
“Perhaps we’re only going without food…”

Moral: The spiritual value of fasting lies not only in enduring hunger, but also in disciplining our speech, thoughts, and behavior. Before judging someone else, try to understand their circumstances and examine your own actions.

title: The Fortieth-Day Rite
paragraphs: In some Turkic communities, the first forty days after childbirth are regarded as a time of special care for mother and baby. Customs concerning outings and visitors vary between regions and families.
One account of the tradition marking the end of these forty days describes a visit to relatives. The hosts prepare small gifts for the baby, each carrying a wish:
Coins, for a life free from want;
Cotton, for a gentle heart and a life long enough to see one’s hair turn gray;
Sugar, for sweetness and happiness;
Rice, for abundance in the home;
Salt, for a life that never loses its savor;
An egg, for nourishment and good health.
These objects do not determine the child’s future. They give a tangible form to the family’s hopes for a happy life.
Moral: A small gift can hold a lifelong wish. The beauty of this custom lies in the care shown to mother and baby, and in the blessings offered for the years ahead.

title: Friend of Allah
paragraphs: An elderly man saw a barefoot child in the street. He took the child to a nearby shop and bought a pair of shoes.
The child held the new shoes and gazed at them in silence. Then, looking up, the child asked:
“Are you Allah?”
The man’s eyes filled with tears. He knelt beside the child.
“No, little one. I’m just a person, like you.”
The child thought for a moment, then said softly:
“Then you must be a friend of Allah. Last night, I was crying, and I told Him I didn’t have any shoes.”
The man could find no words. He helped the child put the shoes on.
Moral: Sometimes the help someone prays for arrives through another person’s compassion. A kindness that seems small to you may kindle a great hope in someone else’s heart.

title: The Gifts of Allah
paragraphs: Every blessing from Allah brings a responsibility. We will be called to account not simply for what we have received, but for how we have honored it:
If given strength—whether we have used it justly;
If given authority—whether we have treated others with compassion;
If given wealth—whether we have used it with integrity and generosity;
If given peace and comfort—whether we have appreciated them and given thanks;
If given a life partner—whether we have shown faithfulness and care;
If given a child—whether we have raised them with love, patience, and responsibility.
Moral: Every blessing is also a test. What reveals our character is how we value what we have been given and what we do with it.

title: The Hajj Pilgrimage
paragraphs: A parable tells of a man on the Hajj pilgrimage who, during the symbolic stoning of the devil, began directing the stones at himself. A young man watching him asked in astonishment:
“Sir, what are you doing? Why are you throwing stones at yourself?”
The man replied:
“My son, casting stones here is not enough. We must first confront the evil within us, discipline our selfish desires, and cleanse our hearts.”

The heat is in the fire, not the iron above it;
Wisdom is in the mind, not the crown upon it.
Whatever you seek, begin by looking within—
Neither holy cities nor pilgrimage can do that work for you.

Moral: Our hardest struggle is with our own ego and desires. In this parable, the stones turned inward symbolize examining ourselves, not harming our bodies. The task is to free the heart from resentment, arrogance, and greed. A pilgrimage finds its deepest meaning in the change it brings within us.

title: A prayer for everyone
paragraphs:
To those whose hearts find no peace, who have no home,
To children without parents, to those who stand alone,
To those in need, with nothing to eat or drink,
To those enduring illness, struggling to make ends meet,
To those who long for a loved one, waiting for their return,
To those whose hope has faded, who can see no way forward,
To those who have lost their way, whose hearts yearn for light,
To those who hold a wish, who still dare to dream,
To those whose faith has faltered, who feel far from You—
Bring Your help, Almighty God.
Moral: Prayer gives voice to our deepest needs and makes room for the suffering of others. As we turn to God, may we remember everyone in need of help.

title: If fate allows
paragraphs: Someone who used to say, “We’ll meet,” now says, “We’ll meet if fate allows.” I find that strange. I have not changed, and my feelings toward him are as warm as before; I would still be delighted to see him. Yet those words seem to place a barrier between us. I know nothing of his fate, and he knows nothing of mine. Do our two fates know each other? Can they arrange a meeting on our behalf?
Perhaps we should not expect anything from fate. Perhaps this is simply another way of saying, “Out of sight, out of mind.”
I did not like the phrase “if fate allows” at all.
Moral: Do not let distance grow between you and those you care about. Do not put off seeing them by saying ‘if fate allows’—meet today and brighten their day.
Bakhtiyar Sirajov

title: The door to the heart
paragraphs: British artist William Holman Hunt’s painting The Light of the World was exhibited at the Royal Academy in London. It depicts Jesus Christ standing at a closed door at night, holding a lantern and knocking. He waits for the door to open.
According to a story told about the painting, an art critic examined it closely and asked Hunt:
“It’s a beautiful painting, but there’s something I don’t understand. How is the door supposed to open? Have you perhaps forgotten to paint the handle?”
Hunt smiled and replied:
“This is no ordinary door. It is the door to the human heart. That is why there is no handle on the outside. It opens only from within. Unless the person inside opens it, no one can enter.”
Moral: The door to the heart opens only from within. Love and kindness may knock, but each of us must choose whether to let them in.

title: A prayer finds you
paragraphs: Our elders used to say:
Be a source of support for someone living in poverty, a door that someone in need can knock on, a hand that gently strokes an orphan’s head, a pair of shoes that keeps a child’s feet warm.
Clear a path for someone in difficulty. Help someone struggling, so that the prayer you need may find its own way to you.
Moral: Kindness offered from the heart becomes gratitude in another person’s heart and a prayer on their lips. Sometimes the blessing we wish for ourselves grows out of the compassion we show others.

title: Moderation and honesty
paragraphs: “Those who eat sparingly have no need of a doctor; those who walk an honest path have no need of a judge,” goes a saying.
Its wisdom lies in moderation at the table and integrity in life.

Eating sparingly does not mean going hungry. It means recognizing your body’s needs and eating enough without excess. Walking an honest path means living conscientiously and fairly, without wronging others.
Of course, moderation cannot prevent every illness, and honesty cannot protect us from every injustice. The saying offers guidance, not a guarantee: it asks us to be mindful of our choices.
Moral: Practice moderation in eating and integrity in life. Care for your health and respect the rights of others.

title: My Alif Has Been Dotted
paragraphs: Turkish has an expression, “elifim noktalandı,” which literally means “my alif has been dotted.” It conveys the feeling of sighing in sorrow, of a heart in pain—a poetic way of saying that joy has turned to sadness.

One explanation draws on the shapes of letters in Ottoman script. When the letter alif (ا) is followed by he (ه), they form the word “ah,” a sigh. Beside the tall alif, the small, rounded he is likened to a dot. This resemblance provides the imagery behind the expression.
In this poetic reading, the upright, slender alif suggests beauty and freedom. The curved he beside it seems to carry the weight of sorrow. Together, the two letters become a sigh.
The shapes of the letters thus reflect a change within the heart: where there was joy a moment ago, there is now sadness.
Moral: Sometimes a small change can express a powerful feeling. Language preserves not only our thoughts, but also the traces of our joy and sorrow.

title: Staying on the Right Path
paragraphs: A man lived idly, spending his inheritance without ever working. Eventually, he grew tired of this life and went to the king, asking for guidance on how to live honestly and with purpose.
The king thought for a moment, then said:
“Take this jar, filled to the brim with olive oil, to the other end of the city without spilling a single drop. If you spill even one, you will be beheaded.”
He sent two soldiers to watch over him.
The man focused all his attention on the jar. Taking each step carefully, he reached his destination without spilling a drop. Then he returned to the palace and appeared before the king.
“Your Majesty, I have carried out your command exactly.”
The king asked:
“What did you see in the city? What happened along the way?”
It was market day, and the streets were packed with people. Yet the man replied:

“Your Majesty, my life was at stake. I was so intent on keeping the oil from spilling that I never took my eyes off the jar to look around. I noticed neither the people nor anything that was happening.”
The king said:

“There is the lesson you were seeking. Bring that same care and sense of responsibility to your work and to every duty you undertake. Give your attention to what you do, and remember that God always sees you. Then you will find it easier to stay on the right path.”

Moral: Staying on the right path begins with everyday choices. Care in our work, a sense of responsibility for fulfilling our commitments, and awareness that we are accountable to God help keep us from going astray.

title: A prayer for relief
paragraphs: O God!
By Your names, the Most Merciful and the Ever Compassionate, bring relief to our troubles.
By Your names, the Ever Forgiving and the Accepter of Repentance, forgive our sins and accept our repentance.
By Your name, the Provider, bless our sustenance.
By Your name, the Healer, grant healing to those among us who are ill.
By Your name, the Opener, open doors of goodness for us.
Moral: Sincere prayer expresses both our vulnerability and our hope. Turning to God can bring comfort to the heart and strength to endure hardship.

title: Give to me last
paragraphs: A prayer is said to have been recited among the Turkic peoples:

“O God, bestow Your blessings first upon the mountains and the stones, the forests, the animals, and the waters. Then give to people, to my next-door neighbor, and to those in need. If anything remains, give to me last!”
Moral: Generosity means more than sharing what we have; it also means making room for others in our wishes. This prayer calls us to care about the sustenance and well-being of all living things.

title: Gratitude at the sink
paragraphs: Pray as you wash the dishes. Give thanks that you have dishes to wash. They are a reminder that there was food on your table, that you fed yourself or someone you love, that you cared.
In that moment, remember those who cannot find enough to eat and those who have no one to share a meal with. Make room for them in your prayers.

Moral: Everyday chores can conceal blessings we overlook. Even a dish waiting to be washed can be a reason for gratitude. Thankfulness begins with noticing these blessings; compassion begins with remembering those who lack them.

title: A Ramadan Prayer
paragraphs: May Almighty God accept our prayers, bless our sustenance, grant healing to those among us who are ill, and forgive our sins. May He open doors of goodness for us and fill our hearts with love and compassion!
Wishing you a blessed Eid al-Fitr!

Moral: Heartfelt prayer strengthens hope and awakens compassion. Praying for blessings, healing, and forgiveness for others as well as ourselves draws us closer both to our Creator and to one another.

title: The Sacrificial Meat
paragraphs: I was in fifth grade. We managed well enough and did not depend on anyone’s help. My father, a bricklayer, had joined a housing cooperative. We counted the days, telling ourselves, “In six or seven months, we’ll move into our own home.”

One morning, we woke to violent shaking. An earthquake had struck. Thankfully, neither our family nor anyone nearby was hurt. Everyone in our building was safe. But the earthquake brought a different hardship: construction stopped, and my father lost his job.
However carefully we spent, the money he earned from occasional repair jobs was not enough. All winter, he searched for work. Each morning he left with hope; each evening he returned discouraged.
A few days before Eid al-Fitr, he came home beaming. He had found a job!
“They told me to bring my documents. I have to get there today!”
He gathered his papers and hurried out.
A few hours later, our next-door neighbor rushed in. The look on his face frightened us.
“Don’t panic. Your father has been in an accident…”
At the hospital, my father was terribly pale. His arm and legs were bandaged. A driver had run a red light and hit him.
We were thankful he was alive. He tried to hide his tears.
“If only this hadn’t happened… Now you’ll have to look after me as well.”

After some time, he came home. Our stove was unlit, and the rooms were cold. A few neighbors had called the municipality to ask for coal for us, but they were told we should have registered beforehand.
And so Eid al-Fitr passed, without sweets or gifts.
The weather gradually grew warmer. The bandages came off my father’s arm, but his leg had still not healed.
Then Eid al-Adha arrived.
I felt hopeful. “There are twelve flats in our building. Many of our neighbors will offer an animal for sacrifice. Surely someone will bring us a share. Mom will make one of the meat dishes I love.”

I watched from the window. In the empty lot opposite, the animals were slaughtered and the meat divided. Full basins were carried into the flats. Whenever a door opened, the smell of cooking meat reached our home.
But no one knocked on our door. Not a single portion came our way.
That day, my grandmother called from the village to wish us a happy Eid. She heard something in my voice.
“What is it, sweetheart? Has your father taken a turn for the worse?”
“No,” I said quietly. “The neighbors didn’t give us any meat.”
We used to spend summers with Grandma. She had one cow and five or six hens. The cow gave plenty of milk. Grandma always sang while she milked her.
Early on the third morning of Eid, someone knocked.
It was Grandma.
We ran to welcome her. With tears in her eyes, she hugged us all.
“My little lambs… I’ve brought you lots of meat!”
We filled the fridge. My sister immediately began cutting some up. Soon, the smell rising from the stove was the very smell I had been longing for over the past two days.
I could not wait for the table to be laid. Standing beside the stove, I picked up a piece with a fork. I was blowing on it, lifting it towards my mouth, when I heard my father say:
“Oh, Mom… Why did you have the cow slaughtered?”
My hand froze.
I felt sick and dizzy. I put down the fork and ran outside.
The cow that helped support Grandma. The cow she milked every day while singing… Had she given her up because I had wanted meat?
When the meal was ready, they called me in. I did not want to come, but they insisted that I sit with them.
Ashamed, I picked up a piece. I could not swallow it. Tears rolled down my cheeks.
“What’s wrong, sweetheart?”
“My tooth…” I managed to say. “My tooth really hurts…”

Moral: A celebration becomes complete when its joy is shared. We should notice those in need around us without waiting for them to ask. A small portion offered in time may spare someone else a heartbreaking sacrifice.

title: Stoning the Devil
paragraphs: During the Hajj pilgrimage, when the time comes for the ritual stoning of the devil, a man begins hitting himself with a stone instead of throwing it. A young man nearby asks in astonishment:
“Why are you hitting yourself?”
The man replies:
“My son, before we stone the devil here, shouldn’t we look at the one within us? First, we must learn to master our selfish impulses and cleanse our hearts.”

Moral: One of our hardest struggles is with our own selfish impulses. Spiritual growth means recognizing our faults and changing our behavior, not inflicting pain on ourselves. Look inward before judging others.

title: The Dervish's Appearance
paragraphs: One day, a dervish was asked:
“Why are your clothes so untidy?”
The dervish replied:
“I’ve been so busy tending to my inner life that I haven’t made time to put my clothes in order.”
Moral: Do not judge people by their clothing alone. A neat appearance is worth caring about, but a person’s true worth lies in the goodness of their heart and the way they treat others.

title: The Devil Out of Work
paragraphs: A dervish was deep in thought when he noticed the devil sitting quietly beside him.
“What’s the matter?” he asked. “Why are you sitting so quietly? Aren’t you leading anyone astray?”
The devil wearily raised his head.
“You humans hurt one another so much and cause such suffering that there’s no work left for me.”

Moral: It is in our hands to reduce the suffering people cause one another. Showing understanding instead of causing hurt, speaking up against injustice, and supporting those in difficulty are ways to lessen that suffering.

title: Life’s Finest Blessing
paragraphs: Someone asked a dervish:
“What is the best thing life can bring us?”
The dervish replied:
“Meeting someone who truly wants to listen to you.”
Moral: Someone who willingly listens gives you their time and attention. Being heard with genuine care makes you feel valued and less alone.

title: The Vizier and the Scholar
paragraphs: One day, a scholar from a distant country came to visit a king. After a lengthy conversation through an interpreter, he asked to meet the local scholars for a scholarly debate.
The king gathered the scholars of his realm, but none dared to take on the visitor. Seeing their hesitation, the vizier finally stepped forward.
“I’ll talk to him!”

The gathering began. The visiting scholar drew a circle on the ground and looked at the vizier. After a moment’s thought, the vizier divided it in half. When the scholar said nothing, he drew another line, making four sections. Then he gestured as though taking three for himself and giving the fourth to the scholar. The visitor nodded approvingly.

Next, the scholar held out his hand, palm upwards, and waited for a response. The vizier turned his own hand palm down, with his fingers pointing towards the ground. The scholar seemed pleased with this answer too.

For his third question, the scholar pointed to himself and mimed eating. The vizier immediately took an egg from his pocket and flapped his arms like a bird. Smiling, the scholar kissed the vizier’s hand, and the vizier left the gathering.
Through the interpreter, the king asked the visitor:
“What were you saying to each other with all those gestures? We understood none of it.”
The scholar eagerly explained:

“By drawing the circle, I indicated that the Earth is round and asked what your vizier thought of this. He drew the equator at once! Then he divided the circle into quarters to show that roughly three-quarters of the Earth’s surface is water and the rest is land.”
He paused, then continued:

“Next, I asked how plants sustain themselves. He explained through gestures that they depend on rain and sunlight. Finally, I asked about human beings and animals. By showing me an egg and flapping his arms, he reminded me to include birds as well. A most learned man!”
After the visitor had gone, the king summoned the vizier.
“Now tell me your side. What were you discussing with the scholar?”
The vizier waved a dismissive hand.

“Some scholar! I thought he would be a man of profound ideas. It turns out all he thinks about is food! First, he drew a circle to say, ‘Wouldn’t a pan of eggs be nice right now?’ So I divided it in half to say, ‘You can’t have it all. There’s me to think of too!’”
“And then?” asked the king.

“He said nothing, so I thought he wasn’t happy with half. I divided the eggs into four portions and took three for myself. That would teach him to be greedy! When he saw his share disappearing, he quickly agreed.”
The vizier continued:

“Then he held his palm upwards to ask, ‘How about a pot of pilaf?’ I turned my hand down to say, ‘I’ll have some if there’s meat and sauce on top.’ Finally, he pointed to his stomach: ‘I’ve come a long way, and I’m hungry.’ So I took out my egg to tell him, ‘Believe me, I’m even hungrier than you, and this is the only egg I have. Don’t ask for it—you’re not getting it!’”

Moral: People can interpret the same words and gestures in very different ways. Agreement does not always mean understanding. Before drawing conclusions, make sure you know what the other person means.

title: The Pleasure of Allah
paragraphs: A saying attributed to Khwaja Ubaydullah Ahrar reads:
“I explored the paths that lead to Allah’s pleasure and found that the shortest was to bring joy to people’s hearts.
“I explored the paths that lead away from Allah’s pleasure and found that the most dangerous was to wound another person’s heart.”
Moral: Seek to please Allah by bringing joy to others. Kindness draws us closer to Him; hurting others takes us further away.

title: The Power of Justice
paragraphs: The sword of justice will not bend, nor will the arm that wields it yield.
Moral: Justice draws its strength neither from rank nor from wealth or force. Times may change, but the value of justice endures. Standing up for what is right gives us moral strength.

title: The Price of a Miracle
paragraphs: Lisa was eight when she overheard her parents talking about her little brother, Oliver. All she understood was that he was seriously ill and that her parents could not afford his treatment.
Only a very expensive operation could save him, and there was no one the family could borrow from. Lisa heard her father whisper helplessly to her tearful mother:
“Only a miracle can save him now.”

She went to her room and took out the glass jar she kept hidden in the cupboard. She tipped her savings onto the floor and counted the coins several times. Then she put them back, closed the lid, and slipped out through the back door to the pharmacy.

Inside, she waited for the pharmacist to notice her. But he was so absorbed in conversation that he did not see the little girl. Lisa shuffled her feet and cleared her throat. Finally, she took out a few coins and placed them on the glass counter. Their clatter made him turn.
“What do you need, little girl?” he asked impatiently. “I’m talking to my brother. I haven’t seen him for a long time.”
“I want to talk to you about my brother too,” Lisa said firmly. “He’s ill. I need a miracle to make him better.”
“A miracle?”
“His name is Oliver. There’s something bad growing in his brain. Dad says only a miracle can save him now. How much does a miracle cost?”
The pharmacist’s voice softened.
“We don’t sell miracles here, sweetheart. I’m sorry. I can’t help you.”
“But I have money. If it isn’t enough, I’ll find some more. Just tell me the price.”
The neatly dressed man who had been listening—the pharmacist’s brother—bent down and asked:
“What kind of miracle does your brother need?”
“I don’t know,” Lisa replied. “I just know he’s very ill. Mom and Dad say he needs an operation, but they haven’t got the money. That’s why I brought mine.”
“How much do you have?”
“One dollar and eleven cents,” she said quietly. “That’s all of it. But I can find a little more if I have to.”
The man smiled.
“One dollar and eleven cents… What a lovely coincidence! That’s exactly the price of the miracle your brother needs.”
He took her money, held her hand, and said:
“Take me to your home. I’d like to see your brother and speak to your parents. Let’s see what we can do about that miracle.”
The man was Dr. Carlton Armstrong, a neurosurgeon.
The family was not charged for the operation. Before long, Oliver had recovered and returned home. His parents were overjoyed.
One day, his mother whispered to his father:
“That really was a miracle. I wonder how much the operation would have cost us.”
Lisa smiled. She knew exactly what a miracle cost: one dollar and eleven cents, and an unshakable belief that her brother could be saved.

Moral: Hope moves us to seek help; compassion moves us to offer it. Sometimes, when a child’s innocent faith meets another person’s skill and kindness, a way forward emerges where none seemed possible.

title: Begin with self-examination
paragraphs: A dervish was asked:
“Where does misfortune come from?”
He replied:
“Begin by examining your own actions.
“Consider your eyes—have you looked at what is forbidden?
“Consider your tongue and your ears—have you spoken ill of others or listened to gossip?
“Consider your hands—have you reached for what is not rightfully yours or tainted your livelihood with dishonest gains?
“Consider your steps—have they taken you somewhere you should not have gone?”

Moral: Not every misfortune is caused by our own actions. Yet we are responsible for examining ourselves honestly, recognizing our mistakes and putting them right. Be mindful of what you look at, what you say, how you earn your living and the path you follow.

title: Why wait?
paragraphs: One day, a lecturer at an American university begins the class with a question:
“Imagine that the world will end tomorrow. By this time tomorrow, everything will be over, and there is no way to escape it. How would you spend the time you have left?”
The students answer one by one:
“I would pray and ask God to forgive my sins.”
“I would say goodbye to everyone I love.”
“I would spend the remaining time with my family.”
“I would visit my parents.”
“I would enjoy my favorite foods one last time.”
“I would finally get all the sleep I wanted.”
“I would walk in the woods and enjoy the beauty of nature.”
“I would watch the sunrise and the sunset.”
“I would look at the stars at night.”
“I would cook my favorite meal and gather everyone I love around the table.”
“I would go somewhere I had always dreamed of visiting and spend my final moments there.”
“I would find the people I had hurt, apologize and ask for their forgiveness.”
The lecturer writes every answer on the board, then asks with a smile:
“So why wait until the world is about to end to do these things?”
Moral: Do not leave what matters most until your final day. Express your love, apologize, make time for those you cherish and enjoy life’s simple pleasures today.

title: A Father's Footsteps
paragraphs: A father said to his son:
“Watch your step, son. Be careful where you’re going.”
His son replied:
“You watch your step too, Dad. I’m following in your footsteps.”
Moral: Guiding a child means more than giving advice; it means walking the path yourself. Children learn from your words and take their example from your actions.

title: A Festive Gift
paragraphs: I asked a wise elder:
“What should I buy for the celebrations?”
He smiled.
“Bring joy to someone’s heart. Make the children smile. If you can, ease the burden of someone in need and receive their blessing. Give others a reason to celebrate too.”
Moral: A gift’s worth lies in the thought and care behind it. The joy we share is often the greatest gift of all.

title: A Mother’s Love
paragraphs: I am one—completely happy. My mother is always beside me.
I am two—she is no longer beside me all the time. What has changed?
I am three—my mother is at work, and my nanny is with me.
I am five—my mother is in a meeting, and I am with my grandmother.
I am seven—my mother is at a seminar, and I am at school. My teacher is with me.
I am thirteen—a teenager. My mother still needs to work. I spend more and more time with my friends.
I am seventeen—my mother comes home tired from work. I am either in class or at a café with friends.
I am twenty—young, caught up in life. When my mother is not at home, my friends are there.
I am twenty-three—I have started working. Now my mother is at home, while I am at work.
I am thirty—and I wonder: when did my mother and I last sit down for an unhurried conversation? When did we last enjoy a day together? Somewhere along the way, I have missed something…
I am thirty-five—married. My mother has her home, and I have mine.
I am forty—my mother waits for me to visit, just as I once waited for her to come home.
I am fifty—I, too, am growing older. But one wish has never aged: to embrace my mother, rest my head in her lap, and be a child again beside her.
I am fifty-five—the mother of my children is beside me. My own mother is no longer alive. I live with the ache of missing her.

Amid everyday demands, we sometimes put off spending time with those dearest to us. There is always more work to do. Visits are postponed; conversations are left unfinished. Meanwhile, children grow up and parents grow older.
Life is like a film unfolding before our eyes. But we cannot rewind its scenes or pause a moment and live it again.
Hold your child today. Take their hand and listen. Make time for your parents today. Do not put off spending time together until tomorrow: tomorrow will be a different day.
To paraphrase Erich Fromm’s view in The Art of Loving, motherly love offers unconditional acceptance and shelter; it cannot be forced into existence or obtained by demanding it.
Moral: Love is felt not only in what we hold in our hearts, but in the time and attention we give. Tomorrow cannot bring back the day we could have shared with someone we love.

title: A mother's lasting lesson
paragraphs: An account of the Turkish writer Fakir Baykurt’s childhood tells how he once said to his mother:
“Mom, I’d love some tea. Shall we have a cup?”
His mother agreed and took him to a nearby teahouse run by Hüseyin, who was known for his limp.
“Please bring my boy a glass of tea,” she asked.
When the tea arrived, the boy eagerly picked up the glass and took a large gulp. It burned his mouth, and he dropped the glass. It landed on the dirt floor without breaking.
He looked anxiously at his mother, expecting a slap. Instead, she calmly called the owner and ordered another glass of tea.
This time, the boy blew on his tea and drank it in small sips.
Years passed, but Baykurt never forgot that day. Whenever he asked his mother why she had neither scolded nor slapped him, she left the question unanswered.
He finally received his answer years later, at the village school where he taught.
One day, his mother, Elif, sat in on a lesson. During the class, Baykurt lost his temper, raised his voice, and scolded the children harshly. Afterwards, he asked:
“Well, Mom? Did you like my teaching?”
“What can I say, son? It wasn’t bad.”
Her answer disappointed him.
“School inspectors observe my lessons and give me high marks. And all you can say is ‘It wasn’t bad’?”
His mother turned to him.
“For years, you’ve asked why I didn’t slap you when you spilled that tea. Now I’ll tell you. Listen carefully.”
She paused, then continued:

“If I had lost my temper with you that day, the lion inside you would have lost heart. If I had beaten you, that lion would have died. Perhaps you would never have become the teacher you are today. Be patient, son. Don’t kill the lions inside these children with shouting and blows.”

Moral: The way we respond to a child’s mistake can strengthen or undermine their confidence. Guidance offered with patience and love helps children learn from their mistakes while still believing in their own worth.

title: Father and Son
paragraphs: After a bitter argument with his father, a young man left home. Hurt and angry, his father refused even to hear his son’s name mentioned.
Every night, his mother went into his room, sat on the edge of the bed, and held his pillow close.
“I miss him,” she would say. “Please, let’s find him and bring him home.”
His father stayed silent and refused to discuss it.
Days became weeks, and weeks became months.
One day, unable to bear his wife’s tears any longer, the father took a folded piece of paper from his pocket.
“Go to this address. You’ll find him there. But don’t tell him I gave it to you.”
He added a few more words. She listened carefully, though her thoughts were already with her son.
The address led to a repair workshop. Her son was busy in his work clothes. For a while, she stood in the doorway watching him. Then she called his name, her voice trembling.
He looked up. For a moment, he could not believe his eyes. Then he hurried over and embraced her.
He asked after everyone, leaving his father until last.
“How is he? Is he still angry with me?”
His mother looked into his face.
“Come home, my dear. We miss you so much.”
His expression hardened.
“No, Mom. I don’t want to go back to someone who hasn’t looked for me even once. He’s probably happier without me.”
She handed him the sweets she had brought. Then she said quietly:

“I won’t force you. But there’s something your father asked me to tell you. He said to be careful of the man you’ve become friends with this past month. And he hopes you’ll make peace with your old friend.”
The young man froze.
“Dad… how does he know about that?”
His mother did not answer. She hugged him once more and left.
As soon as she got home, she asked her husband:
“If you knew where he was, why didn’t you tell me? How long have you known?”
His eyes filled with tears.
“Since the day he left. Sometimes I passed the workshop at lunchtime to see whether he was eating, whether he was all right. Some evenings, I went just to catch a glimpse of him before coming home.”
“Then why didn’t you go over and talk to him?”
He lowered his head.
“My pride wouldn’t let me. I thought he should make the first move… But every day, I hoped he would come home. He’s my son.”
Just then, there was a knock at the door.
The mother opened it and found her son standing outside. He came in and stopped in front of his father. For a few moments, neither spoke.
Then his father stepped towards him.
“I should have come and talked to you, son.”
Tears came to the young man’s eyes.
“And the things I said… I’m sorry, Dad.”
They embraced, and his mother joined them.
The hurt between them had not vanished in an instant. But now they were together, ready to begin talking it through.

Moral: Love that is never expressed in words or actions can feel like absence. What matters most is not who makes the first move towards reconciliation, but that someone makes it before more time is lost.

title: A father's advice
paragraphs: My dear son,

Let good judgment guide you through life. Be thoughtful in your dealings with others, measured in your words, and fair in your actions. Wisdom means looking beyond your own advantage and considering the rights of others.
Value your life. Its worth lies not simply in its length, but in how you live it. Make room each day for learning, love, and kindness.

As fruit sweetens with ripening, we mature by learning from what we experience. Listen to those with a wealth of life experience. But remember: wisdom comes not merely from growing older, but from reflecting on what life has taught us.

A thoughtless act in youth can trouble the heart for years. When making a decision, consider not only what you want today, but what will let you live with a clear conscience tomorrow. If you make a mistake, own it, put it right where you can, and learn from it.
The good you sow when you are young may bear fruit in later years. Honesty, diligence, and respect for others can sustain you throughout your life.
Strength is a gift, but it should serve judgment and conscience. Use it to protect and build, not to crush others.

Remember that none of us is here forever. Cherish the life God has given you. Let the thought of mortality deepen your appreciation of today and of the people beside you, rather than turn you away from life.

In my own life, I have tried to keep two simple habits: eating in moderation and staying active. I offer them not as a cure for every ailment, but as part of caring for myself. Pay attention to your body’s needs, and do not neglect them.
Notice, too, how people approach learning.
Some think carefully, ask questions, and consider the consequences of their actions.
Some have not yet found their way, but are willing to listen and learn. Good counsel can help them find direction.
Others neither recognize what they do not know nor listen to anyone else. Believing they know everything, they close the door to learning.
Strive to be thoughtful. Never be ashamed to ask when you do not know. Listen to advice and weigh it carefully. Above all, guard against the belief that you have nothing left to learn.
This is my wish for you: a clear mind, a peaceful conscience, and a heart open to learning.
Moral: Wisdom is not knowing everything, but recognizing what you do not know and being willing to learn. Let judgment guide you, conscience keep you true, and strength serve them both.

title: Stay calm, Arif
paragraphs: A grandfather was shopping with his grandson at the supermarket. As they walked down the aisles, putting groceries into their basket, the boy demanded everything he saw.
“Get me this! I want that too!”
Whenever his grandfather said no, the boy shouted even louder. Each time, the old man said quietly:
“Stay calm, Arif. We’re nearly finished. We’ll be home soon.”
Eventually, the boy grabbed a chocolate egg from a shelf, threw it on the floor, and stamped on it.
His grandfather took a deep breath.
“Stay calm, Arif. Just a little longer, and we’ll be going home.”
Then he turned to a nearby member of staff.
“I’m very sorry. I’ll pay for that too.”
After paying at the checkout, they left the store. A woman who had witnessed the whole scene followed them outside and approached the grandfather.
“I was so impressed by your patience! No matter how much Arif misbehaved, you never once raised your voice.”
The grandfather thanked her and smiled.
“The boy’s name is Rafiq. I’m Arif.”
Moral: Real strength is keeping your composure when things get difficult. Sometimes the first person who needs to hear “stay calm” is you.

title: Hold My Hand
paragraphs: A father and his little daughter were crossing a bridge. Glancing at the river below, he grew a little anxious.
“Sweetheart, hold my hand tightly so you don’t fall.”
The girl looked up at him.
“No, Daddy. You hold mine.”
“What’s the difference?” he asked, puzzled.
“There’s a big difference! If I’m holding your hand, I might let go when I get scared. But if you’re holding mine, I know you won’t let go, no matter what.”
Moral: Trust means knowing that someone will hold on when you are afraid. Don’t wait for those you love to ask for help. Be there when they need you, and reach for their hand.

title: I’m Tired, Mom
paragraphs: “I’m tired, Mom.”
“Of what, son?”
“Everything. Work, friends, going out, trying to please everyone. I’m exhausted.”
“Rest your head in my lap, son. Let it all go for a moment. Let me share your pain.”
“Thank you, Mom. I’m so glad you’re here. With you, I forget how old I am and everything I’ve been through. May you have many more years ahead of you.”
“A mother gives you life, son. I’ll always be here for you.”
“Mom, we wear you out too. Forgive us.”
“You don’t wear me out. I’m tired because I no longer have a mother of my own. I have no mother’s lap to rest my head in. Don’t wear yourself out, son. Cherish what you have.”
Moral: A mother’s embrace is the most comforting refuge in the world. Whoever has a mother has a place to rest and lay down their burdens. Cherish what you have.

title: Mother and Son
paragraphs: The man set the suitcases against the wall, straightened up, and took a deep breath.
“Mom, this really is a lovely place.”
“Of course it is, son,” the elderly woman replied.
For a while, they stood in silence, looking around the room.
She opened her small suitcase and took out her nightdress, slippers, a few towels, and a framed photograph. She placed the photograph on the bedside table.
It showed a boy in school uniform, standing stiffly at attention. His eyes were full of tears, his lips drawn into a trembling pout.

The man went to the window and pulled back the curtain. Pale daylight entered the room. It was freezing outside. He rested his hands on the radiator and watched mud-spattered cars passing along the street.
“Will this wardrobe be big enough for you, Mom?” he asked without turning around.
She did not hear him. Sitting on the bed, leaning slightly to one side, she was gazing at the frightened child in the worn frame.
The photograph had been taken on his first day of school.

The memory returned as vividly as if it were yesterday. The evening before, she had spent hours telling him what a wonderful place school was. Yet the next morning, she had barely managed to get him into the classroom. She had stayed at school all day, going to him at every break.
“I’m here, son. I’m waiting for you.”
But each time, he had gripped her hand more tightly and cried:
“Don’t leave me, Mom. I’m so scared.”
The sun was setting. The man took his hands off the radiator and rested them against the misted window.
“Open the other suitcase too, Mom. Let’s put your things away.”
“Don’t let me keep you, son. I can do it myself. There isn’t much, anyway.”
She reached out with trembling hands and took his hand. For a moment, she seemed about to say something. Then she changed her mind. She swallowed.
“The children will be wondering where you are.”
The door creaked shut.

The elderly woman was left alone in the room with its peeling paint and the frightened little boy in the photograph. She sat on the edge of the bed for a while, then put on her slippers and went to the window.
Her son was getting into his car.
She was frightened. The day before, she had listened for hours to how lovely this place was. But she was still frightened.
His handprint remained on the glass. Gently, she rested her cheek against it. Her eyes filled with tears, and her lips began to tremble.
“Don’t leave me, son. I’m so scared,” she whispered.
Her words faded against the misted glass. Outside, her son sat in his car and waved.
That night, the other residents on her floor heard her sobbing. Such sounds were not unfamiliar in the corridors of the care home.

Moral: Growing older does not lessen our need for love and closeness. Caring for a parent means more than providing comfort and meeting daily needs; it also means helping them feel remembered and less alone.

title: Only My Mother Truly Weeps
paragraphs: Only my mother’s tears are true; all the rest are just for show!
Moral: These words express the depth of a mother’s love. Her ability to feel her child’s pain as her own is one of the most tender expressions of that selfless love.

title: Raising a Child
paragraphs: A boy often defied his parents. Whatever they told him to do, he did the opposite. Things were not going well at school either: he showed little interest in lessons and left his homework unfinished.
His mother hit him in anger, while his father shut him in his room as punishment. Neither approach made things better.

One day, as his mother was taking him to school, they came across a man performing with a bear. A crowd had gathered around them. The man played a tambourine, and the bear, with a ring through its nose, jumped and danced in response to his movements.
The woman stopped and thought, “I can’t manage one child, yet this man can make even a bear obey!”
She approached him.
“My son won’t listen to me. How did you train this animal?”
The man smiled.
“There’s a way to do everything. I have my own methods.”
“Could you help me too?”
The bear handler looked at the boy.
“Bring him to me for a week. I’ll teach him to do as he’s told.”
Delighted, the woman began taking her son to the man every day.

Within a few days, the boy changed. He no longer argued with his mother and quietly did what she asked. By the end of the week, she thought her problem was solved. She thanked the man and blessed him.
The neighbors were astonished. The once unruly boy now seemed quiet and obedient. His teacher was pleased too and congratulated his mother.
Before long, however, other problems emerged. The boy no longer rebelled openly, but he began secretly taking his classmates’ belongings, covering up what he had done, and lying.
His teacher called his mother.
“I’m concerned about some changes in your son’s behavior. He takes other children’s things and then denies it. We need to understand why.”
Distraught, the woman went looking for the bear handler. But he had already moved on.
Seeing the parents’ distress, an experienced neighbor said:
“I know a kind, wise man. Go and speak to him. Perhaps he can help you find a way forward.”
The mother took her son to see him and explained what had happened. The wise man said:
“Let me meet your son a few times over the coming week. I’d like to get to know him and understand what he has been through.”
After their second meeting, he asked to speak to the mother. He looked deeply concerned.
