“Your son is afraid to admit when he has done something wrong. He believes that telling the truth will always lead to punishment. How have you been treating him?”
She described the punishments at home and then told him about the bear handler.
The wise man sighed.

“You wanted to change your child’s behavior, but you did not try to understand his feelings. Fear can silence a child for a while. But silence is not understanding, and obedience is not the same as learning right from wrong. A child who fears punishment may try to hide a mistake instead of putting it right.”
He paused, then continued:

“Raising a child means building trust, not breaking their will. Listen to your son, make time for him, and show him your love. Explain the rules clearly and follow them yourself. When he makes a mistake, help him understand its consequences and make amends without humiliating him.”
He concluded:
“I can offer guidance, but I cannot change your relationship at home for you. Change begins when your child feels safe, loved, and heard in your company.”

Moral: The aim of raising a child is to nurture understanding of right and wrong, rather than silence born of fear. Love, trust, clear boundaries, and a parent’s own example are the foundations of that process.

title: Puppies for Sale
paragraphs: A little boy saw a sign in a shop window that read “Puppies for Sale” and went inside.
“How much are the puppies?” he asked.
“Between thirty and fifty dollars,” the shopkeeper replied. “Each one has a different price.”
The boy took all the money from his pocket, placed it on the counter, and counted it carefully.
“I only have thirteen dollars and twenty-seven cents,” he said, disappointed. Then he asked hopefully:
“Could I at least look at them?”
The shopkeeper smiled and called to his wife in the back room. A moment later, she appeared with five adorable, plump puppies following her. One lagged behind, struggling to walk.
The boy could not take his eyes off it.
“What’s wrong with its leg?”
“The vet says it was born with a problem in one of its leg bones. It will always have difficulty walking.”
The boy immediately said:
“That’s the one I want!”
The shopkeeper looked surprised.
“I wouldn’t have expected you to choose that one. If you want it, you can have it for free.”
The boy’s expression changed. Looking straight at the shopkeeper, he said firmly:

“I don’t want you to give it to me for free. It’s worth just as much as the other puppies. I’ll give you thirteen dollars and twenty-seven cents now, then pay five dollars a week until I’ve paid the full thirty.”
The shopkeeper tried again to change his mind.
“But it won’t be able to run and play with you like the others.”
“It deserves a chance too. It’s just as valuable as the rest,” the boy replied.
Then he bent down and lifted his trouser leg. His leg, weakened by polio, was supported by metal braces.
He looked at the shopkeeper and said quietly:
“I can’t run and play either. This puppy and I both need a friend who understands us and gives us support.”
Moral: A living being’s worth is not measured by what it can or cannot do. True friendship means understanding and supporting one another, rather than turning away because of differences.

title: The Rotten Seed
paragraphs: After his wife died, a father refused to care for his young son, who was often ill. He dismissed the boy as a “rotten seed” and eventually placed him in a children’s home.
Years passed.
One day, the father saw his grown son outside a school. He could hardly believe his eyes. Before him stood a strong, healthy young man with bright, lively eyes.
Looking at him with regret, he exclaimed:
“I never thought you would recover and grow so strong. Look at you now! How did this happen? How did you overcome all those illnesses?”
The young man’s eyes filled with tears. He looked at the father who had once rejected him, then pointed to an elderly woman approaching them with a smile.

“After you said, ‘A rotten seed will never sprout,’ and left me at the children’s home, this woman adopted me. She said, ‘A seed watered with love deserves a chance to grow.’ She never withheld her love or care from me.”
Moral: A child’s worth is not measured by their health. Cruel words can crush hope, while love and steady care can help a child discover their strength. No child is a “rotten seed.”

title: Spinach
paragraphs: We lived in a remote village without even a proper road. My mother seemed to cook nothing but spinach. In my childish mind, I wondered whether my father’s death had left her unable to think clearly.
“Eat plenty. It will make you strong,” she would say.
Morning, noon, and night, there was spinach and cornbread on our table. I grew so tired of spinach that I could hardly bear to look at it.
One day, I told her:
“When I grow up, get a job, and have a family, I’ll never buy spinach. Nobody will cook it in my house!”
My mother smiled. She said she could hardly wait for that day and promised that, however old she was, she would dance at my wedding.

Eventually, I left the village to continue my secondary education in town. I scraped by on a small scholarship. When I came home once a month, I would not touch the spinach my mother served. I dreamed of returning to the dormitory and eating something different, something tastier.
I kept studying. With a government student loan, I completed university, then a master’s degree and a doctorate. By then, my mother had grown old, and her back was bent.

My fiancée and I returned to the village for our wedding. That day, my mother cried—and danced, just as she had promised all those years before. At the time, I did not understand why tears ran down her face as she danced.
The years passed. My mother died two years ago.
One day, in her old chest, I found a diary she had kept. On one page, she had written:
“All I had left was some spinach seed. I grew spinach and a little maize. We had next to nothing. I cooked the same meal over and over so my children would not go hungry. But I did not complain.
“‘Spinach is very good for you. That’s why I give it to you three times a day,’ I would tell them, and my heart would ache. It was all I could do for them. I love my children more than my own life.”
I learned to love spinach at fifty.
Now my wife often wonders why I buy it so frequently. She thinks I love the taste.
She does not know that whenever I smell it cooking, I remember everything my mother endured to raise us—and the way she danced at my wedding with tears streaming down her face.
Moral: Sometimes a meal we grew tired of as children concealed a mother’s poverty and quiet sacrifice. We should not have to wait years to recognize the love behind it.

title: Teeth falling out
paragraphs: A king dreamed that all his teeth had fallen out. In the morning, he summoned a dream interpreter.
“What does this dream mean?” he asked.
“Your Majesty, all your loved ones will die before you. You alone will remain.”
The king was shaken by these words. Then, in anger, he sent the interpreter away.
He summoned another interpreter and described the same dream.
The second interpreter replied:
“Your Majesty, the dream can be understood this way: you will live longer than anyone else in your family.”
The king’s face brightened. He rewarded the interpreter and sent him on his way.
The two interpretations meant the same thing. But one drew the king’s attention to loss, while the other focused on a long life.
Moral: The impact of words depends not only on their meaning, but also on how they are spoken. Wisdom includes telling the truth with consideration for the listener’s feelings.

title: The Most Beautiful Gift
paragraphs: Moral: The most beautiful gifts cannot always be bought. Respect, love, compassion, and loyalty nurture our relationships; the good we do for others gives meaning to our lives.

title: The Nest Builder
paragraphs: “The female bird builds the nest,” says a proverb. It honors the care and effort a woman brings to family life, turning a house into a home. Appreciating that work means more than saying thank you: it means sharing the care and responsibility.
Moral: Recognize and value a woman’s contribution to her family. A home grows stronger through mutual love, respect, and shared effort.

title: The nail's lesson
paragraphs: In a village there lived a boy who was very quick-tempered and impatient. Even the slightest remark would make him angry, and when he lost his temper, he did not hesitate to hurt the person in front of him.
His father was deeply concerned about this side of his son's character. One day, he gave him a bag of nails and said:
‘My son, whenever you get angry with someone and say something hurtful, hammer one of these nails into the fence around the yard.’

At first, the boy thought this was pointless. But the next day he became angry and hammered a nail into the fence. Then he lost his temper again and hammered in another. As the days passed, the number of nails in the fence began to grow.
After a while, the boy began to pay attention to his behavior. Reaching for a nail every time he became angry made him think. At last, one day he went to his father and said:
‘Father, I will try not to lose my temper anymore.’
His father smiled and replied:
‘Very good. Now, for every day that you control yourself and hurt no one, pull one nail out of the fence.’
The boy did as he was told. Days passed, then months, and at last all the nails had been removed from the fence.
The boy called out joyfully to his father:
‘Father, look! I have pulled out all the nails.’
His father took him over to the fence and said quietly:

‘You have removed all the nails. But look: the marks they left are still there. The same thing happens when you get angry and lash out at someone with your words. You may apologize afterward, you may feel sorry, and that person may even forgive you. But a wound in the heart does not always heal without a scar.’
The boy looked at the holes in the fence for a long time.
From that day on, when he became angry, he learned first to remain silent and then to think.
Moral: A word spoken is like a nail: it is driven in during a moment of anger, but its mark may remain for a long time. That is why we must think before speaking and pause before causing hurt.
Etibar Siracsoy

title: An hour with Dad
paragraphs: One evening, a little boy approached his father.
“Dad, can I ask you something?”
“Of course, son.”
“How much do you earn in an hour?”
His father frowned.
“Why do you want to know?”
“I’m just curious. Please tell me, Dad.”
At last, his father answered:
“I earn a hundred dollars an hour.”
The boy lowered his head and fell silent for a moment. Then he asked hesitantly:
“Could you lend me fifty dollars?”
His father grew angry.
“So that’s why you asked! You probably want another toy you don’t need. I don’t work all day for that. Go to your room and get to bed!”
Without a word, the boy went to his room and quietly closed the door.
His father paced for a while. As his anger faded, he realized he had never asked what his son wanted the money for. Perhaps it was something important to him.
Feeling ashamed, he went to the boy’s room and knocked softly.
“Are you asleep, son?”
“No, Dad. I’m awake.”
His father came in and sat beside him.
“I’m sorry I snapped at you earlier. I had a difficult day and took it out on you. Here are the fifty dollars you asked for.”
The boy thanked him happily. Then he pulled his savings from beneath his pillow and began to count them.
Seeing the money, his father grew angry again.
“If you already had money, why did you ask me for more?”
The boy gathered the notes and looked up at him.
“Because I didn’t have enough. Now I have exactly a hundred dollars. Dad, can I buy an hour of your time? Please come home early tomorrow so we can have dinner together.”
His father’s eyes filled with tears. He held his son close and apologized once more.
Moral: Caring for your family means more than earning money. Children need your love, your attention, and time with you—things no gift can replace.

title: Waiting for the teeth
paragraphs: On a cold winter evening, an elderly couple walked into McDonald’s and sat down. The husband went to the counter and ordered a hamburger, a large portion of fries, and a large Coke.
Back at the table, he cut the hamburger in half and placed one half in front of his wife. He counted out the fries, dividing them equally. Then he took a sip of Coke and passed it to her.
People nearby watched sympathetically. “They must be short of money,” they thought. “They’re sharing a meal for one.”
The husband began eating with a healthy appetite. His wife left her food untouched, watching him and occasionally taking a sip of Coke.
A young employee noticed and approached their table.
“Excuse me, sir. I couldn’t help noticing that your wife hasn’t touched her food. Would she prefer something else? I’d be happy to bring it.”
The man smiled.
“Thank you, son, but we’re quite all right. We’ve been married for sixty years. We share everything.”
Still puzzled, the employee turned to the wife.
“Then what are you waiting for, ma’am?”
She nodded toward her husband and replied calmly:
“The teeth, dear. I’m waiting for the teeth!”
Moral: Everyone has their own way of living, and every family has its own habits. What seems unusual to us may be an ordinary part of someone else’s daily life.

title: Weeds
paragraphs: When we were schoolchildren, we spent the summer holidays with our family in our garden. My late father wanted to teach us the value of hard work, so he left us chores to do while he was at work. We watered the melons he had planted. We carried drinking water from the well in our neighbor Uncle Aghasalim’s garden, since the water in our own well was unfit to drink.
We learned to turn the soil and pull up weeds, but some were difficult to remove. One day, Father explained, “You must dig deeper. Until you remove the roots, the job isn’t finished.”
Moral: Deal with the roots of problems and bad habits. Removing only what is visible above the surface will not keep them from returning.
Bakhtiyar Sirajov

title: Those Who Give Love Receive Love
paragraphs: An old story set in China tells of a young woman named Li-Li who married and moved into a home with her husband and his mother.

Before long, tensions arose between the two women. Their temperaments were very different. A remark that seemed harmless to one would hurt the other, and even small matters turned into arguments. The strain wore down both Li-Li and her husband, who felt caught between two people he loved.

One day, Li-Li visited an old friend of her father’s, a man who prepared herbal remedies. She poured out her troubles, then said bitterly:
“I can’t bear it anymore. I want to be rid of her for good.”

The old man listened and brought her a container of herbs. He told her it was a slow-acting poison. Then he added:
“But there is one condition: you must treat your mother-in-law kindly. Don’t interrupt her or argue with everything she says. Take care of her, so no one notices any hostility between you.”
Li-Li returned home and began adding the mixture to her mother-in-law’s food. She cooked her favorite meals, asked how she was feeling, and listened instead of starting arguments.

At first, she did this only to avoid suspicion. But gradually, she began to notice things about her mother-in-law that she had never seen before. Sometimes there was worry behind her sharp words, and concern behind her criticism.

Her mother-in-law was changing, too. She responded to Li-Li’s kindness with warmth and began treating her like her own daughter. Arguments gave way to quiet conversations, and resentment slowly softened into affection.
One day, Li-Li looked at her mother-in-law and realized she was afraid of losing her.

She hurried back to the old man.
“Please help me! Give me something to save her. I love her. I don’t want anything to happen to her!”
“Don’t be afraid, Li-Li,” he said gently. “The mixture I gave you wasn’t poison. You haven’t poisoned her.”
Li-Li stared at him in astonishment.

“What was poisoning your relationship was the resentment that had built up between you,” he continued. “By changing the way you treated her, you gave yourselves a chance to know and understand each other. At first, kindness was something you chose to practice. Then it became something you truly felt.”
Li-Li’s eyes filled with tears. She could hardly wait to go home and embrace her mother-in-law.

Moral: Resentment can keep us from seeing the good in another person. Listening, understanding, and showing care can open the way to change. Genuine closeness grows where both people treat each other with respect.

catalog_metadata.title: Those Who Give Love Receive Love

title: Before you marry
paragraphs: A young couple preparing to marry received this advice from their elders:

“Don’t compare your marriage with anyone else’s. Don’t say, ‘Look at her husband…’ or ‘Look at his wife…’ From the outside, you can never know what life is really like in someone else’s home. Build your own life together.

“Don’t expect perfection from each other. Everyone has flaws. Learn which differences you can accept with understanding and which problems you need to work on together. Don’t bring up past mistakes every time you argue.
“Don’t expect your partner to read your mind. Speak openly and calmly about your wishes, worries, and hurt feelings. Listen to understand, not just to reply.

“Sharing a life doesn’t mean losing your individuality. You will each have your own thoughts, interests, and need for time alone. Even hedgehogs must find a way to keep each other warm without hurting each other with their spines. Stay close, but give each other room to breathe.

“Neither of you should rule over the other or be expected to obey without question. Be companions who walk through life side by side. Make decisions together, share responsibilities, and respect each other’s right to an opinion.
“Don’t promise, ‘Everything will always be wonderful.’ Instead, say, ‘When things get difficult, you won’t have to face them alone.’

“Even when you’re upset with each other, remember to say goodnight. Not every disagreement can be resolved in one evening, but you can still show kindness while you work through it. Let a new day bring another chance to listen and make peace.”
Moral: A strong marriage is built by two people who know how to listen, understand, and speak with care—not by two perfect people. Sharing a home means supporting each other, not owning each other.

title: Keep your hearts close
paragraphs: Why do we raise our voices during an argument when the person beside us can already hear us?

One way to picture it is this: as hurt grows, so does the distance between our hearts. We raise our voices as though we could shout across that distance. Yet shouting often makes it harder, not easier, to hear one another.

Where there is love and trust, a quiet word can be enough. Sometimes a whisper, a glance, or a hand resting on another’s hand says more than a long speech. When we feel heard and understood, there is less need to raise our voices.
Closeness does not mean never disagreeing. It means treating each other with care even when we disagree.

So when anger rises, pause. Say what you need to say without belittling the other person. Explain your hurt without trying to hurt them in return. If you cannot speak calmly, take a break and return to the conversation later.
Let the argument end—not the bond between you.
Moral: Aim to understand each other, not to silence each other. Choose words that leave a way back to closeness once the anger has passed.

title: Early Marriage
paragraphs: I had just graduated from university and started teaching at a school. One day, I was in the teachers’ lounge marking exam papers. I was erasing and correcting some of the girls’ wrong answers so they could move up to the next class.
A man I did not recognize entered the room. After watching me for a moment, he asked:
“Why are you changing the girls’ answers?”
I put down my pen.

“If some of these girls fail, their fathers will take them out of school and marry them off at twelve or thirteen. If they pass, they may get a few more years of education. In that time, they could learn, gain confidence, and perhaps find a different path for their lives.”
The man was silent for a while. Then he said goodbye and left.
About half an hour later, the principal called me into his office.
“You spoke to someone in the teachers’ lounge. What did you tell him?”
I grew anxious.
“Did he complain about me?”
“No. He had come to inspect the school.”
My heart sank. The principal continued:
“He said there was a young teacher here who cared about the children’s futures. He asked me to pass on his thanks.”

I breathed a sigh of relief. Yet my unease remained. Changing a few answers would not be enough to protect those girls’ futures. Their right to stay in school should never depend on an exam mark—or a teacher secretly altering it.

Moral: A teacher’s care can change a child’s life. But no girl should have to rely on such a chance to protect her childhood and education. We all share a responsibility to oppose child marriage and support girls in learning and shaping their own futures.

title: Friendship and Love
paragraphs: Write your quarrels on leaves, so that autumn may carry them away and take the hurt with them.
Write your anger on clouds, so that it may fall with the rain and your heart may clear with the sky.
Write your hatred on snow, so that it may melt when the sun returns.
But write friendship and love in children’s hearts—through kind words, care, and the example you set. As the children grow, let that love grow with them and find its way into other hearts.
Moral: Nurture love rather than resentment. The kindness we plant in others can live on long after us.

title: I Kiss Your Eyes
paragraphs: Do you know why people say, “I kiss your eyes”?
Because the eyes bear so much of the pain of longing: they watch and wait, shed tears, and search for a loved one. Perhaps that is why they deserve the joy of reunion most of all.
Moral: Our eyes hold the longing we cannot put into words. To kiss a loved one’s eyes is to offer tenderness to the ache of missing someone.

title: I Love You
paragraphs: The story goes that a nightingale fell in love with a white rose. Every night, he perched on her branch and sang of his love. But the rose remained indifferent, offering no answer to his songs.
One day, the nightingale gathered his courage and opened his heart once more.
“I love you with all my heart.”
The rose answered sharply:
“Leave me alone. I don’t love you.”
However much he pleaded, her answer did not change.
Overwhelmed by the pain of rejection, the nightingale saw no way forward and took his own life. According to the legend, his blood turned the white rose’s petals red.
Only after losing him did the rose understand the depth of his love. But it was too late. The song she had heard every night had fallen silent forever.
And so, the tale says, the red rose came to mean “I love you.”

Moral: Unrequited love can hurt deeply, but it does not diminish a person’s worth. Love should never have to be proved through self-destruction. Being gentle with another person’s feelings matters, as does respecting their choices and valuing your own life.

title: Loving from Afar
paragraphs: Two friends meet and start talking.
“I think I’ve fallen for someone.”
“That’s wonderful! Does she know?”
“No.”
“Then why don’t you tell her?”

“I would, but I’m afraid of disturbing my peaceful life. I’d only be asking for trouble. We’d start going to the cinema and the theater, walking hand in hand. Then would come the arguments and the making up: ‘Why were you looking at her?’ ‘Why did you smile at that woman?’ If we’re going to break up in the end, why put ourselves through all that?”
He pauses, then adds:
“I’d rather just love her from afar.”
Moral: Sometimes we fear the end of a love that has not even begun. In trying to protect ourselves from a possible separation, we may also deny ourselves the chance of closeness and joy.

title: The Purple Jacket
paragraphs: A tale about the Yörük communities tells of a purple jacket placed among a bride’s belongings. This short traditional garment was kept at the very bottom of her dowry chest, with the hope that she would never need to wear it.
For the purple jacket was no ordinary piece of clothing. It was a call for help.
When a woman put it on and stood on a rooftop, in the village square, or somewhere everyone could see her, her message was:
“I am suffering in this marriage. I was married against my will, or my husband is mistreating me. I want to leave. Help me!”

In the tale, that call never went unanswered. The villagers would gather around the woman, defend her, and demand an explanation from her husband. The shame lay not in her asking for help, but in his having driven her to that point.

At the sight of the purple jacket, everyday life seemed to stop. People busy milking cows, spinning wool, or weaving rugs would set their work aside. Mothers and grandmothers would leave everything and hurry to her.
If a wedding was taking place, the music would fall silent and the celebrations would pause. One woman’s distress became the concern of the whole community.

A man who had abused his wife would be ashamed to appear in public. Even at the teahouse, no one would meet his gaze. He could not stand in the way of her wish to leave, and if he sought to marry again, few would trust him.
In this tale, the purple jacket is a promise that a woman will not be left alone: “We will hear you. We will stand beside you.”

Moral: There is no shame in asking for help when facing abuse. The shame lies in inflicting it or turning a blind eye. Solidarity begins with hearing a woman’s voice, protecting her safety, and respecting her decisions.

title: The Flower
paragraphs: Water a flower too much, and it rots. Too little, and it withers. Give it the water it needs, and it grows and blooms.
Moral: In love and in raising children, care should respond to the needs of the person receiving it. Neither smothering nor neglect helps them flourish; thoughtful care gives them room to grow.

title: Five more minutes
paragraphs: On a sunny day in the park, a woman pointed out a child on the swings to the man sitting beside her.
“The boy in the red shirt is my son.”
The man smiled.
“And the one in blue is my son, Jamil.”
A little later, he checked his watch and called out:
“Jamil, time to go home.”
“Five more minutes, Dad. Please!”
His father agreed. After a while, he called again. Jamil asked for another five minutes, and his father smiled and nodded.
“You’re a very patient father,” the woman said admiringly.
A sad smile crossed his face.

“It’s more than patience,” he said. “Last year, my older son, Kamal, was killed by a drunk driver on a road near here. I never spent enough time with him. I always thought we had plenty of time ahead of us. Now I’d give anything for just five more minutes with him. I’ve promised myself I won’t make the same mistake with Jamil.”
He fell silent for a moment and watched his son.
“He thinks he’s getting five more minutes to play. But those five minutes are a gift to me, too—a chance to watch him, hear him laugh, and be here with him.”
Moral: Make time for the people you love today. Five ordinary minutes together may be one of life’s most precious gifts.

title: An Eraser for Marriage
paragraphs: One day, a father asked his newly married son to bring him a sheet of white paper, a pencil and an eraser.
“What for, Dad?” his son asked.
“Bring them, and you’ll see.”
The son brought the paper and pencil but could not find an eraser.
“Go and buy one, then,” his father said.
Puzzled, the son did as he was asked and sat down beside him.
“Write something,” his father said.
“What should I write?”
“Whatever comes to mind.”
The son wrote a sentence.
“Now erase it.”
He rubbed it out.
“Write another sentence.”
“Dad, what are you trying to do?”
“Be patient. Write something else.”
The son wrote, and his father asked him to erase it again. After they had done this several times, his father asked:
“Is any of your writing still on the paper?”
“No, Dad. I’ve erased it all. But what does this mean?”
His father rested a hand on his shoulder.

“Son, you need an eraser like this in marriage too. You must learn to forgive your wife’s small mistakes instead of holding on to every hurt. She needs one too, so she can show the same understanding towards you. Otherwise, the pages of your married life will soon be filled with grievances.”
Then he added:
“If you want love and respect, you must both give them freely. When you make a mistake, remember to apologize, put it right and forgive each other. You must each have an eraser.”

Moral: Love and respect in marriage depend not only on forgiving mistakes, but also on recognizing and correcting your own. Mutual understanding keeps small hurts from growing into lasting resentment.

title: The Mother-of-Pearl Flower
paragraphs: A court was hearing the divorce case of a couple in their eighties. Everyone in the courtroom was saddened that two people who had shared fifty years of marriage now wanted to part.
The judge looked at the woman, whose eyes were sunken from crying, and gently asked:
“Tell me, why do you want a divorce?”
She took a deep breath.
“This man has worn me out. I’ve felt alone for fifty years…”
She fell silent. Only the click of a camera broke the stillness. The journalists following the case waited for her to continue.

“I have a mother-of-pearl flower that I cherish,” she said, wiping her eyes. “Fifty years ago, I grew it from a cutting taken from flowers he had brought me. We never had children. I cared for that plant as though it were my child.

“After a while, it began to wilt. My husband told me that if I got up at night to water it, it would recover. So I promised I would. For fifty years, I’ve got up every night to look after it. Not once did he say, ‘You sleep. I’ll take care of it tonight.’”
Her voice trembled.

“The other night, I was exhausted and didn’t wake up. He didn’t wake me either. In the morning, I found that the plant hadn’t been watered. It may seem a small thing to you. But to me, it felt as though nothing I had cherished in fifty years had ever mattered to him.”
The judge turned to her husband.
“Is there anything you would like to say?”
The old man rose, leaning on his walking stick.
“I worked as a gardener during my military service. That was when I met Fatima. I used to make bouquets for her from the loveliest flowers.”
He glanced at his wife, then continued:

“We were newly married when she began having neck pain. I took her to a doctor. As I remember it, he told her not to stay still for too long, but to get up and walk around occasionally. Fatima wouldn’t take care of herself, and I worried about her.

“Then the plant began to wilt. I told her it would recover if she got up at night to water it. I hoped that, if nothing else, the plant would persuade her to get up and move a little. She gave me her word.”
His voice faltered.

“Every night, I woke her and watched how tenderly she cared for it. She was protecting her plant, and I thought I was protecting her. Once she had gone back to bed, I would empty the excess water from the saucer beneath the pot so the roots wouldn’t rot.”
He paused.
“The other night, I didn’t wake up either. We’ve grown old… When I saw how hurt she was in the morning, I didn’t know what to say. I had kept silent for fifty years, and I stayed silent again.”
No one spoke. Even the journalists had tears in their eyes.
After so many years under the same roof, two people were hearing, for the first time, what lay behind each other’s silence.
Moral: Quiet care may come from love, yet remain unseen when it is never spoken of. Love means caring, but also listening, sharing our feelings, and trying to understand one another.

title: The Red Dress
paragraphs: The red dress hung in my mother’s wardrobe. Among the faded, worn clothes she had worn for years, it seemed to glow.
I had come to visit her. The moment I saw her, I knew she was nearing the end of her life.
Looking at the dress, I said:
“Mom, what a beautiful dress! I’ve never seen you wear it.”
“I never have, sweetheart,” she answered softly. “Come and sit beside me. There’s something I want to tell you before I go.”
I sat on the edge of her bed. She drew a deep breath.
“I don’t have much time left. I always thought I was setting you a good example. Now I realize that some of the lessons I taught you were wrong.”
“What do you mean, Mom?”

“Listen, darling. All my life, I believed a good woman should put herself last. Everyone else’s wishes had to come first. Mine were buried beneath theirs. I thought my turn would come one day. But that day never came. My life was spent making sacrifices for your father, your brothers and sisters, and you.”
“You did everything a mother could do for us.”

“I don’t regret loving you or caring for you. But I should have cared for myself too. I never learned to ask for anything for myself. Your father is sitting in the next room now, staring angrily at the walls. When the doctor told him I was dying, he came in and said, ‘You can’t die! Do you hear me? What am I supposed to do without you?’”
She paused to catch her breath, then continued:

“I worked for you seven days a week. I was always the first awake and the last to bed. I took the burnt toast and the smallest portions. Every penny I saved went on your clothes and books, sometimes even when you didn’t need them. I never bought myself something beautiful simply because I liked it.”
Her eyes turned towards the red dress.

“Last year, for once, I bought that dress for myself. I had a little money put aside to repair the washing machine. When I brought the dress home, your father said, ‘Where are you going to wear that? To the opera?’”
Her voice trembled.
“And I thought he was right. As though I needed a special reason to wear something beautiful. Apart from trying it on in the shop, I never wore it.”
She fell silent for a moment.

“I used to think that if I forgot myself in this world, I would find happiness in the next. I think differently now. I want to believe that God wants us to love the life He has given us and make room for our dreams while we are still alive. If a miracle happened and I could get out of this bed, I would live differently.”
Then she took my hand.
“Don’t forget yourself the way I did, darling. Promise me.”
I promised.
Those were her last words to me. A little later, she took her final breath.
Moral: Caring for the people you love does not mean giving up on yourself. Make room for their dreams, but keep your own alive too. Your life, your joy, and your needs matter as well.

title: True Love
paragraphs: Once upon a time, all the feelings lived on an island.
One day, word spread that the island was sinking. Everyone hurried to prepare their boats and leave.

Only Love lingered. As though trusting that a miracle would save the island, Love waited until the very last moment. But when water surrounded everything, there was no choice left but to ask for help.
Just then, Wealth passed by in a large boat.
“Wealth, will you take me with you?” Love called.
“I can’t. My boat is full of gold and silver. There’s no room for you.”
Love turned to Pride, who was sailing away in a beautiful sailboat.
“Pride, please help me!”
“I can’t take you aboard. You’re soaking wet. You’ll spoil my boat.”
Sorrow was passing nearby.
“Sorrow, may I come with you?”
“Oh, Love, I’m so sad… I need to be alone.”
Happiness was not far away either, but was so absorbed in joy that Love’s cries went unheard.
Suddenly, a voice called out:
“Come, Love. I’ll take you!”
Love was so relieved that asking the rescuer’s name never crossed their mind. Upon reaching the shore, the rescuer dropped Love off and continued on.
Only then did Love realize how much was owed to this stranger. Meeting a wise elder, Love told the story and asked:
“Who was it that saved me?”
“Time,” the elder replied.
“Time? Why was Time the one to help me?”
The elder smiled.
“Because only Time knows the true value of Love.”
Moral: The worth of true love reveals itself over time. Love is sustained not merely by beautiful words, but by years of care, faithfulness, and standing by each other through hardship.

title: What women endure
paragraphs: What women have endured in this world…
Even in fairy tales, they were cast as witches or cruel stepmothers.
What wasn’t said about them…
They were not allowed to be themselves. Yet they deserved to be seen as whole human beings, with dreams, thoughts and love of their own.
Woman…
“Long hair, little sense,” they said.
“Your place is in the kitchen. Stay out of matters like these,” they said.
Oh, woman, what you have endured in this world…
Too few recognized your worth.
Too few saw your love, your heart, your kindness.
When you stood up for your rights, you were difficult. When you stayed silent, you were naïve.
When you showed your love, some imagined that they owned you.
Those you lifted to the skies with your love sometimes forgot even to look down at you.
They did not ask, “How are you?”
They barely noticed whether you were there.
They forgot that you, too, had a soul.
They forgot you were human.
They hurt you, crushed you, treated you as though you did not exist…
Yet you wanted to make life more beautiful, to offer support, to change something for the better.
The heart that gave so much love was left longing to receive it.
They spoke to you of heaven and made your life a hell.
They looked into your eyes and denied the pain they saw there.
They did not hear the cry rising within you.
Most of all, you loved being a mother.
You loved looking into your child’s eyes with tenderness.
There were moments when the love in that embrace was the only love in the world you could truly trust.

Moral: Valuing women means more than praising their sacrifices. It means hearing their voices, recognizing their work and respecting their choices and dignity. Love and peace grow where everyone is valued equally.

title: What Is Loyalty?
paragraphs: It is remembering,
not turning away when times are hard,
not closing your door to a friend…
It is caring when a friend is crying,
feeling their pain and sharing their sorrow…
Loyalty is more than a word.
It means being there with a heart that understands.
A balm for the wounded,
water for the thirsty.
Loyalty is understanding—
not abandoning a rose because it has thorns.

Moral: Loyalty means standing by those you love through difficult times and not turning away because of their imperfections. Its worth is shown in the care you give, not merely in the promises you make.

title: Can a Broken Heart Love Again?
paragraphs: One day, a man asked a dervish:
“Can a broken heart love again?”
“Of course it can,” the dervish replied.
The man hesitated.
“But have you ever drunk water from a broken cup?”
The dervish smiled.
“Have you ever given up drinking water because a cup broke?”
Moral: A broken heart has not lost its capacity to love. Give yourself time to heal, but do not let one painful experience close your heart to love forever.

catalog_metadata.title: Can a Broken Heart Love Again?

title: The Woman and the Mirror
paragraphs: One morning, a woman wakes up and looks in the mirror. She sees that she has only three hairs left on her head.
“Lovely! I’ll braid my hair today,” she thinks.
She does, and has a wonderful day.
The next morning, she looks in the mirror and sees only two hairs.
“Today I’ll part my hair down the middle.”
She does, and enjoys another lovely day.
On the third morning, she finds just one hair left.
“Never mind. A ponytail it is!”
She puts it in a ponytail and goes about her day in good spirits.
The following morning, she looks in the mirror and discovers that she has no hair at all.
“Wonderful!” she says cheerfully. “I don’t have to do my hair today!”
Moral: We cannot change every situation, but we can choose how we approach it. Sometimes a little humor and a fresh perspective can make a difficult day easier.

title: Yellow and Red Flowers
paragraphs: It is said that, in the past, flowers placed in a window sometimes carried a quiet message.
Yellow flowers meant, “Someone in this house is ill; please keep your voices down as you pass.” Red flowers meant, “A young woman lives here; please mind your language.”
Moral: A gentle gesture can sometimes say more than many words. Courtesy means not only expressing ourselves thoughtfully, but also noticing another person’s unspoken request.

title: A Compliment
paragraphs: Maria lived with her mother in a small apartment and worked as a secretary at a large company. Her days all seemed much the same. At work, she often felt invisible: she arrived, completed her tasks, and quietly went home.
One morning, she noticed a newly opened hat shop on her way to work. A hat in the window caught her eye, and she stepped inside.
A little girl was there with her mother, while another customer was choosing a hat. Maria tried on several. As she put on the last one, the girl called out excitedly:
“Mom, look! Doesn’t that lady look beautiful in that hat?”
Her mother turned and smiled.
“It really does suit you.”
The other customer nodded.
“As though it were made for you!”
Maria looked in the mirror. It had been a long time since she had looked at herself so closely—or so kindly. She smiled and stood a little straighter.
She decided to buy the hat, went to the counter, paid, and left the shop.
It was the same street, yet everything seemed different. The flowers outside the florist’s looked brighter, and the morning air felt fresher. Even the city’s noise seemed to have a pleasant rhythm.

At the office, she returned the security guard’s greeting with a smile. In the lift, someone pressed the button for her floor, and she thanked them warmly. She spoke more easily with her colleagues and joined their conversations with interest.
“You’re glowing today!” one of them said.
At lunchtime, her manager invited her out to discuss a new project. This time, Maria shared her ideas without holding back.
She was still smiling when she returned home that evening. Thinking over the day, she marveled: “Who would have thought a hat could make such a difference?”
Her mother opened the door and beamed.
“Maria, you look lovely! Your eyes are shining the way they did when you were little.”
“It’s all thanks to my new hat, Mom! I’ve had such a wonderful day.”
Her mother looked puzzled.
“What hat?”
Maria reached up. There was no hat.

For a moment, she was bewildered. Had she left it in the taxi? At the office? Then she retraced the moments in the shop: the mirror, the kind words, the counter… She had taken the hat off and put it down while reaching for her purse.
And there she had left it.
Maria smiled. It had not been the hat that made the difference. A few sincere words had helped her see herself more kindly and let her happiness show.
The world was still the same. But Maria no longer felt invisible in it.

Moral: A sincere compliment can remind someone of a beauty they struggle to see in themselves. Do not hold back a kind word: sometimes a single sentence can give someone’s confidence a much-needed lift.

title: A Glass of Milk
paragraphs: A well-known story associated with Dr. Howard Kelly goes like this:
A young man was selling small household items door to door to pay for his education. One day, hungry and out of money, he decided to ask for something to eat at the next house.
A young woman opened the door. Embarrassed, he lost his courage.
“Could I please have a glass of water?”
She noticed his tired face and sensed that he was hungry. A moment later, she returned with a large glass of milk.
He drank it slowly, then asked:
“How much do I owe you?”
“Nothing,” she said with a smile. “My mother taught us to give without expecting anything in return.”
“Then thank you, from the bottom of my heart.”
As he walked away, it was not only his hunger that had eased. He felt less alone, and his faith in God and in human kindness had been renewed.
Years passed. The woman became seriously ill, and her local doctors referred her to a hospital in a larger city.
Dr. Howard Kelly was asked to consult on her treatment. When he heard where she came from, a distant memory stirred. He went to her room and recognized her immediately.
She was the woman who had given him the milk.
Dr. Kelly took a close interest in her care. After a long course of treatment, she recovered.
On the day she was to leave, he asked to see the bill before it was delivered. He wrote a few words on it and had it sent to her room.
She was afraid to open the envelope. How many years would it take her to pay?
At last, she unfolded the bill. Her eyes filled with tears as she read the note:
“Paid in full with a glass of milk.”
Beneath it was the signature:
Dr. Howard Kelly.
Moral: Give because someone needs your kindness, not because you expect it to return. A small act of care can leave a lasting impression and inspire another kindness years later.

title: A Handful of Roasted Chickpeas
paragraphs: A little boy went into a nut shop with his mother. As soon as he spotted the roasted chickpeas, he began pleading:
“Mom, can I have some? Please!”
When the shopkeeper realized that the boy’s mother wasn’t going to buy any, he decided to treat the boy.
“Come on, help yourself to a handful. They’re on me.”
But the boy kept his hands by his sides.
“I’d rather you gave them to me.”
The shopkeeper scooped up a generous handful and handed them over. Then he asked:
“Why didn’t you take some yourself? Why did you want me to do it?”
The boy grinned.
“Because your hands are bigger than mine!”
The shopkeeper burst out laughing.
“You clever little fellow!”
Moral: Sometimes noticing a small difference can work to your advantage. Being quick-witted means spotting what others overlook.

title: A Pair of Boots
paragraphs: One day, a teacher asked her pupils to write a story on any subject they liked. She promised a pair of boots to the writer of the best story.
The children finished their stories and handed them in. The teacher read them one by one and enjoyed them all. Unable to choose a favorite, she decided to draw lots.
She asked each pupil to write their own name on a slip of paper, fold it, and place it in the box on her desk. She mixed the slips, drew one out, unfolded it, and read aloud:
“Amina!”
The classroom burst into applause. Amina hugged the boots to her chest, unable to hold back her tears of joy.
That evening, the teacher’s eyes filled with tears as she told her husband what had happened. Puzzled, he asked:
“What a lovely way to settle it! But why are you crying?”
She replied:
“Afterwards, I opened all the other slips. Not one child had written their own name. Every single one had written Amina’s—the girl whose family had the least. They all wanted her to win the boots.”
Moral: Finding joy in someone else’s happiness is a victory too. Sometimes true compassion means quietly giving up your own chance for someone who needs it more.

title: Being Lonely
paragraphs: I went to visit someone I knew. When I entered the room, I found him sitting silently with his head bowed. He looked sad.
“Are you unhappy?” I asked.
He raised his head and looked into my eyes.
“No. I’m lonely.”
Moral: Sometimes loneliness lies behind a sorrowful expression. Noticing someone’s silence, listening, and being there for them can be a profound act of care.

title: Discussion and Conflict
paragraphs: As they did every day, Javid Bey and his team gathered in the meeting room to discuss the state of their project. Each person briefly described the previous day’s progress and any difficulties they had encountered.

It was Kamal’s turn. Like the others, he reported on the work he had done, but — as if hoping for help from his colleagues — he spoke in more detail about the problem he faced. As soon as he finished, Nadir accused him in front of everyone: “You are to blame; because of you our work has stopped and we can do nothing.” The room froze. Kamal was deeply embarrassed and did not know what to do.
Before the exchange could escalate, Javid Bey, the project manager, stepped in. “Let’s stop here for today and return to this later,” he said. The team dispersed.

Javid Bey knew what to do: speak to Nadir privately and in a friendly way. He invited him to the company café for a cup of tea. After a little small talk, he said calmly, “My son, the way you treated Kamal today was wrong. You accused him without understanding the situation, and you did it in front of everyone. Put yourself in his place. He was hoping for our help and was accused instead. I’m sure he hoped we would think the problem through together and find a solution.”
Nadir lowered his head in shame. Javid Bey’s words had taught him a lesson: he understood that he had acted wrongly.
Later, whenever Nadir remembered the conversation, he thanked Javid Bey. He was also grateful that their conversation had remained private.
Moral: Conflict focuses on who is right; discussion focuses on what is right. If you want the truth, discuss — do not quarrel.
Bakhtiyar Sirajov

title: Everyone Is Equal Here
paragraphs: The young, newly elected head of the local council decided to explore the neighborhood on foot. After walking for a while, he stopped at a teahouse on a side street and ordered some tea.
A boy of twelve or thirteen approached him.
“Would you like your shoes polished, sir?”
His shoes were already clean, but he did not want to turn the boy away.
“All right. Do a good job, and I’ll pay you double.”
The boy answered calmly:
“I do a good job for everyone.”
The young man looked surprised.
“What do you mean?”
“Our teacher says we should do our work honestly for everyone. It’s not right to do it carefully for one person and carelessly for another.”
Taking out his brush, he added:
“I buy medicine for my mother with this money. I want to earn it honestly.”
The young man fell silent. The boy’s simple words held an important lesson for his own work: good service should not depend on extra money or someone’s status.

When the boy finished, the young man paid him for his work and gave him some additional money to help. As they talked, he learned that the boy’s father had died. The boy attended school and worked afterward to help his mother.

The young man gave him his contact number and said he would visit the family to see how he could support them. Later, he also met the boy’s teacher and thanked him for teaching his pupils the value of honesty.
To remember their conversation, he had a sentence written on the side of his desk nameplate that faced him:
“Everyone matters equally here.”
He tried to keep those words in mind whenever he made a decision: whoever stood before him deserved the same respect and fair treatment.
Moral: You should not need a wealthy or influential customer to do your work conscientiously. Honest service is measured by respect for each person’s rights, not by the promise of extra money.

title: Forgiveness
paragraphs: Forgiving someone does not oblige you to love them, speak to them, or continue the relationship. Nor does it mean accepting that they were innocent or right.
Forgiveness means no longer allowing hurt, resentment, and hatred to rule your life. It means gradually easing the weight of past pain.
Give yourself time. When you are ready to forgive, let go of that burden without forgetting what you have learned. As you make room for peace, protect your boundaries too.

Moral: Forgiveness does not excuse a wrong; it means choosing not to carry its burden forever. You can forgive while recognizing that trusting again and continuing the relationship are separate choices.

title: Beyond first impressions
paragraphs: Of some people, all we can say is:

Meeting them brought us joy;
knowing them brought disappointment.
Moral: A first impression never tells the whole story. An acquaintance begins with a meeting, but character reveals itself over time through actions.

title: Go, but Come Again
paragraphs: A story about Ottoman hospitality tells of hosts placing departing guests’ shoes by the door with the toes pointing towards the house—a gesture reserved for those they hoped to see again.
It was a wordless invitation:
“You may be leaving, but come back soon. Our door is open to you.”
The guests carried away more than pleasant memories of their visit. They left with the joy of knowing they would be warmly welcomed again.
Moral: Warmth does not always need grand words. A small gesture can give someone a precious sense of belonging: “There is a place for me here. They hope I’ll return.”

title: Gossip
paragraphs: A sharp-tongued man had been spreading rumors about someone in his village. When the matter came to a head, he was called before the village elder.
“It was only a joke!” he protested. “People misunderstood me. How is that my fault?”
But the man whose reputation he had damaged would not let the matter rest.
“You have dragged my good name through the mud. I want justice.”
Unable to deny what he had said, the gossip finally backed down.
“All right. I take it all back. Please forgive me.”
The elder listened carefully. Sensing that the man still did not understand the harm he had caused, he said:
“Bring a feather pillow to the marketplace. Cut it open and scatter the feathers on the wind. Then gather every last one and bring them to me. After that, we can talk about forgiveness.”
The man reluctantly agreed. What a strange thing to ask, he thought as he carried the pillow to the square, cut it open, and shook the feathers into the air.
The wind scattered them in every direction. He ran back and forth, trying to catch them, but however hard he tried, he managed to collect only a handful.
He returned to the elder with his head bowed.
“I couldn’t gather the rest. The wind carried them everywhere.”
“Do you understand now how difficult it is to take back your words?” the elder asked.
The man looked at the feathers in his hand and sighed.
“Yes. My words have spread just like these feathers. Saying ‘I take it back’ cannot bring them home.”
Moral: Gossip is like feathers scattered on the wind: easy to spread, hard to gather up again. An apology matters, but it cannot always undo the harm. Think before you speak.

title: Unwelcome gifts
paragraphs: (A parable about a samurai)
An elderly, wise samurai taught his students the ways of wisdom and the art of combat.

One day, a warrior known for his rudeness and cruelty entered during a lesson. He had a favorite tactic: he would insult his opponents until they lost their temper, then exploit the mistakes they made in anger to defeat them.
This time, he used the same tactic to provoke the samurai into a fight. He hurled insults at him, but the samurai paid no attention and continued teaching.
The warrior repeated his insults several times. When he still received no response, he left in frustration.
The students, who had watched closely, asked:
“Master, why did you put up with those insults? Why didn’t you challenge him to a fight?”
The samurai answered with a question:
“If someone brings you a gift and you do not accept it, who keeps it?”
“The person who brought it,” the students replied.
“Think of envy, hatred, and insults in the same way. If you do not accept these ‘gifts,’ they remain with the person who brought them.”
Moral: Do not accept someone else’s insult as the truth about you. Meet hostility with composure rather than hostility of your own, so that another person’s anger does not dictate your behavior.

title: Humanity
paragraphs: Kamal had studied and worked hard for years. At last, the day of the examination that could shape his future had arrived. His father, Kazim, was a demanding man. He followed his son’s studies closely and was certain he would succeed.
Kamal found the examination room and took his seat. He felt nervous when the papers were handed out, but relaxed as he read the questions. He knew the answers and wrote with confidence.
With half an hour left, he looked up and glanced through the window. Suddenly, he sprang from his chair and ran toward the door.
“Come back! If you leave now, your exam will be invalidated! You’ll lose a whole year!” the proctor called.
Kamal did not stop. He raced down the stairs and out through the back of the building.
When he returned home several hours later, his father already knew what had happened. He scolded his son, then lost control of his anger and slapped him.
“Why did you leave? Why did you abandon the exam?”
Kamal remained silent. He did not believe his father would listen to him then. He feared that anything he said would only make him angrier.
Throughout the following year, Kazim kept bringing up the incident. Each time, it hurt Kamal, but he did not argue. He studied again and, the next year, earned a place at medical school.

Years passed. Kamal became a skilled, compassionate doctor. Although he had grown up in the city, he chose to work at a hospital in a remote village. Some time later, his family came to visit. The examination was no longer mentioned.
One snowy, bitterly cold evening, the telephone rang. A woman in a nearby village was ill, and someone was asking for help.
Kamal picked up his medical bag. His father did not want him walking the mountain roads alone in such weather.
“I’m coming with you.”
They walked through the blizzard for almost an hour before finding the house. An elderly man opened the door.
“It’s my wife, Doctor. Please come in.”
Kamal examined the woman, gave her initial treatment, and explained the care she would need.
She looked at him gratefully.
“You came to help us in this terrible cold, my son,” she said in a trembling voice. “What would the world be like without people like you? You remind me of a young man…”
She paused to catch her breath.

“Years ago, I went to the city. I was pregnant. Suddenly, I became unwell in the street and was seized by terrible pains. There was nobody nearby to ask for help. I learned later that an examination was taking place in the building beside me.

“Before long, a young man came running. He went to such trouble to get me to the hospital in that heat. It took us half an hour. The doctor said that any further delay could have put my life in danger. My son was born that very day.”
She fell silent for a moment, then smiled.
“I asked the young man his name. He said it was Kamal. He had seen me through the window during his exam and, realizing I was alone, had run out to help.
“‘I can start my studies a year later,’ he told me. ‘I couldn’t leave you there.’”
Kazim looked up at his son. Kamal was listening without a word.

“I named my son Kamal,” the woman continued. “I brought him up hearing about that young man’s kindness. I wanted him to become just as compassionate. He’s a teacher now. Alongside his lessons, he tries to teach his pupils to care about others.”
Her eyes filled with tears.

“If only I could see that young man again. I would tell him that the year he lost gave two people a future. I would ask him to forgive me for what helping me had cost him. You can learn a profession, my son. What matters is never losing your humanity. He did not leave me alone in that street.”
Kamal gently took her hand.
“You owe me nothing,” he said softly. “Please be at peace.”
Kazim lowered his eyes. Inside the house, he tried to hide his tears. Once outside, he could no longer hold them back.
He wept as he walked beside his son along the snowy road.
“Kamal, my son…”
He could say no more. That night, in a stranger’s home, he had finally heard the answer he had refused to listen to years before.
Moral: Our worth lies not only in our profession, but in the choices we make when someone needs us. What looks like a loss may bring lasting good to many lives. Listen before you judge.

title: I Wish for a Friend
paragraphs:
I ask for neither wealth nor land,
Only a faithful friend.
What fortune ever prayed for the soul of its owner?
I wish for a friend who will pray for mine when I am gone.
Moral: Our truest wealth lies in faithful friends. A friend who stands beside us in life and remembers us in prayer after we are gone is worth more than any possession.

title: Sharing the burden
paragraphs: My mother used to tell me:
“I was very young when I married your father. I could barely cook, and I wasn’t much good at sewing either.
“One day, my mother-in-law—your grandmother—was getting ready to visit a neighbor. She had washed and dried the wool filling for a quilt. She spread the quilt out in front of me and said:
“‘Have this stitched by the time I get back.’

“I picked up the needle and began. But however hard I tried, I struggled to push it through the thick quilt. I kept pricking my fingers. In the end, I started crying. My hand hurt, and I had no idea what I would say to her if I couldn’t finish.

“Just then, your father came home for his lunch break. When he saw me crying, he sat beside me and took the needle from my hand. He finished stitching the quilt himself, ate his lunch, and went back to work.
“He never said a word to his mother. When she returned and saw the finished quilt, she was very pleased.”
Whenever I remember my mother’s story, I think of the saying: “If the road feels easy, thank your companion.”

Moral: Life’s journey is easier with someone who shares your burdens instead of judging you when you struggle. Sometimes love is shown not through grand declarations, but through a quietly offered helping hand.

title: Respecting boundaries
paragraphs: May God never leave us with so little to do that we start meddling in other people’s lives!
Moral: Caring for someone does not mean making their decisions for them. Unwanted advice can become a burden; genuine help begins with respect for a person’s choices and boundaries.

title: Know Your Friend
paragraphs: If you want to know your friend, watch how they behave in hardship, under pressure, and during a disagreement. And when they must choose between your friendship and their own interests…

Moral: The strength of a friendship shows in difficult times and disagreements as well as in happy moments. A true friend considers their own interests without forgetting what is fair to you or the trust you share.

title: Compassion
paragraphs: I was walking home from work on a bitter winter night when I noticed a man struggling to stay on his feet. He swayed, clinging to a post by the roadside to keep from falling.
He looked about thirty and was neatly dressed. Some passers-by assumed he was drunk and made loud remarks about drinking. Others laughed at him. But no one stopped to ask what was wrong.
I approached him.
“Are you all right? Do you need help?”
His lips barely moved.
“I’m ill…”
I put an arm around his waist to steady him, then slowly helped him to a nearby taxi stand.
Snow had begun to fall again. The street was emptying, and the cold was seeping into our bones. I was almost ready to give up hope of finding a taxi when one pulled up beside us.
I explained the situation to the driver. Together, we helped the man into the back seat and headed for the hospital.
The medical staff attended to him immediately. We waited. The driver stayed too.
After a while, the doctor on duty told us:
“It’s a good thing you didn’t leave him out there. His life was at risk in that cold.”
As the man recovered, he looked at us and managed a faint smile. He was still too weak to speak, but his eyes said a great deal.
When the doctors said he could go home, we helped him back into the same taxi.
As we approached his house, we saw his wife and son outside. Knowing that he had diabetes, his wife had grown anxious when he failed to return. She and their son had come out to wait for him.
The moment the taxi stopped, they ran towards us. When the man stepped out, they wrapped their arms around him. For a while, none of them let go.
The hours of weariness vanished. Seeing their joy brought tears to our eyes too.
After we said goodbye, I asked the driver:
“How much do I owe you?”
He shook his head.
“You don’t owe me anything, my friend. I owe you. You let me be part of something good. I don’t think I’ve cried in twenty years… Tonight, you gave me that feeling again.”
I hugged him. When we parted, the night no longer felt quite so cold. I decided to walk home.
Who knew? Perhaps I would meet someone else along the way who needed help.

Moral: Compassion goes beyond feeling sorry for someone. It begins when we stop, ask, and offer a helping hand. Sometimes approaching a person instead of judging them can change a whole family’s world.

title: A request for help
paragraphs: Do not be too quick to resent people who contact you only when they need something. Perhaps they are struggling and asking for help because they trust you. Seeing their request in this light may soften your hurt.
Moral: Do not immediately assume the worst of someone who turns to you for help. Sometimes their request reflects both need and trust. Understanding can ease resentment.

title: Permission or Forgiveness?
paragraphs: Rear Admiral Grace Hopper helped popularize the saying:
“It’s easier to ask forgiveness than it is to get permission.”
This is sometimes understood as: act first, then apologize if anyone objects. But there is a difference between encouraging initiative and using the saying to excuse irresponsibility.
Sometimes, waiting endlessly for approval prevents a good idea from ever being tried.

Imagine a company where the same information is copied manually into several spreadsheets every week, taking hours. An employee realizes that a simple automated process could make the task much easier.

As the proposal passes from one manager to another, a response could take weeks. Instead, the employee builds a separate demonstration without altering existing data or disrupting anyone’s work. They show their colleagues the result: a task that once took hours now takes only minutes.
When someone objects that the trial was not agreed on in advance, the employee explains:
“I built a separate demonstration to see how we could make the work easier. I haven’t changed the existing system. If I should have let you know beforehand, I apologize.”

The point is to test a useful idea responsibly, rather than disregard the rules. When the risk is low, mistakes can be corrected, and other people’s rights are respected, a small initiative can demonstrate more than lengthy discussions.

Moral: Initiative becomes valuable when it is paired with responsibility. Showing what is possible through small, reversible steps can be more effective than waiting endlessly for approval. But apologizing afterwards does not remove the responsibility to think beforehand.

title: How We Treat People
paragraphs: Approach your relationships as you would a fire:

Stay too far away, and you will freeze.
Get too close, and you will burn.
— Attributed to Saadi Shirazi
Moral: Healthy relationships need both closeness and boundaries. Leave enough space to remain yourself, but stay close enough to share their warmth.

title: Mockery Is Unacceptable
paragraphs: Children need to learn from an early age that no one should be mocked or belittled because of their appearance or because they are different. Everyone deserves respect.
Moral: Being different is no reason to be ridiculed. Respect for another person’s dignity is learned in childhood through the words and actions of adults.

title: Relationships
paragraphs: Deep within human life lies a truth: our relationships are a mirror of our inner selves. The warmth born at the family hearth, the bonds rooted in kinship, the mutual understanding that grows in friendship—each is among life's most precious treasures. The respect and kindness shared among colleagues are like an unseen light that brings warmth to our daily work.

Kindness is not simply a way of behaving; it is an expression of a person's inner richness. It is a silent bridge that brings hearts closer, warms cold moments, and makes understanding possible without words.
If we protect and strengthen this bridge, life will become more meaningful, people will grow closer, and the world will become a slightly better place to live.
Moral: Relationships grow stronger through mutual respect, understanding, and kindness. To maintain our closeness, we must remember to care for one another.
Etibar Siracsoy

title: Make time for people
paragraphs: My father needed to transfer some money, so I went to the bank with him. We spent nearly an hour there. Eventually, I lost patience.
“Dad, let me show you how to do your banking online. What do you think?”
He looked at me with surprise.
“What would that do for me, son?”
“You wouldn’t have to come to the bank and wait an hour just to transfer money. You could do your shopping online too. Everything would be easier and more convenient.”
Confident that I could persuade him, I was ready to go on enthusiastically.
“So, if I did what you suggest, I wouldn’t need to leave the house?” he asked.
“That’s right, Dad. You could even have groceries brought to your door. You could order through services like Amazon and have your purchases delivered.”
His reply left me speechless.
“Son, in this hour you consider wasted, I saw four friends and talked to bank staff who have known me for years.

“You know I often feel lonely. I need to see people and have someone to talk to. I enjoy getting dressed, leaving the house, and coming to the bank. I have the time, and these encounters give me pleasure.
“Two years ago, when I was ill, the man I always buy fruit from came to see me. He was genuinely upset that I was unwell. He sat beside my bed, asked how I was, and lifted my spirits.
“A while ago, when your mother fell during her morning walk, our local grocer came to her aid. He helped her up, put her in his car, and brought her home. He knew us and knew where we lived.
“If I did everything without leaving home, how would those connections ever develop? Why should I give up seeing people just to have everything delivered to my door?
“I don’t simply want to buy things, son. I want to know the person I buy them from, ask how they are, and exchange a few words. I need company and a sense of belonging.
“Can Amazon deliver that to my doorstep too?
“Technology makes life easier, but it isn’t life itself. Spend your time with people, son. Let your devices help you do that, not get in the way.”

Moral: Saving time is useful, but an hour spent with people is not necessarily an hour wasted. Enjoy the convenience of technology without forgetting the value of a greeting, a conversation, and being there for one another.

title: The Friendship of Horses
paragraphs: Two horses live on a farm near my home. From a distance, they seem much like any other horses. Only when you come closer do you notice that one is blind.
The owner has continued to care for it, providing a safe, comfortable home. But the horse also has a friend who makes life a little easier.
As you approach the farm, you hear the gentle ringing of a bell. It hangs from the other horse’s halter. The blind horse follows the sound, using it to find its companion and make its way along.
Watch them for a while, and you begin to notice their quiet understanding. The horse with the bell turns now and then to check on its friend. The other walks steadily towards the sound.
In the evening, as they return to the stable, the leading horse does not hurry. It walks a little, then stops and waits. When its companion catches up, it moves on again, as though saying:
“I’m here. I’m waiting for you.”
One offers guidance; the other offers trust. Together, they make their way home.
Moral: Sometimes we feel God’s compassion in the care of a friend. At times, we need a voice to guide us; at others, it is our turn to make sure someone is not left behind.

title: The doorbell
paragraphs: Last winter, I lost my job. To make ends meet, I took temporary work delivering newspapers. One day, I found that the letterbox at one of the houses had been sealed shut, so I knocked on the door. An elderly man answered.
“Why have you sealed your letterbox?” I asked.
“I did it deliberately,” he replied.
Then, with a faint smile, he added:
“May I ask a favor? When you bring the newspaper each day, please knock or ring the bell and hand it to me.”
I was puzzled.
“Of course. But wouldn’t it be easier for both of us if I put it through the letterbox? You wouldn’t have to come to the door.”
“It’s no trouble, young man. I’m home every day.”
He paused before continuing.
“My wife has passed away, and my son lives abroad. I live here alone. Who knows how much time I have left?”
I noticed tears gathering in his eyes.
“But didn’t you subscribe because you wanted to read the newspaper?” I asked.
“I don’t read newspapers, my boy... I subscribed to the sound of the doorbell.”
Then he clasped his hands and said quietly:
“Do me one more kindness. This is my son’s phone number. If you knock one day and I don’t answer, please call him and let him know.”
Moral: Sometimes it is not the newspaper someone is waiting for, but the person at the door. A greeting and a brief conversation can remind someone living alone that they have not been forgotten.

title: Choosing friends
paragraphs: Do not befriend the arrogant. They will not try to understand you, listen to your troubles, or consider your feelings—and you will be hurt.
Do not befriend those who think they know better than everyone else. They talk too much, listen too little, and belittle you with their words—and you will be hurt.
Do not befriend the dishonorable. They break their promises, abandon you in difficult times, and fail to value friendship—and you will be hurt.
Moral: Choose friends by how they treat you and what they do, not by sweet words. A true friend listens, respects you, and stands beside you when times are hard.

title: Thoughtfulness
paragraphs: One of the most precious blessings in a person's life is to receive attention and care. Sometimes even a brief call from a relative, a friend, or an acquaintance, simply to ask how we are, rises like the sun in our hearts. In that moment, we realize that somewhere in this vast world there are people who remember us and value our presence in their lives.

Everyone needs to be loved, remembered, and valued. A sincere greeting, a heartfelt inquiry, or an unexpected call can sometimes be worth more than the most precious gift. For these small gestures give us a sense of belonging and remind us of our place in the hearts of those around us.
A few minutes of attention may brighten someone's day, awaken hope in their heart, and strengthen their love of life.

Sometimes it is not medicine that prolongs a person's life, but words that touch the heart, the care they receive, and the sense of closeness they feel. For one of the surest sources of happiness is knowing that we have not been forgotten.
Moral: Asking how someone is and remembering them may seem like small things, yet they can offer great emotional support. Let us not withhold our care, so that no one feels forgotten.
Etibar Siracsoy

title: Welcome Home, My Dear
paragraphs: When my late father, Hafız Ali, was fighting at Gallipoli, my mother was seven months pregnant with me. I never saw him, never knew him. Not even a photograph of him remained.
Those were terrible years: mobilization, occupation, the struggle for independence, poverty and hardship.
Our childhood passed in want, with the constant worry of finding enough to eat.
Whenever my mother went out, she would come to me first.
“Son, I’m going to the market. If your father comes home, let me know at once!”
“I’m going to your aunt’s. If your father comes home, let me know at once!”
“I’m going next door. If your father comes home, let me know at once!”
My mother never stopped waiting for him.
I grew up, began earning a living and opened a shop. Whenever she went out, she would still stop by, tell me where she was going and add:
“If your father comes home, be sure to let me know!”
The years passed, and my mother grew old. But her habit never changed. Leaning on her walking stick, she would come to me and say:
“If your father comes home, come and fetch me!”
One day she became seriously ill and took to her bed.
In her final moments, she said goodbye to us.
“You have cared for me so well. Forgive me for any trouble I have caused you.”
Then she turned slowly towards me.
“If your father comes home, tell him, ‘Mother waited for you until the end of her life.’”
Suddenly, she raised her head and looked towards the door. A smile spread across her face.
“Welcome home, my dear. Welcome home!”
With those words, she breathed her last.
Recounted as the memories of Cevdet Alkalp, an elderly cobbler who lived in Balıkesir.
The account is attributed to Mustafa Doğru, a researcher, writer and geography teacher at Bursa Çınar Anadolu High School.

In Türkiye, March 18 marks the anniversary of the Çanakkale naval victory and a day of remembrance for the fallen. On that day in 1915, the Allied fleet’s attempt to force its way through the Dardanelles towards Istanbul was repelled.
In remembering this victory, we remember not only those who died on the battlefield, but also the families who waited years for their return.
May all those who fell at Gallipoli rest in peace. May no mother spend her life waiting for someone who will never return.

Moral: The pain of war does not end on the battlefield; sometimes it becomes a lifetime of waiting at home. We owe remembrance and respect both to those who gave their lives for their homeland and to those who waited for them.

title: Why shout?
paragraphs: One day during class, a teacher asked the students:
“Why do people shout when they argue?”
“Because they lose their temper,” one student replied.
“But the other person is right beside them. Why should they need to shout to be heard? Can’t they speak calmly even when they’re angry?” the teacher asked.
The students offered different answers. After listening, the teacher said:

“Think of it this way: as people argue, their hearts grow further apart. It is as though they shout to bridge that distance and make their voices reach each other. Yet the louder they become, the further apart their hearts drift.”
After a brief pause, the teacher continued:

“Now think of people who love each other. They often speak softly because their hearts are close. As that closeness deepens, even a whisper is enough. Sometimes they need no words at all: a glance is enough to understand each other.”
Then the teacher addressed the class:

“When you argue, do not let your hearts drift apart. Do not say things that widen the distance between you. One day, that distance may become so great that finding your way back to each other is difficult.”
Moral: In an argument, try not only to be heard, but also to listen. Patience and respect keep hearts close; hurtful words drive them further apart.

title: Your Friends
paragraphs: A young man was preparing to get married. After a busy week of wedding preparations, he turned to his father.
“Dad, could you do me a favor? I can’t manage everything on my own. Would you call the friends on this list and invite them to my wedding?”
“Of course, son,” his father replied.
On the wedding day, the young man approached his father, visibly upset.
“Dad, I asked you to call all my friends!”
“I did, son. I called every one of them.”
“There were fifty names on the list, but I can only see fifteen of them here!”
His father answered calmly:
“I spoke to all fifty. But instead of inviting them to a wedding, I told them you were facing a difficulty and needed your friends’ help. I asked them to come to this address, today, at this time.”
Then he rested a hand on his son’s shoulder.
