“Look around you, son. These people came here not to share your celebration, but to stand by you in a difficult moment.”
Moral: Friendship is measured in care and trust, not numbers. Treasure those who come to your aid when times are hard; true friendship reveals itself through actions over time.

title: A Generous Man
paragraphs: A generous man was asked:
“When you help people in need, do you expect their gratitude?”
He replied:

“I think of myself as a ladle in a cook’s hand. The food passes through it, but the ladle did not provide the meal. I simply share what God has given me. Rather than expect praise, I am grateful for the chance to help.”
Moral: Do not make kindness a debt others must repay. Share your blessings humbly and respect the dignity of those you help. The opportunity to give is itself a blessing.

title: A Mature Person
paragraphs: There comes a time when you grow to appreciate the sincerity of old friends more deeply. You stop seeking new acquaintances simply to surround yourself with people. You no longer argue with those unwilling to understand, and you step away from relationships that leave you emotionally drained. That is when you realize you are becoming more mature.
Moral: Maturity means valuing genuine relationships, maintaining your boundaries, and protecting your inner peace. Knowing whom to keep close is wisdom; so is knowing whom and what to step away from.

title: Question the question
paragraphs: A story is told of a Berkeley graduate who visited a rabbi in New York and asked for help studying the Talmud.
The rabbi asked:
“Do you know Aramaic? What about Hebrew? Were you introduced to the Torah as a child?”
The young man answered no to every question, then added:
“But I’ve defended a dissertation on Socratic logic. I want to study the Talmud to fill some gaps in my education.”

“Studying the Talmud requires serious preparation,” the rabbi said. “But since you’re so keen, let me ask you a question first. Two men climb down a chimney. One has a clean face; the other’s face is covered in soot. Which one washes his face?”
The young man answered confidently:
“The one with the dirty face, of course!”

“Consider this instead: the clean-faced man sees the soot on his companion’s face, assumes his own face is dirty too, and goes to wash. The dirty-faced man sees a clean face before him and feels no need to wash.”
“Interesting! May I have another chance?”
The rabbi repeated the question:
“Two men climb down a chimney. One has a clean face, and the other has a dirty face. Which one washes?”
“This time I know: the one with the clean face!”

“But both might wash. The clean-faced man looks at his companion and goes to wash. The other notices that his companion went to wash after looking at him and realizes that his own face must be dirty.”
The young man paused.
“I hadn’t considered that. Ask me again.”
The rabbi repeated the question. This time, the young man did not hesitate:
“They both wash!”

“Perhaps neither does. The dirty-faced man sees his companion’s clean face and stays where he is. The clean-faced man notices that his companion isn’t washing and assumes that his own face must be clean as well.”
Thoroughly confused, the young man asked for one last chance. The rabbi began:
“Two men climb down a chimney. One has a clean face, and the other—”
“Neither washes!” the young man interrupted.
The rabbi smiled.

“Again, you rushed to answer. Why didn’t you ask how one man’s face stayed clean when they both came down the same chimney? How do we know what they saw or thought? Each time, I introduced a new assumption, and you accepted it as part of the question.”
He paused, then continued:
“Sometimes the problem is not that we cannot find an answer, but that we seek one without examining the question. First, we must distinguish what we know from what we merely assume.”
Moral: Not every question has a single, definite answer. Clear thinking begins with examining the question and separating facts from assumptions, rather than rushing to a conclusion.

title: Facing a problem
paragraphs: Is there a problem in your life?
If not, why worry?
If there is, can you do something about it?
If you can, put your energy into finding a solution.
If you can’t, what will worrying change?
Moral: Do what you can, and learn to accept what is beyond your control. Constant worry does not solve the problem—it only drains your strength.

title: Avoid These Questions
paragraphs: Pause before asking someone who is looking for work, “Still haven’t found a job?” Think twice before asking an employed person how much they earn, a couple without children whether they have children yet, or someone who is single when they are getting married.
And when someone doesn’t know something, don’t embarrass them by saying, “You didn’t even know that?”
Behind every answer may be a story the person is not ready to share: worry, loss, disappointment, or simply a personal choice they do not have to explain.
A question that satisfies our passing curiosity may reopen someone else’s old wound. Before you ask, consider whether you want to support the person or merely satisfy your curiosity.
Moral: Tact means respecting other people’s privacy. Sometimes care is shown by asking a question; sometimes it is shown by choosing not to.

title: A shared goal
paragraphs: Two people were trying to move a heavy chest through a doorway. However hard they pushed, it would not budge. Eventually, both stopped, sweating and out of breath.
One wiped his forehead and said:
“What a heavy chest! All that effort, and we still couldn’t get it inside.”
The other looked at him in surprise.
“Inside? Weren’t we trying to get it out?”
Moral: Before working together, make sure you are working toward the same goal. Otherwise, you may get in each other’s way while thinking you are helping.

title: Keeping Your Cool
paragraphs: When you find yourself in a difficult situation, pause and think rather than panic. Calmly considering what is happening can help you make a sound decision and find a way to turn things around.
Moral: Composure may not remove a difficulty, but it makes the way forward easier to see. Take a moment to think calmly before you act.

title: Being Human
paragraphs: “Becoming a scholar is easy; becoming a decent person is hard,” the saying goes. But what does it mean to be a decent person?
It means living by your conscience: acting honestly and fairly, preserving your own dignity without diminishing anyone else’s.
It means being considerate, courteous, and humble. Respecting people for their humanity, rather than their wealth or position. Recognizing your own shortcomings, not just those of others.

It means thinking about the consequences of your actions, admitting your mistakes, and taking responsibility for what you do. Keeping your composure in an argument and not losing heart when difficulties arise.
It means keeping your word even when it is inconvenient. Refusing to measure a person’s worth by money or status, to covet what belongs to others, or to take what is rightfully theirs.
It means not lying, spreading slander, or betraying someone for personal gain. Standing up for those treated unjustly, even when staying silent would be easier.
It means not turning people against one another or taking pleasure in someone else’s suffering. Knowing how to love—and showing that love through care and action, not words alone.

Moral: Our knowledge shows what we have learned; our actions show who we have become. Our humanity is revealed in our everyday choices: to be honest, to respect others’ dignity, and to care when someone is hurting.

title: Believe in Yourself
paragraphs: Know your worth!
Do not shy away from hard work!
Build your strength and develop your abilities!
Never lose hope!
Listen to your conscience!
Stay determined!
Keep your intentions pure!
Preserve your dignity!
Hold firmly to your faith!
Moral: Believing in yourself does not mean thinking you can do everything. It means trusting your ability to learn and grow. Let hope, determination, and dignity sustain you along the way.

title: Do not deepen another's pain
paragraphs: Do not boast about your wealth to someone struggling financially, your health to someone who is ill, or your carefree life to someone weighed down by sorrow.
Do not flaunt your freedom before someone deprived of theirs, or your strength before someone feeling powerless.
Speak sensitively about your children with someone longing for a child, and about your parents with someone grieving theirs.
Share your joy, but remain mindful of another person’s pain. Sometimes listening and being present matter more than speaking.
Moral: Do not turn your blessings into boasts that deepen someone else’s hurt. Choose your words with understanding: seek to recognize their feelings rather than remind them of what they lack.

title: Think before speaking
paragraphs: Before you speak, ask yourself: will your words offer comfort, help with a difficulty, or bring clarity where it is needed?
Speaking kindly does not mean hiding the truth. Even a painful truth can be told without humiliating someone. If your words serve only to wound, silence is the better choice.
Moral: The value of words lies in the good they do, not merely in how pleasant they sound. Speak the truth with respect, and never speak simply to hurt.

title: Try again
paragraphs: Days come and go. Some end in joy, others in weariness or sadness. Sometimes our plans remain unfinished, and however hard we try, we do not get the result we hoped for.
At such moments, do not turn “I didn’t finish” into self-blame, or “I couldn’t do it” into a reason to give up. Something that did not work out today may still work out another day.
Rest a little and gather your strength. Tomorrow may bring another chance to try again, take a different approach, or take even a small step forward.
Moral: An unfinished task does not mean you are incapable. Give yourself time: moving forward sometimes means starting again, and sometimes it means resting before you continue.

title: Education or Character?
paragraphs: One day, a king asked his vizier:
“Which matters more in a person: education or character?”
“Character, Your Majesty,” the vizier replied.
The king disagreed. He ordered the finest animal trainer in the kingdom to be brought to the palace.
“How long would it take you to teach a cat to carry a tray and serve guests?” he asked.
“Six months, Your Majesty.”
Six months later, the trainer returned with the cat. The guests assembled, and the gathering began. Holding a tray, the cat calmly approached each guest. Everyone watched in amazement.
The king turned to his vizier with a smile.
“Now tell me: education or character?”
Before answering, the vizier released a little mouse he had brought with him. The moment the cat saw it, it dropped the tray and raced after it.
“Character, Your Majesty,” the vizier said quietly.
The king fell silent. The behavior that had impressed everyone had vanished in an instant.

Moral: Learned behavior is not the same as strength of character. The value of education should be evident not only in knowledge and skills, but also in honesty, responsibility, and the choices we make when tested.

title: In your hands
paragraphs: One day, a young man decided to outwit a wise monk. He caught a little bird, concealed it between his palms, and held his hands behind his back.
“Tell me, wise man,” he asked, “is the bird in my hands alive or dead?”
He thought to himself: “If he says it’s alive, I’ll squeeze it to death. If he says it’s dead, I’ll open my hands and let it fly away. Either way, I’ll prove him wrong.”
The monk looked at him and answered calmly:
“The answer, my son, is in your hands.”
The young man hesitated and lowered his head.
The monk continued:

“You want to prove me wrong, but this bird’s fate depends on your choice. You can hurt it, or you can set it free. Wisdom is shown not by trapping someone with a clever question, but by how you use the power you have.”
The young man brought his hands forward and opened them. The bird spread its wings and flew away.
This time, he did not try to prove himself right. He chose to do what was right.

Moral: Not everything in life is within our control, but we are responsible for our choices. Good intentions gain meaning through the actions that follow. When you have the power to hurt, choose to protect.

title: How We Express Sorrow
paragraphs:
Some ease their sorrow by talking,
some turn it into poetry or stories,
some reveal it in a glance or a sigh,
and some hide it behind a smile.
Sorrow does not speak with one voice. Sometimes the eyes say what the lips cannot; sometimes a weary heart lies behind a smiling face.
Moral: Do not measure someone’s pain only by what they say. A smile does not always mean peace, nor silence strength. Listen without judging, and be there when they are ready to speak.

title: Letting Go
paragraphs: There is grace in letting go—
of those who show no appreciation,
who trample on sincerity,
who change their loyalties for personal gain,
who are swollen with pride and arrogance,
who envy others and spread gossip,
who make a habit of lying,
who know nothing of decency,
who undermine your values,
who turn a blind eye to ignorance,
who scorn their homeland and disown their people,
who forget their mother tongue,
who fail to value a mother’s love, a father’s dignity, and a child’s affection…
There is grace in letting go—
of those who think you could never let them go.
Moral: Walking away from certain people is not weakness; it is self-respect. There is wisdom in refusing to depend on those who do not value you.

title: A king's generosity
paragraphs: One day, a king met a little boy who caught his attention and offered him a gold coin. But the boy would not take it.
“Why not?” the king asked, surprised.
“If I take it home, my parents will ask, ‘Where did you steal that money?’”
“Then tell them the king gave it to you.”
The boy answered at once:
“They certainly won’t believe that! They’ll say, ‘If it came from the king, he would have given you more!’”
The king laughed heartily at the boy’s quick wit and gave him a purse full of gold.
Moral: A well-timed, witty remark can achieve more than a long speech. Wit is at its best when it makes someone laugh without causing offense.

title: Honey or Dry Bread?
paragraphs: Better to share dry bread with a wise person than honey with a fool.
Moral: Good company offers more than a rich meal. Choose companions whose conversation deepens your understanding and broadens your view of the world.

title: Letting go of painful thoughts
paragraphs: One day, a man came to a wise scholar and asked:
“Painful thoughts won’t leave me alone. I feel trapped by them. How can I free myself?”
Instead of answering, the scholar stood up, wrapped his arms around a nearby post, and shouted:
“Help! Someone free me from this post!”
The man stared in astonishment.
“I came to you for advice, and now look at you! The post isn’t holding you—you’re holding it. Open your arms, and you’ll be free!”
The scholar let go and said quietly:

“You’ve just found part of your answer. Sometimes we return to a painful thought again and again, holding it as tightly as I held that post. We don’t have to cling to every thought or follow wherever it leads.”

Moral: We cannot always choose which thoughts arise, but we can learn how to respond to them. Letting go does not mean forcing ourselves to forget. It means learning not to let pain govern our whole lives. Sometimes that takes time and support.

title: Now I Understand
paragraphs: In the words of someone who has weathered life’s ups and downs:
I no longer try to make everyone like me. I understand that, whatever I do, some people simply won’t.
I know my own worth now. I do not owe everyone proof of it.
I keep my distance from people who build themselves up by putting others down.
I can now tell the difference between words and intention: those who want to act look for a way; those who do not often find a “but.”
I do not share my secrets with people who gossip. If they betray someone else’s trust, I cannot assume they will respect mine.
I no longer exhaust myself trying to persuade someone who refuses to listen. Not every conversation needs to become an argument, and not every disagreement needs to become a battle.
I make no room in my life for people who habitually lie, make empty promises, and go back on their word.
I distance myself from those who mistake cruelty and harshness for strength. I value people who can recognize their mistakes, apologize, and change their behavior.
Now I understand that I am happier with people around whom I can be myself.

Moral: Maturity lies less in trying to change others than in recognizing your own worth and boundaries. Knowing whom to welcome into your life and when to step away is a way of respecting yourself and finding peace.

title: Inner housekeeping
paragraphs:
Today I did some cleaning.
Not in my home, but within myself…
I looked into corners of my heart I hadn’t visited in a long time. One by one, I brought to light old hurts, fragments of broken hopes, and grievances I had never voiced.
I began with the disappointments. I didn’t try to relive each one or work out who had been right and who had been wrong. I simply realized that I no longer wanted to carry them.

How much room they had taken up inside me…
I thought I had forgotten them long ago. But forgetting, it turned out, was not the same as being free.
I made room for forgiveness—for others and for myself. Not because what had happened was acceptable, but because I didn’t want to carry the pain for the rest of my life.
Then I faced my envy. How much beauty in my own life had I overlooked while watching other people’s lives! There had been times when I had treated someone else’s success as my own failure.
I put gratitude in its place. I remembered what I had, the people beside me, and all I could still do. It felt as though I had rediscovered something long lost: the value of my own life.
I looked carefully into my heart. Thankfully, I found no deep-rooted hatred or malice. But some old wounds still ached. I didn’t blame myself for them. They needed time to heal.
Then came my fears.

At first, I was afraid even to approach them. I had grown so used to living with them that imagining their absence felt strange. Each was linked to the next: the fear of making mistakes, of losing what mattered, of not being liked…
Every worry had given rise to another fear. And I had let those fears persuade me to put off my dreams, my joy, my life.

“I’ll wait a little longer…”
“Once everything is sorted out…”
“I’ll start later…”
How many todays had I lost while waiting for that later?

I couldn’t make all my fears disappear in a single day. But I tried to listen to them and understand: which were protecting me, and which were standing in my way? I realized that fear didn’t always have to stop me. Sometimes it was possible to take a step while still being afraid.
I didn’t blame myself for the way I had lived before. Yesterday, I hadn’t understood what I understood today.
Today I did some cleaning within myself.

I made room for joy.
For hope, love, and faith in myself…
I made room for kindness, for giving and sharing without expecting anything in return. I promised myself that loving others would not mean forgetting myself.
I welcomed back a little playfulness, a little courage, and a little childlike openness. I remembered that I didn’t need a special reason to laugh.
I made room for silence, too. Sometimes the noise inside me has to settle before I can hear my own voice.
Finally, I began learning to accept myself, my past, and the things I could not change.
That didn’t mean surrendering to everything. It meant ending the struggle with what I couldn’t change, so I could give my energy to what I could.

Today I did some cleaning within myself.
There was still more to do.
But inside, I had room to breathe again.
Moral: Caring for your heart means understanding your feelings, rather than suppressing them, and gradually letting go of what weighs you down. Self-compassion makes room for love, hope, and peace.

title: A sunlit day
paragraphs:
A day,
a beautiful day,
a sunlit day—
I wouldn’t trade it for anything.

That is why I cannot love war,
that is why I cannot love cruelty,
that is why I cannot love lies.

I know that in the sunlight,
I know that alongside love,
none of these can live:
injustice,
fear,
hunger…
— Necati Cumalı
Moral: To cherish the beauty of life is to stand for peace, compassion, and truth. A sunlit day is truly precious when people can enjoy it freely, without fear or hunger.

title: Justice and compassion
paragraphs: According to a tale told about the Gallipoli campaign, morphine was so scarce that it was given only to wounded soldiers who still had a chance of survival.
One day, among the severely wounded brought to Dr. Tarık Nusret was his own son. Seeing that he could not save him, the doctor made no exception for his son and withheld the injection.
Two hours later, his son died of his wounds. The father held his child’s lifeless body and whispered:
“Forgive me, my son... It was not yours to take.”

Moral: Refusing to let personal ties influence a decision can be a painful test. Yet justice and compassion must remain inseparable: even when recovery is no longer possible, a person’s suffering and dignity still matter.

title: Telling Lies
paragraphs: “Do you tell lies?”
“Yes.”
“What kind of lies?”
“A lie I tell only to myself. Every day, I say, ‘You’re stronger, more knowledgeable, and more capable than anyone else.’”
“Perhaps you really are?”
“No, I can’t claim that. There are people who are stronger, know more, or can do things better than I can.”
“Then why do you tell yourself that?”
“Believe it or not, those words motivate me. They make me want to work on myself—to become stronger, learn more, and improve my skills.”

Moral: You do not need to think you are better than everyone else. Saying “I can learn; I can improve” can give you strength too. Self-belief becomes a foundation for growth when it is matched by effort.
Bakhtiyar Sirajov

title: The welcoming smile
paragraphs: A smiling vinegar seller attracts more customers than a scowling honey seller.
Moral: People are drawn not only to what you offer, but also to how you offer it. A sincere smile and a warm welcome can leave a sweeter impression than honey.

title: Keep your self-respect
paragraphs: “Do not become gossip on people’s lips or dust beneath their feet,” says an Azerbaijani expression. It calls on us to preserve our dignity in words and actions, avoid getting caught up in gossip, and refuse to accept humiliation.
But remember: what people say about you does not always reflect how you live. You cannot silence every voice. What matters is staying true to your conscience and keeping your self-respect.

Moral: Do not let other people’s opinions become the measure of your life. Take responsibility for your words and actions, and protect your boundaries. Neither gossip nor someone else’s contempt determines your worth.

title: Every day has meaning
paragraphs: Do not dismiss any day of your life as wasted:

Good days bring joy,
difficult days bring experience,
the hardest days sometimes teach the deepest lessons,
and the happiest days become unforgettable memories.
Moral: A day’s meaning may not be clear while you are living it. Cherish joy and be kind to yourself in hardship. Understanding what an experience has taught you sometimes takes time.

title: Beyond complaining
paragraphs: A man with years of experience wants to teach a lesson to a group of people who keep complaining about the same problems.
He tells them a funny joke. Everyone laughs heartily.
A little later, he tells the same joke again. This time, only a few people laugh.
When he repeats it a third time, no one even smiles.

Repeating the same complaints without looking for a solution can have a similar effect: eventually, the words lose their impact and the listeners grow weary. Speaking about a problem matters, but repeating it does not, by itself, solve it.

Moral: Sharing your troubles can bring relief, but complaining alone does not change the situation. Looking for a way forward, asking for help, and taking a small step where possible can be the beginning of change.

title: Choose your confidant
paragraphs: Not every sorrow is for everyone to hear.
One day, someone may use the pain you confided in them to hurt you again.
Moral: Share your troubles with someone who understands you and honors your trust. Openness matters, but so does choosing whom to trust.

title: Other People’s Thoughts
paragraphs: One day, a man lost his comma (,). His words ran together, and he forgot where to pause for breath.
Another day, he lost his period (.). His thoughts stretched on endlessly; he could no longer finish one before moving to the next.
Then he lost his exclamation mark (!). His joy, anger, and wonder fell silent.
One day, he lost his question mark (?). He stopped asking questions and accepted everything he heard without question.
Next, he lost his colon (:). He forgot how to explain his thoughts or give reasons for what he said.
By the end of his life, all he had left were quotation marks.
And inside them were nothing but other people’s thoughts.

Moral: When we stop questioning, thinking, and expressing our feelings, we begin to lose our own voice. Learning from others is valuable, but repeating their thoughts must not take the place of thinking for ourselves.

title: Strengths and vulnerabilities
paragraphs: The peacock’s enemy is its beautiful tail.
The nightingale’s sweet song draws it into a cage.
The fox’s fine fur lures hunters to set their traps.
The qualities we admire and value in ourselves can sometimes become our vulnerabilities and bring us trouble.
Moral: What we consider an advantage can also leave us exposed to danger. Knowing our worth matters, but so does understanding where our strengths make us vulnerable.

title: Words to Avoid
paragraphs: Disagreements are part of family life. But the words we choose can either help us understand one another or damage the closeness between us.
“Stop talking nonsense!”
This tells your partner, “Your opinion does not matter to me.” You can disagree without dismissing what they say:
“I see this differently. I’d like to understand your point of view too.”
“You’re overreacting!”
Something that seems minor to you may deeply trouble your partner. Rather than dismissing their feelings, ask:
“What worries you most about this? I want to listen.”
“Look at her husband—or his wife! Why can’t you be like that?”
Comparisons can leave someone feeling inadequate and unappreciated. Instead of holding up another person as an example, explain what you need:
“It matters to me that we share the housework. Can we find an arrangement that works for both of us?”
“You wouldn’t understand!”
This closes the door to conversation. If you cannot find the words or are not ready to talk, say so honestly:
“I’m finding it hard to explain how I feel. Please give me a little time, and we can talk later.”
“Don’t go there! Don’t speak to that person! Don’t wear that!”

Your partner’s decisions are not yours to control. Explain your concerns, listen to their perspective, and seek agreement on matters that affect you both. Adding “please” to an order does not automatically make it a respectful request; you must also recognize the other person’s right to choose.
“This worries me. Can we talk about it and try to understand each other?”
Moral: Respect matters even when we disagree. Explain your feelings, make your needs clear, and listen in return. Closeness grows when we hear each other, not when we silence each other.

title: Strength and Sorrow
paragraphs: My God, grant me either the strength to bear my sorrows or only as much sorrow as I have the strength to bear.
Moral: No one can remain strong through every sorrow. Seeking strength, asking for help, and recognizing our limits in difficult times are not signs of weakness.

title: The Flower of Honesty
paragraphs: In a distant kingdom, a young prince was preparing to take the throne. By royal custom, he had to marry before his coronation. He invited the young women of the kingdom to the palace so that he could choose his future wife.
The daughter of a woman who worked at the palace loved the prince. When she heard about the invitation, she told her mother:
“I want to go too.”
Her mother was worried.
“The daughters of wealthy, distinguished families will be there. I’m afraid you’ll be disappointed.”
“I know, Mother. But I’d like the chance to meet him, even just once.”
On the appointed day, the palace hall filled with young women in beautiful gowns. The prince gave each of them a seed.
“Plant this and care for it,” he said. “Return in six months with the flower you have grown. I will marry the woman who brings the most beautiful flower.”
The young women went home full of hope.
The servant’s daughter planted her seed in a pot. Every day, she checked the soil, watered it as needed, and eagerly waited for the first green shoot. But days and weeks passed, and nothing appeared.
She sought advice from gardeners and followed their suggestions. Still, the seed did not sprout.
When the six months were over, her mother asked:
“Will you really go with an empty pot?”
The young woman looked down at it.
“Yes. I’ve done everything I could. I can’t take a different flower and pretend I grew it from his seed.”
At the palace, flowers bloomed in every color. Her own pot held only soil. Embarrassed, she stood to one side.
The prince entered the hall and examined the pots one by one. When he reached her, he asked:
“Where is your flower?”
“I cared for the seed for six months, but it never sprouted,” she replied. “I have no flower to show you.”
The prince listened carefully. Then he turned to the gathering.
“I have made my choice.”
He pointed to the young woman holding the empty pot.
A murmur of astonishment filled the hall.
“But she has no flower!”
“None of the seeds I gave you could grow,” the prince explained. “This young woman had the courage to bring me the result as it was. She has brought me the most precious flower of all: honesty.”

Moral: Honesty sometimes means having the courage to stand before everyone with an empty pot. There is no shame in falling short of the result you hoped for. Pretending you achieved it means betraying your conscience.

title: Plucking the goose
paragraphs: One bitter winter day, a king changed out of his royal robes and went for a walk with his grand vizier. They came upon an old man working beside a stream, dipping hides into the icy water and beating them as he worked the leather.
“Peace be upon you, venerable elder,” the king said.
“And upon you, ruler of the world,” the old man replied.
“What did you do during the six?” the king asked.
“Unless you add six to six, there isn’t enough for thirty-two.”
“And did you never get up in the night?”
“I did, Your Majesty. But other households have reaped the benefit.”
The king smiled.
“If I send you a goose, can you pluck it?”
“Certainly, Your Majesty—and without a squawk!”
The king and his vizier walked on. Once they were out of earshot, the king asked:
“Did you understand our conversation?”
“No, Your Majesty,” the vizier admitted.
“Then work it out before nightfall,” the king said sternly, “or you will answer with your head!”
After escorting the king back to the palace, the frightened vizier hurried to the stream. The old man was still at work.
“What were you and the king talking about?” he demanded. “You must explain!”
The old man looked him up and down.
“Each answer will cost you a hundred gold coins.”
The vizier had little choice. He handed over the money.
“First, how did you know he was the king?”
“I work with hides. One look told me what his fur coat was worth. Only a king could afford such a thing.”
The vizier produced another hundred coins.
“What did six have to do with thirty-two?”

“He was asking what I had done during the six months of summer, if I still had to work in this bitter cold. I told him that unless I worked six months in summer and six in winter, I couldn’t keep these thirty-two teeth fed.”
The vizier paid a third time.
“And what did he mean about getting up in the night?”
“He was asking whether I had children. I told him I did, but they were all daughters. They have married and now have households of their own to look after.”
The vizier paused before asking his final question.
“And the goose he promised to send you—who was that?”
The old man glanced at the gold and smiled.
“That one you can work out for yourself!”
Moral: Hearing the words is not the same as understanding them. High office does not guarantee wisdom; sometimes an ordinary person, taught by life, sees what a royal adviser cannot.

title: The Strongest Shield
paragraphs: Sometimes the strongest shield in life is the distance you know how to keep.
Moral: Keeping your distance in relationships that hurt you is an act of self-respect. Closeness matters, but so does protecting your personal boundaries.

title: The Three Best Things
paragraphs: A father said to his son:
“My son, we should strive for three things in life: to eat the finest food, sleep in the most comfortable bed, and live in the most beautiful home.”
The boy was puzzled.
“But, Dad, we’re poor. How can we have those things?”
His father smiled.

“When you’re hungry, even a simple meal tastes like the finest food. When you lie down tired after a day of hard work, your bed feels wonderfully comfortable. And when you make room for others in your heart and earn a place in theirs, you will find the most beautiful home of all.”
Moral: Life’s pleasures are not found only in expensive things. Savoring a simple meal, resting after honest work, and finding a place in people’s hearts can bring great happiness too.

title: Thought, word, and deed
paragraphs: Think good thoughts, for your thoughts are reflected in your words.
Speak with kindness, for your words pave the way for your actions.
Act with care, for repeated actions become habits.
Cultivate good habits, for they shape your values.
Honor your values, for they guide your choices, and your choices shape your life.
Moral: Our thoughts, words, actions, and habits are connected. By putting good intentions into everyday practice, we help steer our lives in a better direction.

title: Learning to say “yet”
paragraphs: Instead of saying, “I can’t do this,” say, “There are things I still need to learn. With more knowledge and practice, I can get better.”
Instead of saying, “I give up,” say, “What if I tried another way? If this approach hasn’t worked, a different one might help.”
Instead of stopping at “This is too hard,” say, “It’s difficult, but I can take it step by step. I need a little more time, effort, and perhaps some help.”
Instead of saying, “I can’t do any better,” say, “I’m pleased with what I’ve achieved, but I can keep learning and improving.”
Instead of blaming yourself with “I made a mistake—I wish I hadn’t,” ask, “How can I put it right? What have I learned from it?”
Instead of saying, “They’re so clever. I could never be like them,” say, “By looking at how they learn and work, I can find an approach that helps me.”

Moral: The way you speak to yourself influences your next step. Adding “yet” to “I can’t do this” leaves room for learning. A mistake becomes an opportunity to grow when you learn from it and try again.

title: Obstacles and opportunities
paragraphs: Sometimes life runs smoothly; at other times, unexpected difficulties arise. Obstacles are not always easy to overcome, but they can offer a chance to learn, find another way, and move forward.

Moral: Being shaken by hardship is not weakness. Give yourself time, ask for help if you need it, and let what you learn guide your next step. Sometimes an obstacle is where a new path comes into view.

title: The grocer's sticky fingers
paragraphs: A beekeeper brings several containers of honeycomb to a grocer to sell. They agree on a price and begin weighing it.

The grocer has only a one-kilogram weight, so he breaks the honeycomb into pieces by hand and weighs it a kilogram at a time. But before placing each new piece on the scales, he licks the honey from his fingers.
Once, twice, three times…
The beekeeper notices that some of his honey is reaching the grocer’s mouth before it reaches the scales. He objects, but the grocer carries on as though nothing has happened.
At last, the beekeeper loses patience.
“Come on, now! You’ve licked away half my honey!”
Still licking his sticky fingers, the grocer gives him a sly smile.
“No harm intended, my friend. You can’t handle honey without licking your fingers!”
Moral: It is natural to gain something from the work you do. But that is no excuse for helping yourself to someone else’s share.

title: Ali's unreliable rope
paragraphs: There was once a craftsman named Ali who made rope from flax fibers. He was careless about his work, and his ropes were weak. They often snapped and caused accidents. Before long, people began calling him “Ali of the Rotten Ropes.”
One day, a lamb fell into a deep well. A man who offered to rescue it asked the owner to fetch a rope. But as soon as he saw it, he shook his head.
“I know this rope. It’s Ali’s work. You can’t trust his rope to lower you into a well!”
The lamb’s owner smiled.
“Now, don’t be unfair to him. His rope will certainly get you down. Whether it will bring you back up—well, that I can’t promise!”
Moral: Trust is earned through the quality of your work. Carelessness does more than damage your reputation; it puts those who rely on you at risk.

title: Communication
paragraphs: Make time to talk with older people and children alike. In older people’s memories, you may discover lessons drawn from experience; in children’s questions, the beauty of seeing the world with fresh eyes.
Moral: Listening to older people helps us learn from lives already lived. Listening to children helps us rediscover wonder in ordinary things. Every age has something to teach us.

title: Language
paragraphs:
Language is a flower that blossoms on the tongue;
Without water and care, it withers away.
Moral: A mother tongue thrives when it is cherished. Keep it alive in your daily conversations, in the books you read, and in the words you teach your children.

title: Silence
paragraphs: Silence is the answer to some questions.
Either the time to answer has not yet come, or the person asking does not deserve a reply.
Moral: You do not owe an answer to every question. Sometimes wisdom lies in waiting for the right moment; sometimes, in remaining silent with someone who will not value your words.

title: The Silent Corridor
paragraphs: Two organizations were working together: one was the sponsor, and the other was the agency developing the project.

The project team worked tirelessly for months to prepare the documents. When everything was ready, they sent the materials to the sponsor and waited for a response. Days passed, then weeks. Still, there was silence.
The uncertainty within the team grew, spreading like a shadow along the corridor:
“Have the documents arrived? Have they been reviewed?”
No one knew. Inquiries to the sponsor brought only vague, evasive answers.
A few months later, the team decided to go directly to the sponsor’s office to clarify the matter. There, the truth finally emerged:
“Yes, we received the documents, but we have not accepted them. The submission format was wrong, and the required procedure hadn’t been followed.”
The team froze in place.
“Why didn’t you tell us that?” they asked.
“We could have corrected it right away.”
Frustrated, the employees returned to the office and complained to their management:
“We should have followed up, checked the status, and spoken clearly with the other side. Our time and effort were wasted, and our trust was shaken because the corridor between us stayed silent.”

Moral: When communication is unclear, even the best work can go unnoticed. When there is no consistent follow-up, even the strongest partnership weakens. Sometimes the greatest harm to a partnership is done not by failure, but by silence.
Bakhtiyar Sirajov

title: Well-chosen words
paragraphs: Those who choose their words thoughtfully need not regret them and apologize later.
Moral: Before you speak, consider how your words will affect the person listening. Words carry greater value when spoken at the right time, in the right setting, and with respect.

title: Share What You Know
paragraphs: Share what you know, but do not lecture others. Listen carefully, but do not take everything you hear as the truth.
Silence does not mean ignorance, just as talking a great deal does not mean knowing a great deal. Belittling others is foolish; showering them with undeserved praise is a sign of cowardice.

Moral: Share your knowledge with humility, think critically about what you hear, and know when to remain silent. Neither put people down nor place them on a pedestal. See them as they are and give them their due.

title: The Candles' Conversation
paragraphs: Four candles burned slowly in a room. It was so quiet that even their whispers could be heard.
The first candle spoke:
“I am Faith. When people neglect me, my light grows weak. I am about to go out.”
Its flame grew smaller until, at last, it disappeared.
The second candle said:
“I am Loyalty. When promises are forgotten and people turn their backs on one another, I lose my strength. I can hardly keep burning.”
Just then, a gentle draft put out its flame.
The third candle spoke sadly:
“I am Love. When people stop making time for one another and showing that they care, my light begins to fade. Sometimes even those closest to each other forget to say how much they love one another.”
As it finished speaking, its flame flickered and went out.
At that moment, a child entered the room. When the child saw the three unlit candles, their eyes filled with tears.
“You were meant to keep shining… Why have you gone out?”
Then the fourth candle spoke:
“Don’t be afraid. As long as I am burning, we can light the others again. I am Hope.”
The child wiped away the tears, carefully picked up the burning candle, and lit the others one by one. Once again, the room filled with light.
Moral: Hope gives us the strength to restore faith, loyalty, and love. If we keep that light alive and act on it, we can rekindle much that we thought had been lost.

title: Knowing what you know
paragraphs: (A Chinese proverb)
Those who do not know, and know that they do not know, are ready to learn. Teach them!
Those who know, but do not realize that they know, are asleep. Awaken them!
Those who do not know, and do not realize that they do not know, are foolish. Avoid them!
Those who know, and know that they know, can show the way. Follow them!

Moral: Wisdom begins with recognizing what you know and what you do not. Help those willing to learn, encourage those unaware of their knowledge, be wary of those confident in their ignorance, and learn from those who truly understand.

title: The Shepherd’s Word
paragraphs: Once, in a village, there lived a poor but honest shepherd named Hasan. One day, the local landowner summoned him.
“Hasan, I hear you know the mountain pastures well. This summer, I shall entrust my flock to you. If you bring the animals back healthy and well fed in the autumn, I shall give you a cow.”
Hasan agreed. All summer, through rain and heat, he tended the flock and kept watch over it at night. In the autumn, he brought the animals back to the village healthier and better fed than before.
He went to the landowner, hoping to receive the promised cow. But the man gave him a mocking smile.
“I never intended to give you a cow. I only said that to make you work harder. You’re poor anyway—what would you do with a cow?”
Tears filled Hasan’s eyes. Yet he composed himself and answered calmly.
“You’re right, sir. I am poor. But I have a conscience, and I keep my word. You may be wealthy, but if your word is worth nothing, you are the one who is truly poor.”

The shepherd’s words spread throughout the village. The landowner lost people’s respect, and they became reluctant to do business with him. He, too, eventually understood: a person’s worth is measured not by wealth or position, but by how faithfully they keep their word.
Moral: Our true wealth lies in our conscience, the promises we keep, and the trust we earn. Riches cannot guarantee respect, while a broken promise can undermine trust.

title: What Is a Word?
paragraphs:
Some words tear us apart;
some speak straight to the heart.
Moral: Words can hurt or heal. Their worth depends on the sincerity, kindness, and sense of timing with which they are spoken.

title: Words and Silence
paragraphs: Sometimes we say more by remaining silent. Words are more than sounds—they reveal our intentions.
If a word will wound a heart or a sentence extinguish hope, pause before you speak.
If what you are about to say offers neither understanding nor comfort and serves no good purpose, silence may be the better choice.
Remember: not every word blossoms. Some are thorns that wound whatever they touch.
Silence can hold wisdom. Sometimes it is the most meaningful answer.
Words spoken thoughtfully and from the heart can give someone strength. Careless words can leave wounds that take a long time to heal.
Choose both your words and your silences with care. Silence speaks too—sometimes more deeply and more honestly than words.
Moral: The worth of words lies not in how many we speak, but in the good they do. Think before you speak, and be mindful of what your silence says.

title: Call the Shepherd
paragraphs: After many years of study, a student came to his teacher to ask for his blessing before setting out.
“You shall have my blessing,” the teacher said, “but first you must answer a question. Let me see how well you have understood what I have taught you.”
“Please, Master, ask,” the student replied confidently.
“Imagine you are returning to your village. Along the way, a shepherd’s dogs rush at you. What would you do to protect yourself?”
“I would pick up some stones and throw them at the dogs to drive them away.”
“You might drive away one or two. But what if they all came at you together?”
The student thought for a moment.
“Then I would run.”
“And if the dogs ran faster and caught up with you?”
The student fell silent. Unable to think of another way out, he asked:
“What should I do, Master?”

“Call the shepherd,” the teacher replied. “Ask him to call off his dogs. You thought about fighting each dog yourself, but it never occurred to you to ask for help from the person who could calm them.”
Moral: Not every difficulty can be overcome alone or by force. Sometimes the wisest step is to find someone who can influence the situation and ask for help.

title: A Different Path
paragraphs: One day, a cow returning to its barn had to cross a forest where there was no path. It climbed uphill, wandered downhill, and wound its way around trees and bushes, leaving a crooked trail behind it.

The next day, a dog followed the trail to reach the other side of the forest. Then came a flock of sheep. Seeing a path already there, the shepherd led his flock along it without looking for another route.
Before long, people began using it too. They turned this way and that, ducked beneath branches, and complained about the difficult walk. Yet no one stopped to ask:
“Could there be an easier way?”

As more feet passed over it, the trail widened into a road. People and laden animals spent three hours reaching a place they could have reached in half an hour by a more direct route. Still, everyone followed in the footsteps of those who had gone before.

Years passed. A town grew where the forest had stood. The old road became a main thoroughfare and eventually the town’s busiest street. The bends the cow had made while wandering among the trees remained unchanged.
Now cars became stuck along those same bends. Everyone complained about the traffic, but few wondered why the road followed such a route.
At the edge of town, the old forest seemed to whisper:
“One cow’s wandering footsteps have determined the path of generations…”

Moral: A path is not necessarily the best one simply because it has been used for years. Before following a habit, try to understand its purpose. Sometimes progress means changing your route, not walking faster.

title: A Human Being Emerged
paragraphs: I multiplied thought by heart—and the result was love.
I added effort to love—and the result was devotion.
I divided bread with conscience—and the result was justice.
I added love, effort, conscience, devotion, and justice—and the result was a human being.
— Attributed to Yaşar Kemal
Moral: Love, effort, conscience, devotion, and justice make us truly human. Our humanity shows when we put these values into practice, not merely into words.

title: Appearances Can Be Deceptive
paragraphs: A father wolf is teaching his cub about life. He points to a flock of sheep and says:
“Their meat tastes good.”
Then he points to the shepherd.
“But his stick stings. Be careful.”
The cub notices the dog beside the shepherd and exclaims happily:
“Look, Dad! He looks like us!”
The father replies:
“Run when you see him, my boy. We’ve suffered most at the hands of those who look like us but aren’t on our side.”

Moral: Sometimes the greatest harm comes from those who resemble us but have very different intentions. To protect ourselves, we must look beyond outward similarities and recognize deceit before it is too late.

title: Sharpen the axe
paragraphs: A hunter walking through a forest came upon a curious sight. A woodcutter was swinging his axe with all his strength, yet making little progress. Sweat ran down his forehead, and every blow took a tremendous effort.
The hunter approached him.
“Your axe is blunt. Why not stop for a moment and sharpen it? The work would be much easier.”
The woodcutter stared at him in surprise.
“What are you talking about? I haven’t got time to sharpen my axe. I still have twenty more trees to cut down!”
Moral: Working efficiently means thinking about how we work, not just how hard. Time spent preparing and improving our tools is not wasted; it saves effort later.

title: A Windmill Turning Without Wind
paragraphs: When a windmill turns without wind, someone is blowing.
Moral: What you see may have a cause you cannot see. Look beyond the result to understand what sets it in motion.

title: At the Bookstore
paragraphs: After a long search, a medical student found the book he needed in a bookshop. He picked it up eagerly, but his smile faded when he saw the price on the back. He could not afford it.

Hiding his disappointment, he leafed through the pages until he found the section his lecturer had assigned. Seeing that the staff were busy with customers, he stood to one side and began reading. He remembered as much as he could, then put the book back and quietly left.
For the next month, he returned every other day. He studied among the shelves, believing no one had noticed.
A week before his final exams, he came back as usual. This time, the book was missing. He searched shelf after shelf, growing increasingly anxious.
As he was about to leave empty-handed, a member of staff called him over.
“Come and sit down. There’s something we’d like to tell you.”
He took the book from beneath the desk and placed it in front of the student.
“A customer wanted to buy this the other day. But we could see you hadn’t finished reading it, so we put it aside for you. Whenever you come in, you can sit here and study in comfort.”

For a moment, the student could not find the words to reply. He had thought he was going unnoticed. Yet the bookshop staff had understood his difficulty all along and helped him without embarrassing him.
Years later, he became a doctor. He never forgot the kindness he had received at the bookshop: he treated patients who could not afford his care without charging them.
Moral: Kindness that preserves a person’s dignity can leave a lifelong impression. The care you show one person may, through them, reach many others.

title: At the Doctor's Office
paragraphs: I was waiting for my doctor’s appointment. Having missed breakfast at home, I had bought a sandwich and some apple juice from the café.
As I began to eat, I noticed a boy sitting by the window watching me. He kept looking at the food in my hands.
“He must be hungry,” I thought.
I felt sorry for him. I went back to the café and bought him a sandwich and juice too. He thanked me and began eating eagerly. I felt pleased, thinking I had helped someone.
Just then, his mother returned from the reception desk. Seeing the food in his hands, she hurried over, alarmed.
“Did you give him that?”
I nodded.
“The doctor said he mustn’t eat before his examination… I’ve taken time off work, and we’ve come a long way. Now we may have to reschedule.”
Her eyes filled with tears. I did not know what to say. A moment earlier, I had been certain I was doing something kind. Now I realized that I had never asked why the boy had not eaten.
“I’m sorry… I wanted to help, but I should have asked you first.”
I sat there holding my half-eaten sandwich. I had noticed the boy’s gaze, but acted without understanding his situation.
Moral: Good intentions do not always guarantee a good outcome. Asking, listening, and understanding the situation before offering help are also acts of compassion.

title: Another day
paragraphs: The day began... The day ended...

Every morning when we open our eyes, we see that a new day has begun. Yet often we do not notice when evening arrives or when another day slips away from our lives. Time flows like a quiet river, while we stand on its bank, watching the passing moments drift away.

Sometimes we ask ourselves: What wisdom lay behind God's gift of this day to me? Did I cherish this divine trust? What did I add to this day, and what did I take from it? What light did I bring to my soul, and what opportunity did I let slip away?

The greatest treasure in a human life is time. For other things we lose may sometimes return, but not even a single moment that has passed comes back. That is why every day, every hour, and even every breath has its own value and meaning.
And so, I have lived another day... In the endless book of time, another page of my life has turned. Only God truly knows what was written on that page.
Moral: Every new day is a precious trust given to us. Reflecting at the end of the day on how we have spent it helps us live more meaningfully tomorrow.
Etibar Siracsoy

title: Small changes, great value…
paragraphs: A monotonous life quietly wears down the human spirit. When every day is the same as the one before, when the same tasks are repeated, or when time passes without our doing anything at all, an invisible emptiness and a sense of inner unease take hold. For the spirit, like life itself, longs for movement, change, and something new.

Sometimes a small change enters our lives, and it is as though a new window opens within us. Ordinary days suddenly take on color, and our hearts fill with a pleasant excitement, a zest for life, and a sense of well-being. In truth, the beauty of life lies not only in the chance events that come our way, but also in how much beauty and freshness we ourselves can bring into it.

We should not be mere spectators in our own lives. Sometimes choosing a new path, meeting someone new, seeing a new place, learning, creating, or making time for something we love is enough to change the color of life. For something new need not be a major event; sometimes a small step can greatly lift our spirits.

Life is not a page handed to us already written. We write each day ourselves. It is therefore in our own hands to fill the pages of our lives not with repetition, but with new feelings, new dreams, and beautiful memories.
Moral: We do not need to wait for major changes to bring something new into our lives. Even a little time devoted to learning and the things we love can give meaning to our day.
Etibar Siracsoy

title: Seeing without understanding
paragraphs: Some people think that because their eyes are open, they see everything. Yet they miss the meaning of what they see, the pain of those they pass, and the truth right before them.
Moral: Truly seeing takes attention, reflection, and compassion. It means understanding what you notice and caring about the suffering you recognize.

title: The Dry Well
paragraphs: One day, a farmer’s donkey fell into an old, dry well. Hearing the animal’s distressed braying, the farmer called his neighbors for help.
For hours, they tried to get the donkey out. Everyone had a suggestion, but nothing worked. Eventually, they gave up hope and decided to fill the well with earth.
They each took a shovel and began throwing earth into the well. As the first shovelfuls landed on its back, the donkey brayed even louder. Then, after a while, it fell silent.
The farmer peered into the well and could hardly believe what he saw. The donkey was shaking each shovelful off its back and stepping onto the earth beneath its feet.
With every shovelful, it rose a little higher. The earth meant to bury it was becoming a stairway to safety.
At last, the donkey reached the top of the well and stepped out unharmed, to everyone’s astonishment.

Moral: Life sometimes places a heavy burden on your back. When you can, shake it off, find your footing, and take another step upward. Sometimes the very thing that makes life difficult can become part of the way out.

title: The Diderot Effect
paragraphs: In his essay Regrets on Parting with My Old Dressing Gown, the eighteenth-century French philosopher and writer Denis Diderot describes how a single possession can lead to a succession of new expenses.
It all begins with a luxurious scarlet dressing gown.
When Diderot puts it on, the room where he once felt comfortable suddenly looks different. None of his old belongings has changed, yet beside the beautiful gown they now seem shabby and out of place.
The simple furnishings that once served him well no longer satisfy him.

One change leads to another. A leather armchair replaces his plain chair. An ornate cabinet takes the place of his wooden bookshelf. The pictures and decorations change. Eventually, even his old worktable gives way to an expensive writing desk.

The room becomes more elegant, but Diderot feels less at ease. The new gown has changed not only what he wears, but how he sees everything around him. Things he never needed before now seem essential.
He sums up his predicament:
“I was the master of my old dressing gown; I have become the slave of the new one.”
He decides to keep his old rug. Let that modest possession remind him of his former life and keep him from losing himself in luxury.

Today, the urge to follow one new acquisition with other purchases to match it is known as the Diderot effect. Sometimes a purchase does more than meet a need: it creates needs we did not have before.

Moral: One new possession does not require you to replace everything around it. Before buying something, ask yourself: “Do I really need this, or do I only want it to match something else?” Let your belongings make life easier, not dictate your choices.

title: Dreaming
paragraphs: Allah does not make you dream of something that He will not grant.
Moral: Every dream that takes root in the heart has a purpose. Allah does not place in the heart a wish He will not grant — do not lose hope.

title: Free Time
paragraphs: Some people talk to you when they have time to spare. Others make time to talk to you.
Moral: Time is a treasure we cannot recover once it is gone. Cherish those who willingly make room in their lives to listen to you and be there for you.

title: An Istanbul Woman Remembers
paragraphs: It was during the occupation of Istanbul. I had just finished school, and families were beginning to visit ours with marriage proposals.
One day, a young man came with his family. He introduced himself as a lawyer. He was tall, handsome, and quietly composed. We liked each other and became engaged.
I loved him. At night, I worked by lamplight, embroidering linens for the home I imagined we would share. Every stitch held a hope for our future.
Then a rumor spread through the neighborhood.
“Ayşe’s fiancé isn’t a lawyer at all. He earns his living carrying coffins outside the mosque.”
What hurt most was not the work itself, but the thought that he had lied to me.
My father and I went to the mosque. From a distance, we saw him carrying a coffin with several other men.
We took that sight as proof of everything we had heard. Without having an honest conversation with him, we broke off the engagement.
Five years passed. I married and had a son. The occupation was over.
One day, walking through the city with my little boy, I met him again. He stopped when he saw me, then spoke hesitantly:
“If you have time, may I invite you for a cup of tea?”
I agreed. We went to a nearby law office. His name was on the door.
I could not hide my surprise.
“So you really are a lawyer?”
“Yes.”
“Then why were you carrying coffins outside the mosque?”
He was silent for a while. Then he lowered his head.

“I wish I could have explained it to you then. The city was occupied. Roads and goods were being checked. We were helping to send weapons to those fighting for independence in Anatolia. The coffins you saw contained weapons. We carried them as though we were taking part in a funeral. Revealing that secret could have put other people’s lives at risk. I couldn’t even tell you.”
This time, I was the one who fell silent.
The scene I had witnessed years before had not changed. But its meaning had changed completely. I had seen the coffin on his shoulder. I had known nothing of the responsibility he carried.

Moral: What you see may be only part of the truth. Before passing judgment, ask, listen, and try to understand. Behind an ordinary-looking act, someone may be carrying a responsibility you cannot see.

title: Hayat's Life Story
paragraphs: I was six and my brother was eight when our mother left home. Even then, I understood why she had left our father. What I could not understand was why she had not taken us with her.
In my child’s mind, one question kept returning: how could a mother leave her children?
My father beat her. He beat my brother and me too. I thought all men were like that. I thought this happened in every home.
After my mother left, our house felt like four walls and nothing more. No one called in the morning, “Wash your hands and faces. Breakfast is ready.” No one asked whether we had eaten.
The hardest lesson was this: sometimes growing up does not take years. One day of feeling utterly alone is enough.
I grew up at six.
About ten days after she left, the police came. They told us our mother had taken her own life. She had left a letter. On the envelope were the words: “For my daughter and my son.”
I could not read yet. My brother read it aloud. We both cried.
It was much later that I learned what had happened during those ten days. I was nineteen when my grandmother told me, as she lay dying.

My mother had sought shelter at her parents’ home. But her father did not want her there. He believed a woman belonged in her husband’s house, whatever happened. Even with a mouth full of blood, she was supposed to say she had been drinking sweet red sherbet.
My mother had begged him:
“Let me stay for a month. I’ll find a way. Then I’ll bring my children and make a new life.”

But my grandfather cared more about what people would say than about what his daughter had suffered. To him, a separated woman living on her own brought shame on the family. He had even told her she would be better off dead.
That evening, my mother died by suicide.
When my father heard the news, we saw no sign of grief. He told us he was sending us to a children’s home. That would be our home now.
My brother and I were terrified of being separated. We thought we might forget each other. We both needed to keep our mother’s letter.
But how could one letter go to two places?

My brother took a pair of scissors and cut the page down the middle. He gave me the half with the beginnings of the sentences. When I learned to read, he said, I could imagine how they ended. He already knew the whole letter by heart.
When my aunt heard we were being sent away, she came to see my father.
“You can’t send a girl there. I’ll take Hayat.”
I thought I was finally going to have a home. Instead, I learned that my aunt saw me less as a child who needed care than as another pair of hands.
She hardly ever used my name. She called me Slowcoach.
“Slowcoach, fetch some water.”
“Slowcoach, wash these dishes.”
My brother visited once a month. He said he was all right at the children’s home. I said I was all right too. I did not want to upset him.
Was he saying the same thing for the same reason?
I never dared to ask.
When I started school, I was the first in my class to learn to read. My mother’s letter was waiting for me.
My half began:
“Hayat, my beautiful girl, I…”
Every night, I finished that sentence differently.
“…love you so much.”
“…long to hold you again.”
“…am waiting for you.”
From those unwritten words, I built a world. My mother was there. I was not alone. Nobody shouted at me.
Real life hurt enough. At least in my imagination, I could be happy.
When I was fifteen, my aunt decided I had had enough schooling. But I wanted to study, earn a living, stand on my own feet, and share a home with my brother.
That summer, the wife of Hasan, our neighborhood grocer, died of cancer. She left three children: Sami, six; Elif, five; and Zehra, two.
I cried for them. Would they search for their mother’s familiar scent too? Would someone forget their names and call them Slowcoach?
While I worried about the children, the adults were deciding my future.
I learned that I was to be married to Hasan. The price was eight bracelets and three thousand lira.
I was too young for a civil marriage. Forty days later, they arranged a religious wedding.
I was fifteen. Still a child, yet expected to be a wife to a grown man and a mother to three children.
My aunt insisted I should have a baby of my own as well.
“That will secure your place in the family.”
Hasan first slapped me because I called him Uncle Hasan, as I always had.
“What woman calls her husband Uncle?”
I said nothing. I had learned silence long before.
But inside me was another question: what grown man calls a fifteen-year-old child his wife?
The three children clung to their father’s legs.
“Don’t hit Hayat! She plays with us. She tells us stories!”
To them, I was a big sister. And the stories I told them were my own dreams.
After Hasan left, I stood before the mirror and tried to say his name without “Uncle.” I could not. I still saw the older man I had always known, not a husband.
Six-year-old Sami came over.
“Mom used to call him Bey. You could call him that.”
Bey was a respectful form of address. That, at least, I could say.
I bent down and kissed him. Then I called Elif and Zehra over and began a new story.

“Once upon a time, there was a six-year-old girl called Fairy Tale. She had lost her mother and searched everywhere for her. When she could not find her, she went to the land of dreams. There, nobody hurt her or left her alone…”
In my stories, Fairy Tale always smiled. Each day I added a little more happiness to her life. The children listened, and I told my stories. In those moments, we could all breathe.

I called him Hasan Bey now. There were peaceful days and days when he grew angry. For years, I tried to explain his anger, sometimes blaming myself. He thought he had brought home a wife; I was a girl who played with his children and told them stories.
But being a child was not my fault.
My brother kept visiting. Each time, he offered me his half of the letter. Each time, I refused.
I was afraid to read it. For years, I had filled those missing lines with hope. I feared the real words would destroy the world I had built.
By the time I was forty, the children had grown up.
Sami became a doctor and moved to another city. When he was unhappy, he called.
“Hayat, tell me a story.”
Elif became a teacher and married. When her daughter was born, she wanted to name her Hayat. I asked her not to.
“Then we’ll call her Masal—Fairy Tale,” she said.
And that became my granddaughter’s name.
Zehra became a vet.
“When an animal is frightened, I tell it a story,” she would say with a smile. “My voice helps it settle.”
She married too, and I gained a grandson.
I was forty-five when Hasan—the man I had called Bey for so many years—died. I grieved for him. His last words were:
“Please forgive me for the wrong I’ve done you.”
I forgave him sincerely. Over the years, I had known kindness from him too. But forgiving him did not make what had happened to me as a child right.
I cannot extend that forgiveness to those who see nothing wrong with marrying off fifteen-year-old girls;
to those who turn abused daughters away in the name of family honor;
or to those who ignore a helpless child’s plea and defend the people responsible.
My name, Hayat, means “life.”
Yet for so many years, I was not allowed to choose my own.

Moral: No tradition or notion of family honor can justify violence or taking away a child’s future. Children belong in safe homes and classrooms, not forced marriages. Someone asking for help needs protection, not judgment.

title: The cost of indifference
paragraphs: When I asked one of our employees how he was getting on with an assigned task, his reply disappointed me deeply.
“The world won’t fall apart if I don’t do it in the next few days.”

True, I thought, the world would not fall apart. But what about the trust between us? Would that not collapse too? Would that attitude not harm our working relationship, our mutual respect, and our shared work?

A delay of a few days was not the real issue. It was his attitude toward a commitment. Responsibility means not only doing the work but also keeping your word, honoring the trust others place in you, and making sure people can rely on you.

It is wrong to treat a commitment so irresponsibly. Even more troubling was the way he expressed that attitude. To me, such an answer sounds rude, to say the least, and shows too little respect for the other person’s time, effort, and trust.

I admit that these words broke my heart. I knew then that we could not continue working together in quite the same way. A professional relationship depends on trust, and when trust is shaken, the partnership also faces a serious test.

Most disappointing of all, my colleague did not recognize that his words were inappropriate, apologize, or complete the task. Because my trust in him had been shaken, I had to solve the problem another way.

The experience reminded me that an organization’s most valuable asset is not time, money, or technology, but the trust people place in one another. It can take years to build and can sometimes be lost with a single sentence.
Moral: Trust is an organization’s most valuable asset. It can take years to earn and a single sentence to lose. Those who keep their word protect that trust.
Bakhtiyar Sirajov

title: A different door
paragraphs: One day, Jamal went to see his manager, Mr. Selim. He had heard that promotions were coming up and wanted to say that he hoped to be considered.
Mr. Selim listened, then replied:
“Jamal, I’m pleased with your work. But I don’t think this company is the right fit for you. We’ve decided to end your employment.”
Jamal had arrived hoping for a promotion. The news stunned him, and he left the company deeply disappointed.
Two years later, they met again. After exchanging greetings, Jamal told his former manager that he had started his own company and that business was going well. Mr. Selim was delighted to hear it.
Jamal said:

“At the time, your decision was very hard to accept. Looking back, though, I can see that losing my job pushed me to explore other possibilities. I started my own business and began doing work I love. I’m happy with my life now. What felt like an ending became a new beginning, and I’m grateful for that.”

Moral: A door that will not open is not always the end of the road. Sometimes losing an opportunity prompts us to seek a path that suits us better. What matters is not remaining trapped in disappointment, but recognizing new possibilities and taking action.

title: It’s Pointless
paragraphs: There is no point in advising someone who refuses to listen, arguing with someone unwilling to understand, or befriending someone who is two-faced.
Moral: Who you give your time and trust to shapes your life. Time spent in relationships without mutual respect and sincerity cannot be reclaimed.

title: Never Lost
paragraphs:
Kindness offered from the heart,
an act shaped by love,
a sincerely spoken word,
a gesture of courtesy,
a smile full of affection,
a step taken in the name of justice,
respect for the values we hold dear—
none of these is ever lost. They light the way for others and bring warmth to your own life and peace to your heart.
Moral: Sincere words and kind deeds leave a lasting mark. The light you bring into someone else’s life brightens your own as well.

title: An audience of one
paragraphs: A lecturer was invited to give an educational talk in a village. When he entered the hall, he found just one man sitting there. He greeted him and asked:
“No one else has come. What do you think—should we go ahead with the lecture?”
His sole listener replied:
“Sir, I’m a stable hand. I look after twenty horses. If nineteen ran away and only one remained, I wouldn’t leave it hungry and thirsty. I’d still feed it and give it water.”
Encouraged by these words, the lecturer began. He talked at great length. When he finally finished, he asked:
“Well, did you enjoy my lecture?”
The stable hand replied:
“I look after horses, so I didn’t understand much of what you said. But I do know one thing: just because only one horse is left, I wouldn’t give it enough feed for twenty!”
Moral: Speaking well is not the same as speaking at length. A useful talk meets the listener’s needs and offers as much as they can understand and absorb.

title: Life Is Short
paragraphs: Life is short. Spend it with people who bring you joy and make you feel loved.
Moral: The worth of a life is measured not only in years, but in the love and joy we share. Genuine relationships bring meaning to our lives and peace to our hearts.

title: The Liver
paragraphs: Why do Azerbaijani speakers call a close friend jan-jiyar, a beloved child jiyargusham, or someone precious to them jiyarparam? And why can aghjiyar, the word for “lung,” also describe a coward?
In Azerbaijani, jiyar is more than an anatomical term. It also appears in expressions of affection, closeness, sorrow, and character.

Similar associations existed in ancient cultures. In Mesopotamia, the liver was regarded as a seat of life, the soul, and emotions. When people sought to explain their inner world, they gave symbolic meaning not only to the heart but also to the liver.
Yet not every expression involving the liver can be traced to a single belief. Each expression has its own history and development.

Today, someone saying jiyarparam—literally “a piece of my liver”—is not thinking about anatomy. They mean that another person is as precious as a part of themselves. This is the power of language: a word for part of the body becomes an expression of our deepest feelings.
Moral: Language carries not only our thoughts but also the ideas of earlier generations. An everyday word can hold generations of love, sorrow, and ways of understanding the world.

title: Living in the Past
paragraphs: Living in the past is like walking while looking over your shoulder. With your eyes fixed on what is behind you, you miss the obstacles ahead and stumble. You can neither change what has happened nor see the opportunities opening up before you.
Moral: Learning from the past can guide you; remaining trapped in it holds you back. You cannot change yesterday, but you can choose the step you take today.

title: Newton’s Second Law
paragraphs: A physics teacher walks into the teachers’ lounge after a lesson and complains to his colleagues:
“These students just don’t get it! I explained Newton’s second law three times. By the end, even I understood it—but they still didn’t!”
Moral: Teaching begins with understanding. Before blaming students for not understanding, teachers should examine their own grasp of the subject and how they explain it.

title: Learning from loss
paragraphs: Do not see life only in terms of what you have lost. Recognize your successes and the lessons your setbacks have taught you. Even when things do not turn out as you hoped, the experience can help you find your next step.
Moral: A setback does not mean all your efforts were wasted. If you learn from what happened, you carry that experience with you as you move forward.

title: The Pawn and the King
paragraphs:
Do not look down on a pawn—
one day, he may rise to be king.

Do not feel secure just because you are king—
one day, you may be checkmated.
Moral: Never belittle someone because of their present position, or assume your own is unshakable. Those who seem powerless today may rise tomorrow, while the mighty may face defeat.

title: Draining the Coffers
paragraphs: One day, a king went out with his courtiers. As they passed through a village, they came upon an old man planting saplings in his field. The king called out:
“Why work so hard at your age, grandfather? You have been blessed with a long life, but you may not live to taste the fruit of these trees.”
The old man replied:
“We need not eat the fruit ourselves, my son. Those before us planted, and we enjoyed the harvest. Now let us plant so that those who come after us may enjoy it.”
The king was pleased with this answer and ordered that the old man be given a purse of gold.
Pointing to the purse, the old man smiled.
“You see, my son? Our saplings have already borne fruit.”
The king liked that answer too and ordered a second purse of gold to be brought.
The quick-witted farmer continued:
“Other people’s trees bear fruit once a year. Mine have borne fruit twice in a single day!”
The king laughed and ordered a third purse of gold. This time, the vizier hurriedly intervened:
“Your Majesty, we must leave! At this rate, the old man won’t just fill his field with trees—he’ll empty our coffers!”
Moral: You may never taste the fruit of every tree you plant. But just as you have benefited from the efforts of those before you, leave something good for the generations to come.

title: The Qualities of Water
paragraphs: Consider the qualities of water:
When it reaches a tree’s roots, it gives life.
When it meets fire, it puts it out.
It washes away dirt.
Mixed with flour, it becomes dough—the beginning of bread.
Its droplets form a rainbow in sunlight.
It brings life to the places through which it flows.
Left stagnant and unrefreshed, it can turn murky and foul.
The human heart is like water: honest conversation, shared joy, and mutual care renew it. If it goes too long without warm human connections, it too can grow stagnant.
Moral: Genuine connection, sharing, and mutual care nourish the heart. Solitude can bring peace, but we also need understanding and closeness.

title: Do you remember me?
paragraphs: “Hello, sir! Do you remember me? I used to be one of your pupils.”
“Yes, I do. I taught you in primary school. How lovely to see you after all these years! What do you do now?”
“I’m delighted to see you too. I became a teacher, just like you.”
