“That’s wonderful! What made you choose teaching?”
“You did. You were my example. I wanted to help children grow and teach them to believe in themselves.”
“That makes me very happy. But tell me, how did I become your example?”

“One day, a boy in our class came to school with a new watch his parents had bought him. My family couldn’t afford one. I liked that watch so much that, during the long break, I took it from his pocket.
“After the break, my classmate told you his watch was missing. You addressed the whole class:
“‘Whoever took it, please give it back.’
“No one said a word. So you closed the door and told us you would check all the boys’ pockets. I thought the most humiliating moment of my life had arrived.

“You lined us up along the wall and asked us to cover our eyes with our hands. Then you checked our pockets one by one. Even after you found the watch in mine, you carried on checking everyone else’s.
“Finally, you returned the watch to its owner. But you never said who had taken it. You didn’t speak to me or my parents about it that day—or at any time during the rest of the school year.
“You spared me the shame of being exposed in front of everyone. You didn’t let one thoughtless act define me as a thief. I understood how wrong I had been, but I didn’t feel worthless.

“It was a lesson I never forgot. I realized that teachers do more than pass on knowledge. They help children recognize their mistakes, learn from them, and believe they can become better people. I wanted to be a teacher like you.”
The teacher listened closely. Noticing his surprise, the young man asked:
“Don’t you remember? You found the watch in my pocket.”
“I remember what happened. But I didn’t know the watch was in your pocket.”
“How could you not know? You found it yourself!”
The teacher answered quietly:
“Because while I was checking your pockets, I had my eyes closed too.”

Moral: True teaching does not mean overlooking a mistake. It means helping someone put it right without stripping them of their dignity. Sometimes a single act of sensitivity towards a child can shape the course of a lifetime.

title: Living with loss
paragraphs: When two people love each other wholeheartedly and one dies, the one who truly dies is the one who survives.
Moral: The one left behind lives with longing and feels dead while still alive. Separation can make the depth of that love painfully clear.

title: A place in loving hearts
paragraphs: The most beautiful places in the world are the places you hold in the thoughts, prayers, and hearts of those you love.
Moral: The most beautiful places are not always found on a map. Being remembered with love, included in someone’s prayers, and cherished in someone’s heart brings a sense of belonging and peace.

title: Beyond the cotton field
paragraphs: We could barely read or write when a new teacher came to our village. We did not yet know that he would become more than a teacher to us—someone who would support us like an older brother or a father.
Mr. Aydin was saddened by the state of our school and the hardship we faced. When he learned that we were all expected to work in the cotton fields after leaving school, his eyes filled with tears.
He pointed to a road leading out of the village.
“Where does that road go?”
“To the cotton field,” we answered.
Then he pointed to another.
“And that one?”
We had no answer. We had never been beyond our village. As far as we knew, it was the whole world.
That day, he also asked what we wanted to be when we grew up. Again, we fell silent. We had never thought about it.
Mr. Aydin soon taught us to read and write. As the days passed, we read more confidently and learned to put our thoughts on paper.
One day, he brought a bundle of letters to class. He said they had been written by doctors, engineers, scientists, and people in other professions.
“From now on, they will be your pen friends,” he told us.

For years, we received letters from people we had never met. They wrote about their work, what gave life meaning, and the importance of knowledge and education. Each letter opened a window onto a world we had never known.
Until then, we had never even dreamed of continuing our education or doing anything other than growing cotton. We believed there was only one road ahead of us: the road to the cotton field.
Through our pen friends, we began to dream. We started to understand where that other road out of the village might lead.

With Mr. Aydin’s help, we finished school and continued our studies. Years passed. Some of us were preparing to become doctors, others engineers or teachers. A future we had once had no words for was beginning to take shape.
Then, one day, another letter arrived:
“My dear children,
“Never stop dreaming. Your dreams can give you direction; your effort and determination will bring you closer to them.
“My heartfelt congratulations to you all. I have always believed you could succeed.

“Your pen friend,
Mr. Aydin.”
We were astonished. All those letters we had believed came from people in different professions had been written by Mr. Aydin himself.
It was our own teacher who had shown us that other roads existed.

Moral: A good teacher offers children more than knowledge: they reveal possibilities the children cannot yet see. Discovering that there is more than one path gives a child the courage to choose a future.

title: Living well
paragraphs: Eat in moderation, walk twice as much, laugh three times as often, and love without limits.
A saying commonly described as a Tibetan proverb.
Moral: Eat moderately, stay active, remember to laugh, and love wholeheartedly. Sometimes it is these simple habits that make life richer.

title: The price of belonging
paragraphs: One day, a kindly old man receives a warning from above:
“Tomorrow, the water will taste different. Everyone who drinks it will lose their mind.”
He hurries home and fills every jar and vessel he can find with water.
The next morning, the warning comes true: one by one, those who drink the water lose their minds. The old man drinks only from the supply he has stored.
A week or two passes. Tired of being alone, he leaves his house to seek company. But whenever he exchanges a few words with anyone, they laugh at him.
“Have you gone mad? You belong in an asylum!”

He cannot make anyone understand. At last, unable to bear the pressure, he returns home and smashes the jars and vessels holding his water. Then he goes to the fountain everyone else drinks from, drinks its water, and lies down to sleep.

Moral: Widespread agreement does not turn wrong into right. Sometimes people give up their own judgment and convictions just to be accepted. The real test is to preserve independent thought under pressure, rather than simply become like everyone else.

title: The empty boat
paragraphs: My teacher used to tell this story:
“When I was young, I often went to the lake to be alone with my thoughts. I had a small boat and would spend hours on the water, finding peace in the stillness.
“One morning, just as dawn was breaking, I was sitting in my boat with my eyes closed, lost in thought.
“Suddenly, another boat struck mine. I jolted out of my reverie, furious. I opened my eyes, ready to scold whoever was steering it. But the boat in front of me was empty.
“There was no one to take my anger out on.
“I closed my eyes again. The collision that had made me so angry a moment earlier now seemed different: no one had done it deliberately. By sunrise, I was calm again.
“That empty boat taught me a lesson I never forgot. Ever since, whenever someone upsets me, I tell myself:
“‘This boat is empty too.’”
Moral: Do not look for malice behind every unpleasant incident. Giving yourself a moment to understand what has happened can help you respond without being swept away by anger.

title: Three Questions
paragraphs: One day, a king summoned his vizier.

“I shall ask you three questions,” he said. “If you cannot answer them by tomorrow, you will be dismissed from court. First: what does God bear patiently? Second: what does God keep hidden? Third: what does God change through His wisdom and power?”

However hard the vizier thought, he could find no answers. He returned home that evening in distress. He had a clever, perceptive servant who noticed his troubled expression and asked what was wrong. The vizier told him what had happened.

“I know the answers to all three questions,” the servant said. “I shall give you two now and the third tomorrow. God bears patiently the complaints His servants utter in sorrow, and He keeps their faults hidden.”
The following day, the vizier went before the king and gave these two answers. The king was pleased.
“Did you think of those yourself, or did someone teach you?”
The vizier told the truth.
“My clever servant taught me, Your Majesty.”
The king had the servant brought to court and ordered the vizier:
“Take off your robe of office and give it to him.”
The vizier removed his robe, and the servant put it on. The vizier, in turn, dressed in the servant’s old clothes.
Bewildered by what had happened, he asked:
“What about the third answer? What does God change through His wisdom and power?”
The servant smiled.
“Have you still not understood? In an instant, He makes a vizier a servant and a servant a vizier!”
Moral: No position is ours forever, and wisdom is not confined to those of high rank. Never take your status for granted or look down on someone because of theirs.

title: Three Scenes
paragraphs: A young man set out on a journey and encountered three strange scenes along the way.

First, he saw people sowing wheat in a field. As soon as the grains touched the soil, they sprouted, grew, and formed ears of wheat. Yet instead of harvesting the ripe crop, the farmers set the field on fire.

A little farther on, he came across a man struggling to lift a large stone. No matter how hard he tried, he could not raise it. But when he placed a second stone on top, he lifted them both. After adding a third, he lifted the load even more easily. Unable to make sense of what he had seen, the young man continued on his way.

The third scene was stranger still. A man was riding a sheep, with several people clinging to his shoulders. The sheep was running swiftly. Others ran behind them, but however hard they tried, they could not catch up.
Pondering these sights, the young man reached a city. At its entrance, he greeted a kindly old man, who stopped to speak with him. The traveler described the strange scenes and asked what they meant.
The old man said:
“The farmers represent people who do good and then diminish its value by boasting about it. With their own hands, they burn the harvest they have grown.”
He continued:

“The man lifting stones represents how people become accustomed to wrongdoing. The first time someone does wrong, their conscience weighs heavily on them. Unless they feel remorse and change their ways, doing it again becomes easier. An unrepented sin can open the door to another.”
“And the sheep and the people riding it?” the young man asked.

“In that symbolic scene,” the old man replied, “the sheep carries people towards Paradise. Those riding it represent religious scholars, while those clinging to their shoulders represent believers from all walks of life. Those running behind, unable to catch up, represent people who remain distant from faith.”

Moral: Do not overshadow your kindness with boasting or silence your conscience by growing used to wrongdoing. When seeking guidance, turn to people whose knowledge, integrity, and actions are in harmony.

title: Three Statues
paragraphs: The rulers of two neighboring countries were close friends. One day, one of them decided to send the other a birthday gift. He summoned his finest sculptor and asked him to make three gold statues, each a handspan tall and identical in appearance. Yet there was to be a hidden difference known only to the ruler and the craftsman.
When the statues were ready, they were sent to the neighboring ruler with a letter:

“To celebrate your birthday, I present you with these three gold statues. At first glance, they look exactly alike. Yet one is more valuable than the other two. When you discover which one it is, please let me know.”
The recipient first had the statues weighed. All three weighed exactly the same. They were measured and examined from every angle, but no difference could be found.
The ruler invited people knowledgeable about art to his palace. Everyone studied the statues carefully. Days passed, but the mystery remained unsolved.
At last, he heard of someone who might be able to solve the riddle and had the man brought to court.
After examining the statues, the man asked for a thin wire. He inserted it into the ear of the first statue. It emerged from the other ear.
When he inserted it into the second statue’s ear, it came out through the mouth.
But when he put the wire into the third statue’s ear, it stayed inside and did not emerge anywhere.
The mystery was solved. The ruler sent his friend this reply:
“These three statues represent three kinds of people.
“With the first, whatever is heard goes in one ear and out the other.
“The second repeats whatever is heard without thinking.
“The third keeps what is heard in the heart, knowing when to remain silent and when to speak.
“The third statue is the most valuable, for it represents someone who knows how to listen, honor another’s trust, and speak at the right moment.
“Thank you for this meaningful gift.”
Moral: Wisdom lies not only in listening, but in what we do with what we hear. Protect what is entrusted to you, think before speaking, and choose the right words at the right time.

title: Stronger together
paragraphs: By sharing, we are fed;
divided, we fade away.
— Attributed to Yunus Emre
Moral: Sharing brings abundance to our tables and strength to our unity. We grow weaker when we drift apart and stronger when we support one another.

title: Searching
paragraphs: Looking for something where it cannot be found is not searching; it is deceiving yourself—like seeking loyalty in the disloyal, decency in the shameless, or compassion in someone without a conscience.
Moral: See people as their actions reveal them to be, rather than as you wish they were. Do not build your hopes on expectations alone; consider both their words and their deeds.

title: Two Bowls of Water
paragraphs: Long ago, there lived a ruler renowned for his wealth. Wherever he went, he took some of his treasure with him and delighted in displaying it.
He had a wise teacher whom he trusted deeply. One day, he asked him:
“You have seen much of the world. Tell me, what do you think of my power and wealth?”
Instead of answering, the teacher asked a question:
“Imagine, Your Majesty, that you are in a vast, scorching desert, on the verge of dying from thirst. Would you give half your wealth for a bowl of water that could save your life?”
“Of course I would!”
“And if your journey continued, your water ran out, and you once again faced death from thirst? Would you give the rest of your wealth for a second bowl?”
The ruler thought for a moment.
“To stay alive, I certainly would.”
The teacher smiled gently.
“Then do not boast too much of your riches, Your Majesty. It seems there are circumstances in which your entire fortune is worth no more than two bowls of water.”
Moral: Sometimes a blessing we take for granted is worth more than everything we own. Do not boast of your wealth; cherish the simple things that make life possible.

title: Not my concern
paragraphs: Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent had made the Ottoman Empire one of the most powerful states of his time. Yet one thought sometimes troubled him:
“Could the Ottoman Empire one day weaken and fall?”

According to tradition, he decided to share his concern with Yahya Efendi, a respected scholar whose mother had also nursed Suleiman as a baby. The sultan trusted his learning and spiritual insight, and wrote to him:
“What causes a state to collapse? Could the Ottoman Empire itself fall one day? I would like to hear your thoughts.”
Yahya Efendi’s reply was very short:
“What has it got to do with me, my sultan?”
Reading the letter at Topkapı Palace, Suleiman was astonished. He could not believe that Yahya Efendi would dismiss such a serious question.
“There must be a meaning in these words that I have missed,” he thought, and went to visit him at his Sufi lodge in Beşiktaş.
“My brother, I wrote to you about an important matter. Please give my question a serious answer,” he said, with a note of reproach.
Yahya Efendi replied:
“My sultan, how could I treat your question lightly? I considered it carefully and sent you my conclusion.”
“But I understood nothing from your answer. You wrote, ‘What has it got to do with me?’ It sounded as though you were telling me to leave you out of it.”
Yahya Efendi explained:

“My sultan, when oppression spreads through a state, when injustice runs unchecked, and those who witness it turn away saying, ‘What has it got to do with me?’, that state’s foundations begin to shake.

“When sheep are devoured not by wolves, but by the shepherds entrusted with their care; when those who know the truth remain silent and conceal it; when the cries of the poor, the needy and the defenseless rise to the heavens, yet only the stones seem to hear them—then the end draws near.

“In such a land, the treasury is depleted and the people lose trust. When rulers no longer respect the people, and the people no longer believe in the state, order breaks down and the state collapses from within.”
The sultan’s eyes filled with tears as he listened. He lowered his head in acknowledgment. Then he departed, thanking God that there was a scholar who would speak the truth to him without fear.

Moral: Injustice spreads not only through the power of those who commit it, but also through the indifference of those who say, “What has it got to do with me?” Protecting a society begins with each of us recognizing our own responsibility.

title: Before it is too late
paragraphs: Being late means not doing something when it needs to be done. In our relationships, however, delay can carry a much greater cost.

There is a time to express our love, to welcome the love offered to us, to forgive those who have hurt us and to apologize to those we have hurt. When we keep putting these things off, the distance between us can grow, and the opportunity may pass.

None of us is immune to making mistakes. We can all misjudge a situation, speak without thinking or hurt someone’s feelings. What matters is not delaying when it is time to admit a mistake, put it right and make amends. Life is short.
Let us try to live so that, looking back, we say “I’m glad I did” more often than “If only I had.” Making room for love, reconciliation and fairness today leaves less room for regret tomorrow.
Moral: Do not put off expressing love, apologizing or making amends. One sincere gesture today may spare you regret tomorrow.

title: What Matters in Life?
paragraphs: A teacher enters the classroom, greets the students and takes a glass jar from his bag. He places it on the desk and says:
“We each have one life. How we spend our time determines what we make room for.”
He fills the jar with golf balls and asks:
“Would you say the jar is full?”
“Yes!” the students reply together.
The teacher pours some pebbles into the jar and gently shakes it. They settle into the spaces between the golf balls.
“Is it full now?”
“Yes!” the students answer.
This time, he pours in some sand. It fills the remaining gaps between the pebbles.
“And now?”
Once again, the students agree that the jar is full.
The teacher explains:
“This jar represents your life. The golf balls are what matters most: your family, your friends, the people you love and your health.
“The pebbles are other important things, such as your work, your home and your possessions.
“The sand is the small stuff: everyday tasks and less important concerns.

“If I had filled the jar with sand first, there would have been no room for the balls or the pebbles. Life works much the same way. If you spend all your time and energy on the small stuff, you will have no room left for what matters most.
“First, decide what the ‘golf balls’ in your life are and make room for them. Then fit in the rest.”
Moral: When there is no time left for what matters most, sometimes it is your priorities that need another look. Do not let everyday concerns push family, love and health into the background.

title: Life's lessons
paragraphs: Throughout life, we keep learning:
from some people, patience, love, loyalty, faithfulness and decency;
from others, how to recognize hypocrisy, deceit, malice and betrayal.
Moral: The people we meet teach us different lessons: some show us who we want to be; others show us who we do not want to become. What matters is what we take from those lessons.

title: Where Does This Road Go?
paragraphs: A young man walking along a road comes across an elderly man sitting by the roadside.
“Excuse me, where does this road go?” he asks.
“Nowhere, son.”
“What do you mean? How can a road go nowhere?”
“Well, I’ve been here for fifty years, and that road hasn’t moved an inch. It’s the people who come and go.”
Moral: A road will not take you anywhere by itself. You must choose where you want to go—and take the steps to get there.

title: Without a plan
paragraphs: An organization without an action plan is like a ship with a known destination but no chart, no chosen route, and no assigned duties for its crew. It may reach port thanks to luck, a skillful captain, or favorable weather. But that would not be the result of systematic management. Lasting success needs more than fortunate circumstances: it requires careful planning and consistent action.

Over time, an organization without a plan also begins to lose its members. People are sustained not only by ideas, but by the hope of seeing those ideas put into practice. When hope fades, people leave; when people leave, the organization gradually weakens and eventually ceases to function.
Moral: A goal provides direction; a plan defines the path toward it. An organization may advance by chance without a plan, but lasting success requires deliberate and consistent action.
Bakhtiyar Sirajov

title: At the Fish Shop
paragraphs: On his way to the bus stop after work, a man paused outside a fish shop. Remembering how much his wife and daughter enjoyed fish, he went inside.
“A kilo, please… Actually, make it two.”
Just then, an elderly woman in a worn coat approached him hesitantly.
“Could you buy me a little fish too, please?”
Without hesitation, he turned to the fishmonger.
“Make that four kilos. Two for my family and two for her.”
Then he asked the woman:
“Do you have any bread at home?”
She shook her head. He went to the shop opposite, bought four loaves, and gave her two.
“Is there anything else you need?”
She took an empty bottle of eye drops from her pocket.
“I last bought these two months ago. I can’t afford another bottle. My sight hasn’t been as good lately…”

He took the bottle and went to the pharmacy. When he returned, the woman was sitting on a chair. The fishmonger had brought it out so she would not have to stand while she waited. The man smiled at the gesture.
He handed her the medicine, then put the money he had left into her palm.
She thanked him again and again, blessing him as she set off home.
The man picked up his bag of fish and headed towards the bus stop. Then he stopped short: he had forgotten to pay. He returned to the shop, embarrassed.
“I’m sorry—I forgot to settle up. I’ve given away all the money I had with me. I’ll bring it later.”
The fishmonger smiled.
“No need, my friend. Let me have a share in the kindness. The fish is on me.”
The man thanked him. With nothing left for the bus fare, he started walking home. He called his daughter.
“I’ve bought some fish. Tell Mom I’m on my way, but I’ll be a little late.”
Rain began to fall. As he walked, the day’s weariness seemed to lift. He felt grateful that he had been able to ease someone’s burden—and that another person had chosen to help too.
The tears on his cheeks mingled with the rain.

Moral: You do not have to be wealthy to show kindness. Whatever help you can offer may lighten someone’s burden and inspire another person to give. Sometimes compassion is what we pass from hand to hand.

title: Baklava
paragraphs: When I was a child, my family had very little money. One day, my father brought home some baklava. That evening, we gathered for tea. There was a small piece for each of us.
The next day, we were having a celebration at school. My mother packed a piece of bread, a few olives, and a slice of baklava in my bag.

My classmates had brought all sorts of food. One boy looked at my little portion and laughed.
“Did you bring that baklava for the mice?”
The whole class burst out laughing. I felt as though everyone was staring at my tiny slice. My face burned with shame. Unable to hold back my tears, I ran home.

As soon as I stepped through the door, I shouted at my mother:
“Why did you give me just one little piece? Everyone else had so much food! You embarrassed me!”

My mother looked at me and said softly:
“That was my piece, sweetheart. I saved it for you.”
I fell silent.
So she hadn’t eaten her share the night before. She had put it aside so I would have something sweet for the school celebration. And I had taken out on her the hurt that others had caused me.
I wanted to hug her and apologize. But I was too ashamed to lift my head or say a word.
Years have passed since that day. Whenever I remember it, I hear my mother’s gentle voice again, and silently ask her forgiveness.
I have never been able to eat baklava since.
Moral: Never mock someone for being poor. A small portion may hold a great deal of love. And do not take out the hurt others cause you on those who love you.

title: Investing in people
paragraphs: The chief accountant asked the CEO:
“What if we invest time and money in developing our employees, and then they leave?”
The CEO replied with a question:
“What if we don’t, and they stay?”
Moral: Investing in employees’ development is investing in the company’s future. Saving on learning today may cost far more tomorrow.

title: More than money
paragraphs: Cherish your parents while they are still here. Ask whether they have enough money, but do not let your care end with that question. Sometimes they may keep their needs to themselves because they do not want to burden you.

Help where you can, respect their wishes, and preserve their dignity. Remember that their needs are not only financial: hearing your voice, talking with you, and sharing a meal can mean a great deal to them too.

Moral: Show your parents love while you have the chance—through both practical help and the time you spend together. Sometimes the best thing to add to “Do you need anything?” is “I’ve come to spend some time with you.”

title: Everyone Has Work to Do
paragraphs: I have been fortunate to learn from wise teachers. One was my literature teacher, the esteemed Baladadash. He taught us: if someone asks you for something or assigns you a task and you cannot do it, never say, even if it is true, “I had so much work that I had no time and I could not get it done.” Those words make the other person think, “Don’t I have things of my own to do? Am I bothering you for nothing?”

Everyone has things to do. When someone asks for help, it is usually because they need you, not because they have nothing better to do. Do not ignore the request or leave them waiting in silence. If you cannot do it, say so at once and do not leave them in uncertainty, because they are counting on you and trust you. Coming back much later to say “I had no time” destroys that trust.
Moral: It is painful to live knowing that others regard you as unreliable and untrustworthy.
Bakhtiyar Sirajov

title: The plastic cup
paragraphs: A former minister invited to speak at a seminar stepped up to the lectern holding a plastic cup of coffee. After a few sentences, he paused, looked at the cup, and smiled.
“If you’ll allow me, I’d like to share something that’s been on my mind. I spoke here last year too. Back then, I was a minister.”
The room grew quiet.

“They booked me a business-class flight. A car was waiting at the airport. A comfortable hotel room had been arranged. The next morning, I was driven here, welcomed, and shown to my seat. Before my speech, someone brought me coffee in a beautiful porcelain cup.”
He raised the cup in his hand.

“This time, I bought my own ticket and took a taxi from the airport to the hotel. This morning, someone checked my name on the list and let me in. I found an empty seat. When I asked about coffee, they pointed me towards the machine in the corridor. So I went and filled this cup.”
A ripple of laughter passed through the audience.
“At first, it felt strange. Then I realized: last year, the porcelain cup wasn’t for me. It was for my position.”
He paused before continuing.

“I’m not telling you this because I feel slighted. I’ve still been invited to speak, and you’re here listening. I can simply see more clearly now the difference between the attention given to me and the privileges attached to my office.”
He set the cup on the lectern.

“When you hold a senior position, it’s easy to mistake the open doors, the praise, and the special treatment for proof of your own importance. Yet some of those things belong to the role. Tomorrow, someone else will occupy it, and the cup will be theirs. What stays with us is the kind of person we are and how we have treated others.”

Moral: Do not confuse the privileges of office with your worth as a person. A porcelain cup does not make you greater, nor a plastic one make you less. Lasting respect is earned through conduct, not titles.

title: The Garden and the Gardener
paragraphs: A teacher said to his students:
“Imagine a gardener tending a garden: loosening the soil, watering the trees, and pruning dead branches. The garden grows, blossoms, and bears fruit. Who makes it grow?”
“The gardener,” one student answered.
“The trees grow by themselves,” said another.
The teacher smiled.

“A gardener cannot grow in a tree’s place. But that does not make the gardener’s work unnecessary. It creates the conditions for growth. The tree has life within it; the gardener helps that life flourish.”
He paused, then added:
“People grow in much the same way. We should recognize both their own efforts and the support they receive along the way.”
Moral: Growth owes something to our own efforts and something to the care we receive. Value your hard work, and remember those who helped you flourish.

title: The butter price war
paragraphs: An elderly woman ran a small grocery shop in our neighborhood. One day, a large supermarket opened directly across the street.
Both shops displayed their prices on boards outside. As soon as the supermarket advertised “Butter — 70 dollars,” the woman put up her own sign:
“Butter here — 60 dollars.”
The next morning, the supermarket dropped its price to 50 dollars. The woman changed her sign:
“Butter — 40 dollars.”
Watching this price war unfold, a worried neighbor spoke to her.
“You shouldn’t try to compete with them. They have deep pockets and can afford to take a loss. You could lose everything.”
The woman smiled, perfectly untroubled.
“But I don’t even sell butter. I just want people to get it cheaper over there!”
Moral: Not every reward ends up in your pocket. Sometimes the satisfaction comes from helping others rather than gaining something for yourself.

title: Henry Ford’s Choice
paragraphs: A story told about Henry Ford describes how he once invited two young friends to dinner. Both hoped to work for his company. They had graduated from the same university and were equally talented and well qualified.
They talked about all sorts of things that evening. As they left the restaurant, Ford offered one of them a job. He wished the other well but said he would not be hiring him.
Disappointed, the young man summoned the courage to ask:
“Mr. Ford, we didn’t discuss cars or our engineering skills all evening. Why did you choose my friend?”

“There are two reasons,” Ford replied. “During dinner, I watched you both. Your friend tasted his food before adding salt. You added salt without tasting it. I want to work with people who understand what is in front of them before deciding to change it—people who observe rather than assume.”
He paused, then continued:

“The second reason is how you treated people. Your friend was courteous to the waiters too. You gave me your full attention but barely acknowledged them. To me, respect is not something reserved for people in important positions. We should value people for who they are, not for what they can do for us.”
Moral: Character reveals itself in small actions. Seek to understand before making a decision, and show respect regardless of someone’s position.

title: Busy but unproductive
paragraphs: A man bought ten eggs for ten coins and sold the lot for nine. His friends were puzzled.
“You lose money on every sale. What’s the point?”
“Never mind the loss!” he replied. “People see me buying and selling, so they think I’m a merchant. What matters is that everyone sees I’m busy!”
Moral: Looking busy is not the same as doing something useful. Judge work by what it achieves, not by the impression it creates.

title: Hot Bread
paragraphs: The smell of freshly baked bread filled the street.

An elderly man stopped outside the bakery. His grandson had been asking for warm bread for days. He checked the coins in his pocket and joined the queue. He had just enough for one loaf. If he could have afforded it, he would have bought two.
When his turn came, he held out his money. Instead of taking it, the baker handed him a bag.
“Here you are, sir. Enjoy.”
There were three loaves inside.
“But I only asked for one.”
“Take all three. You can share them at home.”
The old man leaned closer and lowered his voice.
“I only have enough money for one.”
The baker smiled.
“There’s nothing to pay. It’s Friday—we give away fresh bread every Friday. These three are for you.”
“May God bless you, my son.”
“Amen. Enjoy your bread!”
He had walked only a few steps when a young man called after him.
“Sir, just a moment!”
The old man turned.
“This is my mother’s zakat—her charitable offering. We’d be grateful if you would accept it.”
He slipped an envelope into the old man’s pocket.
“May God accept her gift and bless her,” the old man said.
As he passed the market, a woman stopped him. She was carrying two full bags of groceries.
“We’re giving out food for Ramadan. Please take these home with you.”
“May God bless your kindness, my daughter.”
By the time he reached home, he was breathless with the effort of carrying everything. His daughter opened the door and took the bags.
“Welcome home, Dad.”
“Where’s your mother?”
“In the kitchen, making eggs for iftar. You know how much Orkhan loves them.”
His grandson came running.
“Grandpa, did you get warm bread?”
“Yes, my boy. Three loaves!”
“Hooray for Grandpa!”
His daughter looked inside the bags in astonishment.
“Dad, you hardly had any money this morning. How did you buy all this?”
“God provided, my daughter.”
His wife came out of the kitchen, and he told them everything that had happened.

When the call to prayer sounded, the family gathered to break their fast. There were eggs and warm bread, and the bags held butter, cheese, halva, and other groceries. It had been a long time since their table had been so full or their hearts so much at ease.
After the meal, Orkhan stood up.
“I’m going to my room to pray.”
His grandfather smiled.
“You can pray before bed, my boy. It’s still early.”

“No, Grandpa. I prayed at this time yesterday. I asked God for warm bread and cheese, and today they came. Now I’m going to ask Him to send money to have your teeth fixed. It’s so hard for you to chew.”
A wistful smile crossed his mother’s face.
“If only your father were alive to see you now…”
“I see Dad in my dreams, Mom. In my dreams, he tells me to pray.”
Suddenly, the old man remembered the envelope. He went to his coat, hanging by the door, and took it out. Inside was far more money than he had expected.
His eyes filled with tears.
“What is it?” his wife asked anxiously.
He handed her the envelope.
“Look… There’s enough here for both of us to have our teeth fixed before Eid.”
Then he looked at his grandson and whispered:
“Thank You, God. So many kind hands brought joy into our home today.”

Moral: A child’s prayer and the kindness of strangers met at this family’s table. When we notice someone’s need and offer help, we may help make their hopes come true. The bread we share can bring both nourishment and joy to a home.

title: The Credit Ledger
paragraphs: One day during Ramadan, a stranger in plain clothes walked into a neighborhood shop and approached the shopkeeper.
“Brother, would you let me have bread, tea, and eggs on credit?”

“Of course,” the shopkeeper answered kindly. “There’s a woman who’s been taking bread on credit for three months. Honestly, I don’t know whether she’ll ever be able to repay me. But she’s raising three children without their father. We can’t let them go hungry. God will provide for us too. If you’re in need, take what you need. Don’t worry about paying for the bread. You’re welcome to it.”
The stranger smiled. “I think I’ve found the right place,” he thought.
“How much do the debts in your ledger come to?”
The shopkeeper looked surprised.
“Why do you ask?”
“I’d like to pay them all.”
The shopkeeper glanced from the stranger to the old ledger he had taken from beneath the counter.
“All of them?”
“Yes, brother. Please add them up.”
Seeing that the man was serious, the shopkeeper calculated the total. The stranger took money from his inside pocket, counted it, and laid it on the counter.
“May God bless you. You’ve stood by these people through difficult times. Let this be my Ramadan gift. Tell them their outstanding debts have been paid. They don’t need to know my name.”
Then he pointed to the ledger.
“Let me take that too. There’s no need for their names to become a subject of gossip or for these debts to trouble them again. It is enough that God knows our intentions.”
He took the ledger and quietly left.

Even after putting the money in the till, the shopkeeper could hardly believe what had happened. He looked through the little window. The stranger was gone. It was almost time to break the fast, and everyone was hurrying home.
Just then, Surayya’s seven-year-old daughter appeared in the doorway. Her father had died, leaving her mother to raise the children alone.

“Uncle Ahmed,” she said shyly, “Mama asks for a loaf of bread and three eggs for iftar. We’ll pay you next month, when my uncle comes.” Her words brought the shopkeeper out of his daze. Out of habit, he reached beneath the counter for the ledger. Then he paused and smiled.
“Come, my child. Take the bread, the eggs, and some butter too. Tell your mother that her brother came by.”
Moral: True generosity protects the dignity of the person receiving it. A burden quietly lifted from one person’s shoulders can inspire kindness in another.

title: Mercedes
paragraphs: “Mercedes” was neither a company founder’s surname nor the name of an existing car manufacturer. It was the name of a girl whose father was passionate about cars.
Austrian businessman Emil Jellinek first used his daughter Mercédès’s name as a pseudonym in motor racing. Later, a new car he commissioned from Daimler also came to bear her name.

Mercedes cars achieved remarkable success at Nice Race Week in 1901. The name was registered as a trademark in 1902. When Daimler and Benz merged in 1926, the name “Mercedes-Benz” was born. A girl’s name had become part of motoring history.

Yet while her name became famous, Mercédès Jellinek’s own life was far from easy. Her first marriage ended in divorce, and her second husband died just months after their wedding. She died of bone cancer in 1929, aged thirty-nine, and was buried in Vienna’s Central Cemetery.
Her life was brief, but her name lived on. Behind a name known around the world were a father and his beloved daughter.
Moral: Behind a world-famous name, there may be a deeply personal story of love. Remembering the people whose names became famous brands gives those names a human meaning.

https://www.secret-classics.com/en/120-years-of-mercedes-as-a-brand/

title: Pay Rent for the Water
paragraphs: A man buys a well from a farmer. But when he tries to draw water, the seller stops him.
“I sold you the well, not the water in it!”
An argument follows. Unable to settle their dispute, they go before a judge.
After hearing both sides, the judge turns to the seller.
“If the water belongs to you, why are you keeping it in someone else’s well? Either take your water away or pay the owner rent!”
Moral: Someone who tries to cheat another out of what is rightfully theirs may be caught out by their own words. Fair-minded reasoning exposes the contradiction behind the trick.

title: The Scarf Seller
paragraphs: A bitter winter night had settled over the town. Ice covered the ground, and it was difficult even to keep my footing. It felt as though my breath might freeze. Taking careful steps, I finally reached the bus.
“Thank goodness I made it without falling,” I thought.
Just then, a boy carrying scarves approached me. I had no energy to listen to him. All I wanted was to get on the bus and warm up.
“Would you like one, miss?” he asked, holding out a scarf.
“No, thank you,” I said, hoping to end the conversation.
“Go on, miss. It might come in handy.”
“I haven’t got any money,” I said, hoping he would leave me alone.
“That’s all right. Take it. I don’t want any money. It’s a gift from me.”
“No, I couldn’t. I already have a scarf.”
With that, I hurried onto the bus. At that moment, I was thinking only of myself. I walked towards my seat without giving the boy another thought.

Before sitting down, I reached into my coat pocket for my phone. My hand touched a small packet. I took it out and stared: there was a scarf inside. The boy had slipped it into my pocket without my noticing.
I quickly got off the bus. He was still standing in the same spot, offering scarves to the passengers.

He could not have been more than twelve or thirteen. His coat was thin, his hands were bare, and his nose was red with cold. His dark eyes shone like stars in the night, and when he smiled, his teeth gleamed white.
I went over, rested a hand on his shoulder, and held up the scarf.
“Did you put this in my pocket?”
He smiled.
“Yes, miss. You might need it. It’s a present.”
“But how will you earn anything if you give your scarves away? Isn’t it hard standing out here in the cold?”
“I’ll be all right,” he said, looking at me kindly.
I held out some money.
“No, miss. I don’t want it. I gave you that scarf.”

Had he asked, “But didn’t you say you had no money? Where did this come from?” I would have wished the ground would swallow me. Yet he did not question me. He had believed what I said, thought I needed help, and shared what he had.
“Please take it,” I said, firmly this time.
Seeing that I meant it, he accepted the money. Then he reached into his pocket for change.
“Keep the change.”
“No, miss. This is too much. I can’t.”
He began hurriedly sorting through his coins. A few slipped from his fingers and fell to the ground.
“It’s all right. This is my gift to you,” I said with a smile.
A little shyly, he smiled back—a smile that seemed warm enough to melt the ice.
“Thank you, miss. God bless you.”
“Thank you, too, my young friend,” I thought. “You have so little, yet such a generous heart, and you ask for nothing in return.”

I got back on the bus and sat down. Outside, the cold was as fierce as ever. The boy was still standing there—a child who had not lost his trust in people, whose smile could turn winter into spring, and who was trying to earn something to help his family.

We pulled away. The town and the scarf seller disappeared into the darkness behind us. I thought of him, and of everyone who had nowhere to shelter on a night like this. A lump rose in my throat, and I struggled to hold back my tears.
The bus traveled on, following the winding road between mountains blanketed in snow.
Moral: Generosity is measured not by how much we own, but by our willingness to share. Sometimes the person we think needs our help is the one who reminds us what kindness means.

title: The Weight of the Butter
paragraphs: A baker regularly bought butter from a farmer. After a while, he noticed that the portions were getting lighter. He accused the farmer of cheating him and took his complaint to the judge.
The judge summoned the farmer and asked:
“How do you weigh the butter you sell?”
The farmer replied:
“I have no weights for my scales. Every day, I put the one-kilogram loaf I buy from this baker on one side and the butter I’m going to sell him on the other. I add butter until the scales balance.”
Moral: The measure you use for others may one day be used for you. The bread you give determines the butter you receive.

title: We Are Rich
paragraphs: According to legend, Emperor Nintoku of Japan once climbed a tall tower to look out over the surrounding land. When he saw no smoke rising from the houses, he understood that his people were living in poverty: they had nothing to cook.

He immediately decreed that, for three years, the people would pay no taxes and owe no labor to the imperial court. He even postponed repairs to the palace so that they could devote their efforts to supporting themselves.
Three years passed. The people’s circumstances improved, and their homes were well provided for again.
Nintoku climbed the tower once more. Seeing smoke rising from houses in every direction, he turned joyfully to his wife.
“Now we are rich!”
The empress pointed to their neglected palace, with its leaking roof.
“You call this wealth?”
Nintoku replied:
“If our people are poor, so are we. If our people are rich, so are we.”
Moral: True wealth is measured by the well-being of the people, not by the riches in the treasury. A leader’s greatness lies in what they do to improve people’s lives, not in the title they hold.

title: Giving without money
paragraphs: In a story told about the Buddha, a poor man approaches him and asks:
“Why am I poor?”
“Perhaps you do not recognize the riches you already possess or share them with others.”
“But I have nothing to give!”
“You have five treasures you can share.”
“What are they? Please explain.”
The Buddha replies:
“With your face, you can offer someone a smile.
“With your eyes, you can look at them with compassion and love.
“With your words, you can comfort and encourage them.
“In your heart, you can wish them happiness.
“With your hands, you can help them and do good.”
Moral: You do not have to be wealthy to be generous. A smile, a kind word, a compassionate glance and a helping hand are valuable gifts too. There is always some kindness you can share.

title: Belling the Cat
paragraphs: One day, the mice gathered to discuss how to protect themselves from the cat that never left them in peace.

Everyone had a suggestion, but none seemed suitable. At last, a young mouse spoke up.
“Let’s hang a bell around the cat’s neck! Whenever it comes near, we’ll hear it and hide. It won’t be able to catch us by surprise anymore.”
The mice looked at one another in delight. What a wonderful idea! Why hadn’t they thought of it before? They all applauded the young mouse.

When the excitement had died down a little, an old mouse who had been listening quietly in a corner spoke.
“A fine idea. With a bell around its neck, the cat won’t be able to sneak up on us. But one question remains: who will put the bell on the cat?”
Everyone fell silent. Not a single mouse answered.
Moral: A good idea is only part of the task. Before applauding a plan, consider who will carry it out—and how.

title: Humanity
paragraphs: How full the world is of wonders and delicate beauty... In every flower, in every whisper of the wind, in the color of the sky, there is a hidden wisdom. This beauty is like a silent trust placed in the human soul. Sadly, however, people sometimes disrupt this harmony with their own hands, burning not only the land but also hopes, destinies, and memories.

War damages not only the land but also the light within us. Every life lost is, in truth, a part of the world falling silent. Yet our purpose in life is not to destroy, but to protect, create, and sustain life.

Perhaps the greatest question is this: When will humanity find its strength in sustaining life rather than destroying it? When will the earth be filled with the sound of peace rather than silence? Perhaps then the world will be not only beautiful, but also a place that is cherished.
Moral: Humanity is elevated by protecting life and serving peace and goodness. The more we devote our strength to sustaining life, the more beautiful the world becomes for us all.
Etibar Siracsoy

title: Who was keeping watch?
paragraphs: Long ago, an elderly woman’s home was robbed. Distraught, she went before the king to complain.
After hearing her story, the king asked indignantly:
“Why were you sleeping so soundly that you didn’t even notice a thief entering your home?”
The woman replied:
“Your Majesty, we thought you were keeping watch. That is why we slept so peacefully at home.”
Moral: People’s peace of mind rests on their safety, not on promises. A ruler’s duty is to fulfill their responsibilities, not to blame those who have suffered.

title: Land and Homeland
paragraphs: Mix soil with water, and it becomes mud. Let blood be shed in its defense, and it becomes a homeland.

Moral: A homeland is more than the place we live. It holds the sacrifices and memories of those who protected it and entrusted it to us. Honoring that legacy means remembering them and building a peaceful future for generations to come.

title: Sharing Justice
paragraphs:
Let no one shed a tear,
or let those who always smile remember those who weep.

Let there be no curse called money,
or let those with wealth learn how to share.

Let no one say “I love you,”
unless their actions show what love truly means.

Let no festival come,
unless there is meat for every table.
Moral: Justice means that everyone has a share in joy, sustenance, and love. True humanity is remembering another’s hardship even in our own happiness—and sharing what we have.

title: The judge's answer
paragraphs: According to an old tale, a merchant lost a purse containing 800 guilders in Frankfurt in 1506. A carpenter passing along the same road found it. An honest, devout man, he reasoned that anyone who had lost so much money would surely come looking for it. He kept the purse safe, intending to return it to its owner.
One day, after a church service, the priest made an announcement:
“A merchant visiting our city has lost 800 guilders. He promises a reward of 100 guilders to whoever returns the money.”
As soon as the carpenter heard this, he went home, fetched the purse, and handed it to the priest.
The merchant came to the church when he heard the news. He counted his money, but instead of the promised 100 guilders, he offered the carpenter just five. The carpenter asked him to honor his word.
Unwilling to pay the reward, the merchant protested:
“There were 900 guilders in my purse, not 800. You’ve already taken your hundred!”
The priest intervened. He had known the carpenter for years and vouched for his honesty. When the dispute grew heated, the matter was brought before the town court.
The judge first addressed the merchant:
“Will you place your hand on the Bible and swear that your purse contained 900 guilders?”
The merchant took the oath without hesitation.
Then the judge turned to the carpenter:
“And do you swear that the purse you found contained 800 guilders?”
The carpenter also placed his hand on the Bible and swore.
As everyone waited for the ruling, the judge said calmly:

“The matter is clear. The carpenter found 800 guilders, while the merchant has sworn that he lost 900. Therefore, the purse that was found cannot belong to this merchant. It will remain with the carpenter until its rightful owner comes forward. The merchant may continue searching for his missing 900 guilders.”
Moral: Greed can cost us what we already have while we reach for more. Those who lie to deny others their due may find that their own words expose them.

title: The Lambs’ Skins
paragraphs: “Better to shear the rams than skin the lambs.”
This saying appears in a tale associated with Asad Pasha al-Azm, an Ottoman governor of Damascus.
According to the tale, one day Asad Pasha discovered that the treasury was empty. He summoned his advisers to find a solution. They proposed imposing an additional tax on the city’s weavers.
“How much would that raise?” the Pasha asked.
“Fifty or sixty purses of gold.”
“But these people can barely make ends meet. How would they pay?”
“They could sell whatever gold and jewelry they have at home, Pasha.”
Asad Pasha rejected the proposal.
“I shall find the money another way.”
The next day, he sent word to the mufti, inviting him to a private meeting that night. When the religious official arrived, the Pasha said:

“Mufti, we have received information that you drink alcohol secretly in your home. That goes against both your office and the rules you uphold. I must report the matter to Istanbul, but I wished to speak to you first.”

Alarmed, the mufti began to plead. He offered a thousand gold coins to keep the news from reaching Istanbul. The Pasha refused. The mufti doubled his offer, but the Pasha refused again. Eventually, they settled on six thousand gold coins.
The following day, the Pasha summoned the judge.
“We have learned from reliable sources that you accept bribes and use your position for personal gain.”
Fearing for his office and reputation, the judge also began to plead.
“Please do not dismiss me, sir. I would be disgraced.”
After much bargaining, he too agreed to pay six thousand gold coins.
Next, the Pasha summoned the treasurer, the chief of public order, merchants, and other wealthy men, one by one. According to the tale, he collected two hundred purses of gold in this way.
Then he called his advisers together again.
“Have you heard of me imposing an additional tax on the people of Damascus?”
“No, Pasha.”
“And yet I have collected not fifty, but two hundred purses of gold.”
“How did you manage that?”
The Pasha replied:
“Better to shear the rams than skin the lambs.”

Moral: Justice means sharing burdens according to people’s means, rather than taking the last morsel from those who have little. Ill-gotten gains should be dealt with through laws that apply equally to everyone, not through secret bargains.

title: The stolen camel
paragraphs: A Bedouin was riding his camel across the desert when he came upon a man who could barely stand. His lips were cracked with thirst.
“Water… Please give me some water,” the stranger begged.
The Bedouin dismounted and handed him his waterskin. The man drank his fill. Then, without warning, he shoved his rescuer aside, climbed onto the camel, and rode away.

Realizing he could not catch him, the Bedouin called out:
“Take the camel! But I ask one thing: don’t tell anyone how you got it!”

Surprised, the thief stopped the camel and looked back.
“Why?”
“If people hear that you repaid kindness with betrayal, they may be afraid to offer water to someone dying of thirst. I have lost my camel. I don’t want others to lose their hope of finding help.”

Moral: When we betray someone who helps us, we hurt more than that person—we weaken other people’s faith in kindness. Value the kindness you receive, and never let someone’s ingratitude make you indifferent to others.

title: A market of good neighbors
paragraphs: One day, a king disguises himself and goes into the city to see how his people are faring. He walks through the market, asking about the quality of the goods, their prices and the shopkeepers’ livelihoods.
He enters the first shop on the street and greets the owner.
“I’d like half a batman (a traditional unit of weight) of butter, half a batman of honey, and some cheese.”
The shopkeeper welcomes him warmly and weighs out the butter. Unaware that his customer is the king, he says:

“Sir, I can certainly sell you the honey and cheese as well. But this butter is my first sale of the day, while my neighbor has sold nothing yet. I would be grateful if you bought the rest from the shop opposite.”
Pleased by these words, the king pays for the butter and crosses the street. There, he asks for honey and cheese.
The elderly shopkeeper weighs the honey and hands it over.
“Thank God, you have brought me my first sale of the day. May I ask a favor? Please buy your cheese from the shop next door. Its owner is still waiting for his first customer.”
The king goes to the third shop and buys the cheese. He is deeply moved by the care these shopkeepers show for one another’s livelihoods.
As he leaves the market, he says with satisfaction:
“With such a people, the world could be conquered!”
Moral: A community grows stronger when people care about their neighbors’ livelihoods as well as their own. True success lies not in leaving others behind, but in moving forward together.

title: Choose justice
paragraphs: Words attributed to Hacı Bektaş Veli:
Why hatred when there is love?
Why war when there is peace?
Why strife when there is brotherhood?
Why enmity when there is friendship?
Why intolerance when there is tolerance?
Why captivity when there is freedom?
Why injustice when there is justice?
Moral: Love, peace and justice are more than wishes; they are values to uphold through our everyday choices. Choosing them—and defending them through our actions—is our responsibility.

title: Aging
paragraphs: Growing older is like climbing a mountain: the higher you go, the heavier your steps and the harder it is to catch your breath—but the wider the view becomes.
Moral: Our strength may diminish with the years, but experience teaches us to see further and understand life more deeply.

title: Life flows silently
paragraphs: Time is a strange wonder... We can neither see it, nor hold it, nor bring it back. It passes silently—in the movement of clock hands, in the changing days, in the gray appearing in our hair, in children growing up, in memories receding into the distance...

Often, we understand time only after we have lost it. A day that seemed ordinary yesterday becomes our most treasured memory years later. A conversation, a glance, a smile that we once considered insignificant, or a simple evening spent with someone we love, may later become one of the most beautiful moments of our lives.

Time stops for no one. It yields neither to wealth, nor to fame, nor to human desire. It is the greatest treasure, given to everyone in equal measure, yet valued differently by each of us. A person's life is measured, in truth, not in years but in the meaningful moments they have lived.
Sometimes we think that life still lies ahead and that we have plenty of time. We will do it tomorrow, go next week, talk someday, meet later... But the time we call ‘later’ does not always come.
Time takes much from us: our youth, certain people, certain dreams, certain opportunities... Yet in return it gives us memories, experience, and the chance to understand the true meaning of life.

So let us not measure time simply by the years that pass. Let us value our time not by how long we live, but by how we live. Let us tell our loved ones today that we love them. Let us not put off meeting our friends. Let us look at beautiful landscapes, watch the sunrise, listen to the sea, and savor the moments that bring joy to our hearts.
For time passes...
Moral: Let us not put off expressing our love or making time for our loved ones. A moment that has passed does not return; we must appreciate today.
Etibar Siracsoy

title: Life after sixty
paragraphs: Turning sixty is not a signal to step aside. It may be a chance to make room for wishes you have postponed for years and to give yourself more care.

Let yourself enjoy some of what you have worked for. Keep future needs in mind, but make room for comfort, pleasure, and things you have long wanted to do. You need not deny yourself everything simply to leave everything to others.

Keep loving your children and grandchildren and helping where you can. But you do not have to carry every worry for them. Give your adult children room to make decisions, take responsibility, and find their own way. Spending time and resources on yourself does not make you less caring.

Pay attention to your body. Move in ways that suit your health and abilities, take walks, and rest. Discuss your health needs and appropriate check-ups with your doctor. Avoid pushing yourself unnecessarily, but do not let age alone persuade you to give up activities you enjoy.
Look after your appearance for your own sake. Wear clean, comfortable clothes that feel like you. Being older does not mean giving up your sense of style or the colors you love.

Keep your curiosity alive. Read, listen to music, and learn something new. Use technology, if you wish, to stay close to people and discover more of the world. You do not have to follow every new trend; choose what is useful or enjoyable to you.

Listen to younger people. Their lives need not follow the pattern of yours. Share your experience, but leave room for questions before offering advice. They may have as much to teach you as you have to teach them.
When you say, “In my day…,” remember: this is your day too. Your memories may belong to the past, but your life is happening now.
Nurture relationships with people who respect you and let you be yourself. Care about others’ troubles, while setting limits with people who repeatedly belittle or exhaust you.
Make time for what you enjoy. Garden, cook, write, dance, or travel—whatever your circumstances and interests allow. Even a day without grand plans can hold small pleasures.

Go out when you can. Meet a friend, sit in a park, or visit an exhibition. If getting out is difficult, a phone call or a cup of tea with someone at home can also bring connection. Stay involved in life in ways that work for you.

Try to ease the weight of old hurts. Apologize when you have hurt someone. Being ready to forgive may take time, so do not rush yourself. Forgiveness does not have to mean forgetting what happened or returning to a hurtful relationship.
Talk when you are sad. Ask for help when you need it. You do not owe anyone constant strength or a permanent smile.

Love, laugh, stay curious, and make plans. Give yourself permission not only to rest, but also to begin again. Live this part of your life according to your values and circumstances, rather than other people’s expectations.
Moral: Caring for yourself does not require loving others less. At every age, your time, comfort, and hopes matter. This is still your life.

title: What Changed After Sixty
paragraphs: I asked a friend who was nearing seventy what changes he had noticed in himself as he grew older. This was his answer:
I no longer tell older people, “You’ve already told me that story.” I let them tell it. Sometimes sharing a memory allows them to relive a beautiful moment.
I no longer try to correct every mistake. It is not my job to make everyone perfect. Peace of mind is often worth more than having everything just right.
I am generous with kind words. A sincere compliment lifts the other person’s spirits—and mine too.
I no longer fret over a small crease or a spot on my clothes. Being presentable matters, but there is more to a person’s worth than appearance.
I have learned to step back from relationships that leave me emotionally drained. I do not have to be close to everyone. I treasure relationships built on mutual respect and understanding.
I am no longer ashamed of my feelings. Joy, tenderness and longing are all part of being human.
I have learned to set needless pride aside for the sake of a relationship. Being right every time does not make you happy. Sometimes reaching out matters more.
I make time for things that bring me joy. I have come to understand that my own happiness needs care too.
Before helping, I ask whether my help is needed and wanted. Good intentions do not excuse me from respecting another person’s choices.
I no longer complain endlessly about my health, my neighbors, my relatives or retirement. I do not ignore life’s difficulties, but I am also grateful to be alive and to have people I love beside me.

I am slower to tell young people, “When I was your age…” as though my life should be their model. Nor do I say, “I gave you the best years of my life,” to make someone feel indebted to me. Every generation faces different circumstances. The present cannot be judged solely by the standards of the past.

I give my wife more attention. I remember how young, strong and full of joy she once was. If the years have tired her and she needs more care now, I try to be there for her. I cherish the life we have shared.
I have stopped blaming myself for everything. I have made mistakes, but I have also done my best for myself and my children. I learn from the past instead of using it to punish myself.
And finally, I have learned to ask God for strength to change what I can, patience to accept what I cannot, and wisdom to tell the difference. I accept that I am human and cannot do everything.

Moral: Growing older can teach us that peace matters more than perfection, and understanding more than always being right. Life becomes richer when we learn to treat ourselves and others with compassion.

title: A Fly in a China Shop
paragraphs: A fly could never wreck a china shop on its own. But if it flew into the ear of a bull standing inside and sent it into a panic, the thrashing animal could smash everything.
In this image, the fly represents lies, superstition, and prejudice. The bull represents someone who accepts what they hear without question and acts out of anger or fear.
Sometimes the destructive power of a lie comes from the strength of those who believe it and act without thinking.
Moral: Do not act on everything you hear. Check the source, examine the claim, and then decide. Do not let someone else’s lie cause harm through your actions.

catalog_metadata.title: A Fly in a China Shop

title: The Elephant and the Rope
paragraphs: A parable tells of a traveler who came upon a curious sight: enormous elephants, each tied to a stake by a thin rope around one front leg. There were no chains and no cages.
“Animals this strong could easily break those ropes,” he thought. “Why don’t they even try?”
He asked a nearby trainer.

“When they’re young, we tie them with ropes like these,” the trainer explained. “However hard they pull, they cannot break free. Eventually, they stop trying. As they grow, their strength increases, but their belief that they cannot break the rope remains.”
The traveler looked at the elephants again. It was not only the ropes that held them in place. It was their belief that what had been impossible in the past must still be impossible today.
Moral: Do not assume that what you could not do yesterday is beyond you today. Your experience, strength, and circumstances can change. Do not let a past failure set the limits of your future.

title: The Donkey’s Law
paragraphs: One day, a donkey became king of the forest. A few days after taking the throne, he issued a decree:
“Everyone must go to sleep at six in the evening and wake at six in the morning. For those twelve hours, not a sound may be heard in the forest. Anyone who breaks this law will be punished!”
The animals were bewildered, but none objected. As evening fell, silence settled over the forest.
Then, one morning, a rooster crowed at five. Uproar followed. The rooster was brought before a court and executed on the king’s orders.
After that, no one dared break the law. Every animal arranged its life around the hours the donkey had chosen.
Years passed. The donkey grew old and weak. Near the end of his life, a lion came to visit. After asking how he was, the lion said:

“One question has troubled us for years. What wisdom lay behind making everyone sleep from six in the evening until six in the morning? Many times, we wanted to challenge the law. But we feared disturbing the peace. We thought you must know something we didn’t understand.”
The donkey gave a bitter smile.
“There was no wisdom in it. I made that law out of sheer foolishness. What astonished me was that you spent years looking for wisdom in my stupidity.”
The lion fell silent. The donkey continued:
“First, you feared me. Then you grew accustomed to the rule. In the end, you forgot that any other way of living was possible.”

Moral: Not every command contains wisdom, and not every old rule has a sound reason behind it. A rule accepted out of fear can become a habit, and a habit can become an unquestioned truth. Keep asking: “What purpose does this rule serve?”

title: The lion's untold story
paragraphs: Until the lion learns to write, every story will praise the hunter.
— Commonly described as an African proverb

Moral: Those who tell the story often cast themselves as the hero. To understand the truth, listen to those whose voices have gone unheard as well. If you do not tell your own story, others will tell it from their perspective.

title: The Lion’s Tracks
paragraphs: A timid hunter who liked to boast went into a forest looking for a lion. He came across a woodcutter and asked:
“Have you seen a lion around here? Or at least come across its tracks?”
The woodcutter replied:
“I’ve seen the lion itself. Come along, if you like. I’ll take you to it.”
The hunter turned pale.
“No, no, thank you! I was only looking for its tracks, not the lion itself.”
Moral: Courage is revealed when it is tested, not when it is talked about. A reputation for bravery built on boasting can crumble at the first sign of difficulty.

title: The Tortoise’s Miscalculation
paragraphs: Someone asked a tortoise:
“How long will it take you to reach the nearby village?”
“Allowing for rain, mud, wind, and all the hills, it’s a three-day journey. But let’s say six days, just to be safe,” the tortoise replied.
Six days passed, but the tortoise had not arrived. They went looking and finally found it only halfway there.
“What happened? You haven’t managed a three-day journey even in six days?”
The tortoise answered miserably:

“Don’t ask, my friends. I allowed for the rain, the mud, the wind, and the hills. What I forgot was people with cruel intentions. Whenever I picked up a little speed, someone would grab me and turn me onto my back.”
Moral: Difficult conditions are not the only things that can hold us back; other people’s malice can too. May God bring you people who help you up when you fall, rather than those who knock you down.

title: Two Donkeys
paragraphs: Two donkeys were walking down a road when they spotted a monkey sitting in a tree. One said to the other:

“Let’s have some fun at his expense. We’ll ask whether he has any friends. If he says yes, we’ll say, ‘What fool would be friends with you?’ If he says no, we’ll say, ‘Who would be foolish enough to be your friend anyway?’”
They walked up to the tree and called out:
“Monkey, do you have any friends?”
The monkey looked down at them and replied:
“Everywhere I look, all I see are asses. Who am I supposed to be friends with?”
Moral: Those who try to make others look foolish sometimes become the laughingstock themselves. Putting others down does not make you any better.

title: The Ant Carrying Water
paragraphs: According to legend, the cruel ruler Nimrod ordered a huge fire to be built in the town square, intending to throw the prophet Abraham into the flames. The fire rose higher and higher, and every creature hurried away from the unbearable heat.
Only one little ant was heading towards the fire. It carried a drop of water in its mouth.

Another ant called out:
“Where are you going? Can’t you see those flames?”
“Nimrod wants to burn the prophet Abraham. I’m taking water to put out the fire.”
“With one drop?” the other ant scoffed. “It’ll evaporate before it even reaches the embers! What difference could you possibly make?”

The ant carrying the water paused.
“Perhaps this drop won’t put out the fire. But at least it will be clear whose side I’m on.”
And with that, it went on its way.
Moral: We may not always have the power to stop cruelty, but we can choose not to be indifferent. Even the smallest act in defense of someone in danger matters.

title: A Remarkable Lesson
paragraphs: A tale is told about the Ottoman sultan Murad II and his son Mehmed.
As a child, the future Mehmed the Conqueror would fidget and misbehave during lessons. Whenever his teacher, Akshamsaddin, reprimanded him, he would reply:
“You can’t tell me what to do. I’m the sultan’s son!”
Akshamsaddin was troubled by the prince’s behavior. At first, he hesitated to complain to the sultan, but eventually he gathered his courage, requested an audience, and explained the situation.
Murad thought for a moment, then whispered a plan into the teacher’s ear. Akshamsaddin protested:
“Your Majesty, I couldn’t possibly do that!”
But the sultan stood firm.
“We must do this so that my son learns.”
The next day, the prince disrupted the lesson again. When his teacher warned him, he gave his usual reply:
“I’m the sultan’s son!”
At that moment, the door opened and Murad II entered the classroom.
As they had agreed, Akshamsaddin pretended to be angry. He scolded the sultan for entering without permission, even slapped him, and ordered him to leave.
The sultan lowered his head, apologized, and stepped outside.
Mehmed was astonished. His father, before whom everyone bowed, had accepted the teacher’s reprimand and obeyed the classroom rules.
A little later, there was a knock at the door. This time, Murad asked permission to enter and apologized again.

According to the tale, the prince’s behavior changed from that day on. Without a lengthy lecture, his father had shown him that being the sultan’s son did not give him the right to treat others disrespectfully.

Moral: In raising a child, example speaks louder than a lengthy lecture. A parent’s authority comes not from placing themselves above the rules, but from showing the respect and responsibility they expect of their child.

title: Albrecht Dürer
paragraphs: A legend about Albrecht Dürer

The story goes that two brothers, Albrecht and Albert, grew up in a poor family with many children near Nuremberg. Both dreamed of becoming painters. Their father worked from morning until night, but could not afford to pay for their studies.

Night after night, the brothers talked by candlelight, searching for a way to pursue their dreams. Finally, they decided to draw lots. One would study painting; the other would work in a mine to pay for his brother’s education. After four years, they would exchange roles.
Albrecht won the draw.

He left to study art, while Albert began working in the mine. One learned to handle a brush and explored the world of color. The other descended underground each day, working hard so his brother could continue his studies.

Four years passed. Albrecht’s talent attracted attention, and his work began to bring him recognition and an income. When he returned home, he embraced his brother and said joyfully:
“Now it’s your turn, Albert. Go and study. Follow your dream. You supported me; now I’ll support you.”

But Albert slowly shook his head.
“No, brother… It’s too late for me.”

He held out his hands. His palms were calloused, his fingers bent from years of heavy labor.
“These hands can no longer hold a brush the way they once could.”
Albrecht gently took his brother’s hands in his own. He wanted to speak, but no words came. His tears fell onto Albert’s work-worn hands.
Only then did he fully understand what the fulfillment of his dream had cost his brother.
The legend connects Dürer’s famous drawing Praying Hands with this sacrifice. In the story, those hands symbolize brotherly love, gratitude, and the quiet labor behind another person’s success.

Moral: Our achievements also belong, in part, to those who have generously given us their time, strength, and support. True gratitude means recognizing their sacrifices, remembering them, and returning their care with care of our own.

title: Mihrimah and Sinan
paragraphs: A beautiful legend links two mosques in Istanbul: the story of Mihrimah Sultan and the architect Sinan.
Mihrimah, the daughter of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, bore a name of Persian origin: mihr means “sun,” and mah means “moon.”
According to the legend, when Mihrimah was seventeen, two men wished to marry her: Rüstem Pasha and Sinan. She married Rüstem Pasha in 1539.
The tale says that Sinan, already married and approaching fifty, kept his love to himself. Unable to share his life with Mihrimah, he gave his feelings expression through his art.
Sinan first built a mosque bearing her name in Üsküdar, then another in Edirnekapı. Both buildings are indeed his work; the idea that they express a secret love belongs to the legend.

Those who tell the story see a woman in flowing skirts in the silhouette of the Üsküdar mosque. In the slender minaret, luminous interior, and delicate ornamentation of the Edirnekapı mosque, they look for echoes of Mihrimah’s beauty. Some even liken its decorative patterns to her long hair.
The most memorable part of the story is the meeting of the Sun and Moon.

It is said that from a certain spot in Istanbul, the Sun can be seen setting behind the Edirnekapı mosque while the Moon rises behind the mosque in Üsküdar. The legend associates this scene with the spring equinox and presents it as Sinan’s silent declaration of love.
Mihrimah—the Sun and Moon…
Did Sinan deliberately plan this view, or did people later give his work this romantic meaning? We cannot present that interpretation as established history.
Yet the legend lives on. Looking at the two mosques, people see more than stone, domes, and minarets. Sometimes they also search for the trace of a feeling never put into words.
Moral: Not every love leads to a life together. When people channel their feelings into creativity, those feelings can live on in works that bring beauty to others.

title: Sinan's waterless house
paragraphs: A legend about Mimar Sinan

During the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent, Istanbul was growing rapidly, and its water shortage was becoming increasingly severe. According to legend, the sultan summoned the architect Sinan and asked:
“People pay dearly for water and suffer great hardship. Is there a way to free Istanbul from this shortage?”
Sinan asked for time to survey the surrounding countryside. With his assistants, he examined springs, riverbeds, and valleys, searching for ways to bring water into the city.

Then he returned to the sultan.
“It can be done,” he said. “But it will require a great deal of work and money.”
“As long as it is possible,” the sultan replied, “the money will be provided.”

Sinan set to work. In time, water flowed through the channels and aqueducts he built to the city’s public fountains. Water that had once been so difficult to obtain now supplied people’s everyday needs.

The sultan ordered that the public water supply be protected and forbade private connections without permission. But he made an exception for Sinan: in recognition of his service, he gave him verbal permission to bring water directly to his home.
Years passed. Suleiman died, and fewer and fewer people remained who remembered his permission.
